articles.title_orig: The World’s Growing Patchwork of Age Bans and What It Reveals
articles.title_zh: The World’s Growing Patchwork of Age Bans and What It Reveals
articles.content_orig:
Two pupils stand in a classroom at Goethe-Gymnasium and look at their smartphones; the TikTok logo appears on one of the displays. Photo by: Marcus Brandt/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images
New York University professor Jonathan Haidt’s proposal for an under-16 ban in his 2024 best-selling book, The Anxious Generation , drew widespread attention. Australia’s first-of-its-kind social media ban for children under 16 went into effect nearly a year ago . Now, policymakers around the world are considering social media age restrictions.
I’ve given up some sleep to track policy action around the world, relying on desk research and collaboration with Internet Society colleagues in more than 30 countries and a global community of more than 110 active chapters across six continents.
Across the globe, social media bans, or delays, clearly resonate with parents and politicians. They see children (and adults) tied to their phones and computers. Nearly everyone agrees something needs to be done to improve children’s online safety.
The concern is real. The attention and headlines are global. But a closer look at policy trends tells another story about the direction of social media age restrictions.
While we can’t dismiss the attention social media bans have received, the trend is much more nuanced than a proliferation of “Australia-style” bans:
More than 60 countries are formally exploring restrictions, but only seven countries have actually implemented bans to date.
Of those few countries, the minimum age, covered services, and age verification requirements all vary. Research on effectiveness is limited, but there are now initial findings from government and academic studies in the UK and Australia .
While nearly one-third of the world’s countries are formally considering or taking action on social media age bans, fewer than a dozen have passed or implemented national social media age restrictions — Australia, Brazil, China, Egypt, Gabon, Indonesia, Malaysia, Turkey, United Arab Emirates, United Kingdom, and Vietnam.
In countries with active legislation, proposals often lack support from a political majority or the ruling party. The recently introduced EU KIDS Act , with an under-13 ban and under-15 restrictions, would preempt proposals and draft legislation across the 27 countries in the EU.
Why have so few countries taken action despite widespread calls for social media bans, including from heads of state on the world stage ?
Of course, regulation can take a long time. Powerful companies are also pushing back on these rules. Those are important factors, but there’s more to it.
In fact, a growing number of countries have ruled out or oppose a full ban, including Estonia , Mexico , and South Africa . The new EU KIDS Act proposal and Canada’s Safe Social Media Act also offer prominent alternatives to bans that focus on accountability for safe design.
Policymakers considering bans must recognize three types of implementation challenges: technical feasibility, legal requirements, and broader societal values.
Social media age restrictions are difficult to enforce and require collective buy-in . That’s difficult when teens generally find it uncool and unhelpful to comply . Policymakers must decide whether to prioritize stricter age checks or focus on measures that make online services safer for children and all users.
In Australia, more than 80% of children and teens under 16 continued to use social media accounts in the first few months after the ban went into effect, according to eSafety government research and a British Medical Journal study .
In Malaysia, a social media ban requiring government ID checks was quietly postponed from June 2026 to January 2027 after companies declined to comply. Social media companies reportedly raised data security concerns about processing IDs, arguing the current requirements are unworkable.
While there is a lot of discussion about VPNs, government reports found only 7% of children in Australia and 5% in the UK reported using VPNs to circumvent age restrictions. While these figures are self-reported and the actual percentages may be higher, the research finds that children don't have to use VPNs because there are easier ways to get around age restrictions.
You have successfully joined our subscriber list.
VPN downloads often spike when social media restrictions go into effect. This likely means adults are more likely to use technical tools to circumvent age verification requirements than children and teens. Research and media reports find young people draw mustaches or use other simple methods to avoid detection.
Data breaches and tracking
Security breaches and privacy violations are not theoretical. Multiple high-profile incidents occurred in the past year.
At least 70,000 photos of government IDs and other sensitive personal information were exposed when a third-party customer service provider for the social media company Discord was breached in October 2025. The incident happened shortly after age verification requirements went into effect under the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act.
Discord broke ties with the age and identification provider Persona earlier this year after reports that the company accidentally left some of its code and capabilities publicly exposed. The decision came just ahead of Discord’s planned global age verification rollout that was delayed until September.
While the EU age assurance system is open source, making it easier to identify and address vulnerabilities, a security researcher found significant vulnerabilities within a few hours of the code going live.
Legal restrictions include jurisdictional, children’s rights, freedom of expression, and privacy protections that limit complete bans and strict age verification.
Reddit and Australian teenagers are challenging the under-16 social media ban in separate legal cases. The lawsuits raise concerns about access to political communication and privacy risks, which they argue could be more narrowly and effectively addressed by focusing on safety by design. The challenges call attention to a disproportionate impact on vulnerable and rural communities, including those with disabilities and indigenous young people.
A French constitutional court blocked a planned social media ban due to freedom of expression and privacy concerns. The European Commission previously warned the legislation would breach European law . There are also many First Amendment free expression legal challenges against social media bans passed in US states .
Government consultations have been nearly unanimous in calling for safer design and accountability over blanket bans. They also frequently emphasize that efforts to protect children must not restrict their rights to free expression and access to information.
An Irish parliamentary committee reported that none of the experts it consulted recommended a social media ban for children under 16.
Legislation to ban children under 15 from using social media was blocked in Mauritius following consultations that raised concerns about freedom of expression.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum rejected an outright ban following public consultations and engagement with researchers, including The Anxious Generation author Jonathan Haidt and Meta whistleblower Arturo Bejar.
Canada initially pursued a ban on social media access for children under 14 but announced a more nuanced approach , allowing access for under-16s where companies can demonstrate that their services are safe.
Following expert consultations , the European Commission rejected an outright ban. The EU KIDS Act proposes a developmental approach with an under-13 ban, parent-controlled accounts for 13- and 14-year-olds, and safety design requirements for teens under 18.

articles.title_orig: World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
articles.title_zh: World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
articles.content_orig:
Archaeologists working off the coast of Turkey have found a shipwreck dating back around 4,700 years, making it the oldest in the world.
A number of ancient storage vessels known as amphorae were recovered during excavations at the wreck, which was found at a depth of around 100 feet near Kekova Island off the coast of southern Turkey, according to a statement from the country’s culture ministry, published Wednesday.
The amphorae date from 4,400-4,700 years ago and provide new information on maritime history, the daily lives of mariners and trade connections at the time.
The vessels are thought to mainly have been used for transporting olive oil or wine. However, one amphora features a distinctive set of marks and two holes in its body, which suggest it could have been used to make cheese or butter.
Researchers said the presence of this amphora may mean that sailors took goats with them on their voyages, using their milk to make dairy products.
The excavations were led by Hakan Öniz, a professor at Akdeniz University, Antalya, who told CNN that the shipwreck was first discovered four years ago.
The amphorae were initially thought to be much more recent, but then Öniz read a publication on amphorae that had been found near the Giza pyramids in Egypt — the oldest of which was believed to have been under construction at the same time as the ship sank.
“These resembled the amphorae in our shipwreck,”  Öniz told CNN on Wednesday, adding that a team of researchers made a follow-up dive at the site.
They then invited a leading expert on amphorae, Australian archaeologist Karin Sowada, to visit the shipwreck and examine the evidence.
“We reached a consensus and proceeded with further analysis,” said Öniz, who added the team are “generally confident” that this is the oldest shipwreck in the world.
“It is not just the amphorae; the anchors and other artifacts found at the shipwreck site also point to the same centuries,” he said.
Turkey’s culture and tourism minister, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, said the amphorae appear to have moved around the Eastern Mediterranean.
“Clay analyses indicate that the amphorae were likely produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley,” Ersoy said in the statement.
“The fact that similar examples have been found in Egypt, Troy, and Crete is of great importance for understanding the trade networks that connected different geographies via sea routes,” he said.
Researchers believe the ship may have been traveling from the Levantine coast, which runs from Turkey in the north to Egypt in the south, to Troy or Crete when it was wrecked.
CNN’s Gul Tuysuz contributed to this story.

articles.title_orig: Real-World Treatment Choices for AMD
articles.title_zh: Real-World Treatment Choices for AMD
articles.content_orig:
— Studies show big early drop in adherence to anti-VEGF therapy, increased bevacizumab use
October 14, 2026 • 5 min read
Poor adherence to anti-VEGF therapy for neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) remains a major limitation of existing therapies, a review of a large clinical database showed.
Almost 40% of patients stopped treatment during the first year, rising to a majority by the end of the second year. By year 5, only about a quarter of patients remained on therapy. Visual acuity worsened with decreasing number of injections, reported Andrew Moshfeghi, MD, of Keck Medicine of USC in Los Angeles, at the recent American Society of Retina Specialists (ASRS) meeting.
"This real-world data tells us that the largest drop in anti-VEGF treatment adherence really occurs during the first year, with 40% of patients already going more than 180 days without an injection," said Moshfeghi. "This declining injection frequency over time is associated with reduced durability of the early vision gains. Delayed treatment initiation was associated with poorer vision outcomes and greater likelihood of non-persistence."
Anti-VEGF non-persistence was associated with worse fibrosis and atrophy at baseline as well as a more frequent treatment interval at latest follow-up.
A separate study of recent trends in use of anti-VEGF therapies showed a surge in bevacizumab (Avastin) use, increased use of biosimilars, and variation in therapy choices by indication.
Rapid Increase in Non-Persistence
Moshfeghi reported findings from an analysis of the Vestrum Health Retina Database , encompassing patients who had a diagnosis of nAMD from January 2015 through June 2025 and who received at least one anti-VEGF injection. The analysis excluded patients who had a history of diabetic retinopathy, diabetic macular edema, retinal vein occlusion, or myopic choroidal neovascularization.
The study included 201,768 eyes in 158,727 patients (mean age 80 years). The fellow eye had treated nAMD in 16.9% of cases and untreated nAMD in 24%.
Within 12 months after initiating anti-VEGF therapy, 38.9% of patients had become non-persistent, defined as no injection for more than 180 days. Non-persistence increased to 52.6% at the end of 2 years, 72.9% at 5 years, and 80.1% at 7 years. The steady increase in non-persistence came with a steady decline in number of intravitreal injections, from a mean of 8.4 during year 1 to 6.6 in year 2, and 6.2-6.3 for years 4 through 8. Non-persistent patients lost four times as many letters of visual acuity from baseline (-8.0 vs -2.1).
"Suboptimal long-term nAMD vision outcomes are driven by poor real-world anti-VEGF adherence, emphasizing the urgent need for longer-lasting, more durable therapies," said Moshfeghi.
During a discussion, Vivienne Hau, MD, PhD, of Kaiser Permanente Bernard J. Tyson School of Medicine in Pasadena, California, noted: "The best drug is the one that the patient actually received. Your study demonstrated very well about how a lot of patients are not getting the medication. How do you think newer drugs coming out can change things?"
The problem is multifactorial, but newer drugs might help if they address one of the biggest issues: transportation for frequent treatment, said Moshfeghi.
"A lot of these patients can't drive because they don't have good vision," he said. "They have to have a medical assistant or family member come with them, and that person often has to take time off from work. If we can do anything to remove some of these barriers, like having longer-lasting, more durable treatment ... then they will have a lot more faith in the fact that the drug is still having the intended effect and less onus on the patient to come back and forth so frequently."
Real-World Treatment Choices
A real-world study of recent trends in intravitreal therapy for nAMD showed that bevacizumab (Avastin) accounted for 30% of all injections in 2025, more than any other agent. Bevacizumab's share of injections increased during the 3 years analyzed. In contrast, use of aflibercept 2 mg decreased by more than 50% from 2023 to 2025, but use of aflibercept 8 mg (Eylea) increased by 50% from 2024 to 2025, reported Anton Kolomeyer, MD, PhD, of NJRetina in Lawrenceville, New Jersey.
During the discussion, a member of the audience asked Kolomeyer about the potential reasons for the increased use of bevacizumab.
"Obviously the Good Days issue [with depletion of co-pay support] has been a big burden to the patients," said Kolomeyer. "I keep having conversations with them, and they don't understand why they now owe something for the injection, whereas before they didn't. I never used to discuss this with patients."
"I don't think [bevacizumab is] our preference, as first line, but maybe we have to use it for a certain percentage of the population," he added. "You definitely have to ask why the rate increased so dramatically in '25 compared to '23 and '24."
A study reported at the American Academy of Ophthalmology meeting in October supported Kolomeyer's caution about switching to bevacizumab. An analysis of medical records for 177 eyes (152 patients) switched to treatment with bevacizumab showed a decline in visual acuity within 3 months of the switch, continuing out to 12 months. Retinal thickness initially increased before decreasing to a mean value below the baseline at 12 months. The frequency of intravitreal injections increased over time after the switch, which might explain the decline in retinal thickness, Adam Weiner, MD, of Associated Retinal Consultants and Corewell Health William Beaumont University Hospital in Royal Oak, Michigan, and colleagues reported in a poster presentation.
The findings were consistent with a report last year from an ASRS-supported analysis of treatment patterns involving more than 300,000 eyes. The study showed an increase in switching to bevacizumab for patients with AMD, diabetic macular edema (DME), and geographic atrophy. Based on Vestrum data, the analysis showed a decline in visual acuity after the switch in one-fourth of eyes treated for AMD and 19% of eyes treated for DME.
Kolomeyer's analysis also involved records from the Vestrum database. The 2025 data encompassed 81 ophthalmology practices, 384 physicians, 930,606 patients, 2.8 million visits, and over 1.4 million intravitreal injections, a 6.1% increase in injections versus 2024 and 7.9% higher than 2023.
The most common indication for injection was nAMD (52.0%), followed by DME (28.3%), and retinal vascular occlusion (RVO) with ME (12.2%).
After bevacizumab, the next most commonly used agent was aflibercept 2 mg, at 21.9% in 2025 as compared with 36.9% in 2024 and 45.6% in 2023. Faricimab (Vabysmo) came in third at 18.9% (vs 18.4% in 2024 and 11.4% in 2023), followed by aflibercept 8 mg at 12.7% (vs 8.5% in 2024 and 0.6% in 2023, after an August 2023 approval). The biosimilar aflibercept-ayyh (Pavblu) accounted for 11.8% in 2025, an increase from 0.2% in 2024 (after an August approval).
An analysis of injections by indication showed that bevacizumab (23.6%) and faricimab (23.4%) accounted for almost half of all injections for nAMD. Bevacizumab (34.4%) and aflibercept 2 mg (24.7%) were used in a majority of injections for DME, and the same two drugs accounted for a majority of injections for RVO with ME (aflibercept 2 mg 35.9% and bevacizumab 26.5%).
Biosimilars accounted for 14.6% of all injections in 2025 (compared with 10.2% in 2024 and 3.5% in 2023), and the most common indication was nAMD (59% vs 70% in 2024). Aflibercept-ayyh was the biosimilar used in 80.8% of cases.

articles.title_orig: WCC reference group leaders discern what joint witness means today
articles.title_zh: WCC reference group leaders discern what joint witness means today
articles.content_orig:
Leaders from three World Council of Churches (WCC) reference groups, following a recent conference in Chiang Mai, reflected on what it mean to witness together, and what they hope churches will do.
Rev. Hanna-Maria Pauliina Parhiala (Finnish Evangelical Lutheran Mission), co-moderator of the WCC Ecumenical Diakonia Reference Group, Thandiwe Soko-de Jong (Protestant Church in the Netherlands), co-moderator of the WCC Gender Justice Reference Group, Very Rev. Fr Hrant Tahanian (Armenian Apostolic Church/Holy See of Cilicia), co-moderator of the WCC Reference Group on Overcoming Racism, Xenophobia, Casteism, and all forms of Discrimination
Rev. Hanna-Maria Pauliina Parhiala, from the Finnish Evangelical Lutheran Mission, co-moderator of the WCC Ecumenical Diakonia Reference Group, said that the reference group contributed a distinctive focus on ecumenical diakonia as shared witness, shared agency, and institutional transformation.
“ In a context marked by polycrisis, shrinking civic space, polarization, and unequal power, our group highlighted that credible Christian witness requires moving beyond charity and service delivery towards prophetic action alongside communities,” she said. “ The group helped connect theological reflection with lived realities, emphasizing that diakonia is constitutive of the church and inseparable from justice, advocacy, peacebuilding, ecological responsibility, and visible unity.”
One of the conference ’ s greatest achievements, Parhiala added, was bringing together diverse commissions and reference groups to develop a common reading of the signs of the times and a renewed ecumenical response to today ’ s global crises. “ The conference articulated a shared call to prophetic action for life, justice, and peace, while linking issues of climate justice, gender justice, health, racism, international affairs, and diakonia into one coherent ethical vision,” she said. “ My hope is that churches leave Chiang Mai with a strong sense that unity is not an end in itself but a shared public witness.”
Thandiwe Soko-de Jong, from the Protestant Church in the Netherlands, is co-moderator of the WCC Gender Justice Reference Group.
She reflected that gender justice is not imported into the church from outside, but flows from the heart of our faith. “ Gender justice is therefore a matter of God ’ s justice and mutual enrichment,” she said. “ Our commitment is thus an act of faith and a confession of what we proclaim.”
The reference group reaffirmed its current focus on climate justice as a critical issue that disproportionately affects women and girls because it amplifies gendered inequalities. “ Our voice on this issue drew attention to gendered dimensions of the climate crisis, such as the limits placed on community and societal progress where women and girls lack access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation infrastructure,” she said. “ Because each church walks this path according to its own context and tradition, our approach builds bridges rather than walls.”
One of the conference ’ s major successes, Soko-de Jong reflected, was convening distinct commissions, reference groups, and dedicated individuals to focus on contemporary ecumenical social ethics. “ I hope churches continue to promote this spirit of deep listening and wholehearted engagement in their communities.”
Very Rev. Fr Hrant Tahanian, from the US and the Armenian Apostolic Church (Holy See of Cilicia), serves as co-moderator of the WCC Reference Group on Overcoming Racism, Xenophobia, Casteism, and all forms of Discrimination. “ Societal issues have been a matter of concern for the ecumenical movement since its inception,” he said. “ It grapples with the same challenges the broader inhabited world struggles with. Similar to most things in human life, the level of commitment our societies have in improving them goes through ebbs and flows.”
In recent times, he noted, we are noticing a "recession of interest" in the issues and their solutions.
“ But what of the social ills that are not the talk of the day, or are hidden underneath layers that render them un-perceivable to the naked eye?” he asked. The reference group takes to heart the mission of unearthing all that is necessary for the welfare of societies and churches, both the seen and the unseen. “ An example we broached this past week was climate colonialism—seldom discussed, yet crucial to holistic emancipation,” he said. “ As such, the ecumenical movement continues to not only be a voice for the voiceless, but also a beacon to all things that yearn for the light of Christ.”

articles.title_orig: How one of the world’s biggest music stars is transforming the Spanish language
articles.title_zh: How one of the world’s biggest music stars is transforming the Spanish language
articles.content_orig:
According to the Royal Spanish Academy (RAE, under its Spanish acronym), a “piquete” is either a sharp object, a small wound, or a  group of striking workers blocking access to a workplace. It is a word, generally speaking, of conflict and harm.
But when Puerto Rican musician Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio – more commonly known as Bad Bunny – intones on his song NUEVAYoL “Tú tiene’ piquete mami, yo también” (“You’ve got piquete mami, and so do I”), he is not talking about trade unions or pointy sticks. He is referring to something else altogether, a way of moving through the world with a certain self confidence, attitude and style.
In Puerto Rico’s boricua dialect, the meaning of piquete is totally divorced from the RAE’s official uses. But unapologetic use of his native dialect is what defines the music of the world’s biggest Spanish-language musician.
Bad Bunny has put Spanish on more global stages than any other artist in recent history, yet he is also widely criticised for his way of speaking. This is rife on social media, where users complain that he “doesn’t talk properly” , he is “deforming the language” , and “doesn’t enunciate clearly” .
But these critiques say much more about the narrow confines of “proper Spanish” and its place in the world than about how one particular artist speaks.
Read more: Who is Bad Bunny? Why the biggest music star in the world sings in Puerto Rican Spanish
Comments like these point to a linguistic clash: on one side what was, until recently, regarded as standard, codified, academic Spanish; on the other, the Spanish spoken on the street corners of Puerto Rico, in the voice notes sent across any Latin American city, and in countless neighbourhoods across the US, Spain and beyond. It is from this latter perspective that Bad Bunny expresses himself.
Since his earliest hits, criticism has focused on the dialect he uses. Certain aspects of his Caribbean Spanish – aspirating or leaving out final consonants, boricua slang, “Spanglish” vocabulary, and replacing the rolled Spanish “r” with “l” in certain positions – have been held up as examples of his supposedly “bad” Spanish.
However, what was once perceived as local or marginal has quickly become a global phenomenon. Today, millions of people around the world now recognise and use typically Puerto Rican expressions, pronunciations and structures – not necessarily because they understand their nuances, but because they form part of a recognisable cultural identity.
According to data from our report on Bad Bunny’s impact on global Spanish , after Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl half-time show , songs like NUEVAYoL were searched for on Shazam around the world, including in Germany, Italy, France and the UK. In other words, listeners in non-Spanish-speaking markets who may not fully understand the language were consuming and actively searching for his music.
For much of the world, the singer has managed to upend decades of prejudice surrounding urban Latin music.
With Bad Bunny’s linguistic impact reshaping Spanish as a whole, can people learn to accept the music whilst rejecting the accent?
Sheila Rodríguez Madera is a researcher specialising in socio-cultural studies on Puerto Rico, and co-authored the 2024 book The Bad Bunny Enigma . She argues that:
“[Bad Bunny] does not disavow Puerto Rico’s colonial condition; rather, he performatizes it. Working within colonial structures—the global cultural industry and the North American market — he subverts them from within by asserting his accent, his slang, and his local perspective. This tension positions him as a figure of symbolic resistance: through songs such as ‘El Apagón,’ he makes visible the island’s precarity and the extraction of its energy resources, even as he expands the possibilities of what spectacle can accomplish.”
By singing and speaking in distinctly Puerto Rican Spanish on primetime TV in the US, at the Grammies, the Oscars, and the Super Bowl, Bad Bunny is not refusing to adapt and meet the demands of Anglophone listeners and markets. On the contrary, it proves that his music can reach them without any need for translation.
The same cannot be said for previous Latin American music stars. For decades, any Latin artist who wanted to reach international audiences had to release music in English (or a mixture of Spanish and English). But Bad Bunny’s catalogue is exclusively in Spanish, and he uses a mixture of English and Spanish in his public appearances to make himself understood.
His lyrics do include common boricua English slang and expressions, but most would be unrecognisable to English speakers: “janguear”, for example, is derived from “hang out”.
This idea, which has been explored in depth by the Cuban-American linguist Ofelia García , refers to the practice of bilingual or multilingual speakers who draw on a single, fluid linguistic repertoire, without treating their languages as sealed, segregated compartments. It is not merely a question of code-switching , but a way of engaging with language that reflects complex life stories, hybrid identities, and histories of migration and resistance.
Bad Bunny can be understood in this light. He does not adapt his language to suit the global market – he has instead shifted the conditions of what can be understood within that market.
On February 18, 2026, the Puerto Rican Academy of Letters honoured Bad Bunny for his “contribution to the global dissemination of the Spanish language”. Its reasons were very clear:
“Martínez Ocasio’s cultural output has helped to overcome prejudices against the forms of communication characteristic of popular, urban and youth dialects, or those influenced by other languages. Despite the distinctly local nature of the references and linguistic forms used in his works, his message has managed to transcend geographical, national, generational and ideological boundaries”.
The Academy thus recognised the singer for his way of speaking, not in spite of it.
If the purpose of a language is to communicate and foster a sense of community, Benito Martínez Ocasio’s impact is undeniable. He has succeeded in making words like bellaquera , chambear and piquete understood from Madrid to Tokyo, and in gaining acceptance among a global audience.
Read more: Rosalía: raising reggaetón’s ‘global cachet’ or robbing it of its roots?
However, as Dr Nathaly Gómez Gómez highlights in our study : “It is not enough for the market to open up to Spanish-speaking voices; we must also ask ourselves which variety of Spanish we are talking about, from which territories, under which aesthetic frameworks, and which bodies are once again becoming dominant.”
Her argument is that this expansion may consolidate a Caribbean and Puerto Rican hegemony within the Spanish language, leaving out the diversity of other Latin American dialects. “Rather than broadening plurality,” she says, “the system may end up encouraging other versions of the same thing and reinforcing a hegemonic idea of what it means to be Latin.”
Bad Bunny’s success should therefore prompt us to check our ideas of neutrality in the spread of Spanish, while also moving away from linguistic elitism.
However, the data and cultural evidence cannot be ignored: the Spanish heard by most people around the world is not the RAE’s “standard”, but the dialect of a Caribbean island with a population of three million.
Certain segments of Spanish society may read this as a sign of decline or marginalisation. In reality, nothing could be further from the truth: it is proof of our language’s extraordinary health and elasticity, and grants modern-day Spanish the kind of piquete that can only come from the streets.

articles.title_orig: Low-level clouds could make wind farms more efficient
articles.title_zh: Low-level clouds could make wind farms more efficient
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for registering with Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account
Low-level sea clouds can make offshore wind farms more efficient, say researchers at the University of Twente in the Netherlands. This increase in efficiency is due to atmospheric mixing effects that shrink the wake of slower air behind nearby turbines, and the team say it could help wind farm designers make the most of ambient conditions.
Scientists have known for decades that multiple wind farms can be significantly less efficient than a single, isolated one. This is because air slows down as it moves through turbine blades, creating a wake that impairs the performance of wind farms downstream. This slow-air wake may extend for tens of kilometres, and in extreme cases it can even stretch beyond 100 km. “How quickly the wake recovers depends on how effectively atmospheric mixing pulls air from the stronger wind above and on the sides,” explains Davide Selvatici , a physicist who co-led the research with his colleague Richard Stevens .
In their latest study, which appears in PRX Energy , Selvatici and Stevens show that the presence of low-level stratocumulus clouds can enhance this mixing via a process called radiative cooling. This occurs when air at the top of a cloud radiates heat into space and becomes cooler, much like the ground does on a clear night. Because cooler air is denser than the surrounding air, it sinks, generating an enhanced downward motion that intensifies atmospheric turbulence. This ongoing mixing helps sustain the cloud by drawing moisture up from the surface below.
To piece together this picture, Selvatici and Stevens needed to accurately model the turbulence in cloud tops and the way that air flows through a wind farm. They used large-eddy simulations to study how low-lying clouds impact the length of a wind farm’s wake. They also performed high-resolution simulations of stratocumulus-topped boundary layers across a range of atmospheric conditions: clear skies, cloudy skies without radiative cooling; and cloudy skies with radiative cooling.
These simulations are fully three-dimensional, and Selvatici explains that creating them meant solving equations within the model to determine how wind moves in all three directions, while also incorporating changes in temperature, water vapour and liquid water suspended within the cloud. For this, they relied on the Navier-Stokes equations (the standard equations used to describe the movement of fluids such as air) with some modifications. “We use an extended set of equations to include the effects of heat and moisture and to represent the energy and momentum extracted by the wind turbines under local wind conditions,” Selvatici explains.
The pair’s results indicate that the effects of cloud-top cooling can be significant. When these effects are present, the mean wind speed within a wake returns to approximately 90% of the incoming wind speed about 17 km beyond the end of the wind farm. In simulations without cloud-top cooling, however, the mean wind speed remained below 90% even 32 km beyond the end of the farm.
“Clouds are inherently coupled to the atmosphere, making it difficult to isolate their effects, but by comparing simulations with and without cloud-top cooling, we identified cloud-top cooling as an important process for wind farm wake recovery,” Selvatici explains.
So you want to install a wind turbine? Here’s what you need to know
Since wind farm power production increases with the cube of wind speed, even a modest reduction in wind speed can have a considerable effect, he adds. The problem is that most existing wind-farm models either simplify cloud-related processes or exclude them altogether. “Our results demonstrate that these should be taken into account,” says Stevens, “particularly in regions with frequent low-level clouds as over the North Sea, where many wind farms are found and where the annual cloud coverage is higher than 30%.”
Stevens adds that a better understanding of these effects could improve wind farm design and inform how far individual wind farms should be placed from each other. However, Selvatici notes that they’re not yet able to offer definite practical advice. “We cannot conclude whether wind farms should indeed be placed closer together in cloudy regions because our simulations represented idealized conditions,” he says.

articles.title_orig: Atlanta theatre opens true crime show
articles.title_zh: Atlanta theatre opens true crime show
articles.content_orig:
The musical "Like Father" makes its world premiere at the Alliance Theatre on the Hertz Stage in Atlanta.
ATLANTA, Ga. - A teenage girl's deepest secret – that her father is a notorious serial killer – comes to light in the new musical "Like Father."
Created by Atlanta native Jacob Ryan Smith and featuring a book, music, and lyrics co-written by Smith and Caroline Pernick, the show is making its world premiere now on the Hertz Stage at Atlanta's Alliance Theatre .
"The evil plan was always to debut this on home turf," laughs Smith. "So, to be here is very exciting!"
"Like Father" centers on a teenager in Dahlonega, Georgia whose father is a notorious serial killer — a secret that’s revealed through a hit podcast. The fallout from that revelation forces 17-year-old Chris and her mother and stepfather to face issues they’ve long kept buried, and to confront the public’s obsession with true crime.
"I watched this [program] where a very notorious serial killer's daughter gave an interview, and my mind ignited," says Smith of his inspiration for the show. "So, in beginning to storyboard this thing and figure out what was the story I wanted to tell about this young girl experiencing this kind of betrayal from the most important person in her life, I started looking out and needing to find the perfect writing partner."
That perfect partner was Pernick, who says working with Alliance Theatre has been a dream.
"The Alliance really spans all decades and audiences, and I think for a show that's kind of about family – about spanning decades and audiences – to be in a space and with a team that believes in that so wholeheartedly, is really, really special," says Pernick.
Prior to its world premiere here in Atlanta, "Like Father" won the Open Jar Studios Broadway Shark Tank and was a semi-finalist at the National Music Theater Conference at the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center. The current production is directed by Alliance Theatre’s co-artistic director Tinashe Kajese-Bolden is being produced on the Hertz Stage, the Alliance’s 200-seat black box theatre. Performances are set to continue through November 15th.
For more information on "Like Father" — including showtimes and ticket info — click here . And click the video player in this article to check out our interview with Jacob Ryan Smith and Caroline Pernick.
The Source: This is a FOX 5 Atlanta original report, based on Paul Milliken's interviews with Jacob Ryan Smith and Caroline Pernick.

articles.title_orig: Judge extends White House access to banned media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico
articles.title_zh: Judge extends White House access to banned media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico
articles.content_orig:
District court judge Timothy Kelly was ruling after Trump administration blocked access to three outlets last month
A federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue allowing journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to access the building as the media coalition’s lawsuit against the Trump administration plays out.
Timothy Kelly, a district court judge, had on 24 September granted a 14-day reprieve for the news organizations, which six days earlier had been banned by the president in an extraordinary move from entering the White House grounds “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”.
“Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN , MS NOW, and POLITICO, thereby maintaining the status quo since the Court’s entry of a temporary restraining order on September 24, 2026,” the judge wrote in granting a preliminary injunction requested by the plaintiffs.
The organizations filed a lawsuit on 21 September seeking to overturn the ban as a violation of their rights under the US constitution. But that temporary restraining order expired on Tuesday, bringing the media companies into court late last week to ask for a preliminary injunction that would lift the ban during the duration of the lawsuit, which could take months.
During arguments at the E Barrett Prettyman federal courthouse in Washington, Kelly seemed inclined to lift the ban indefinitely , telling a lawyer for the federal government that his side had “a notice problem” that was “probably the biggest hurdle” they had to overcome.
The Trump White House gave no advance notice to the media companies affected to say that they were at risk of losing their press badges, which the news organizations have said are essential to their ability to cover the administration. While the White House sent letters to the media companies informing them of the ban, they did so post-hoc, after building access had already been cut off, in violation of binding court precedent.
In his ruling on Tuesday, Judge Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs “are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims”. While access to the White House is not guaranteed, court precedent dictates that once it is provided to journalists, it cannot be taken away for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.
During arguments for a preliminary injunction on 8 October, media lawyer Theodore J Boutrous told the judge that Trump had offered a “confession” – in a Time magazine interview last week – that he was banning the media companies explicitly because of the content of their reporting, not because of any other considerations, such as national security.
“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge.
The judge seemed to agree. “President Trump’s own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before,” he wrote.
Although the White House has largely adhered to the judge’s prior ruling restoring access on a temporary basis, journalists for CNN and Politico have on occasion been prevented from performing “pool duty” – covering the daily activities of the president – because the administration has interpreted the judge’s temporary restraining order to solely require access to the White House complex, not smaller spaces like Air Force One or the Oval Office.
The judge required the media plaintiffs to post a bond of $1.
In a statement, Boutrous said of the judge’s ruling: “When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers.”
The court, he added, “was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future”.

articles.title_orig: Best photographs of 2026 to be showcased as part of World Athletics Awards
articles.title_zh: Best photographs of 2026 to be showcased as part of World Athletics Awards
articles.content_orig:
Photographers at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship ( © Getty Images )
An award for the best athletics photograph of the year will once again be presented as part of the World Athletics Awards in 2026.
Any professional photographer who has attended an athletics event in 2026 can take part in the World Athletics Photograph of the Year.
Photographers are requested to submit one photograph via the online form and include a caption, the date the photograph was taken, the image's technical information and a short photographer bio (no more than 50 words). Entries should be no larger than 5MB and must be received by 11:59pm Monaco time on 30 October.
A panel of five experts will judge all eligible photographs and select three finalists. The finalists will be revealed on 9 November and a fan vote to help determine the winner will be held on World Athletics’ Instagram channel from 9-15 November.
The winner will be announced on 28 November, ahead of the World Athletics Awards taking place in Monaco on 29 November.
Usain Bolt Jamaican sprint superstar Bolt has been the subject of some of the most iconic photographs in athletics. The fastest man of all time, he set his world 100m and 200m records of 9.58 and 19.19 during the 2009 World Championships in Berlin to win two of the 19 senior global titles he claimed throughout his sensational sprinting career. He retired in 2017 but remains involved in the sport, most recently through his role as Ultimate Legend for the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest.
Christel El Saneh El Saneh is the digital creative manager at World Athletics, managing photography and visual content across digital platforms. She joined World Athletics in 2021 and covered the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 Olympic Games as a photographer. The long jumper has spent most of her life in athletics and her journey has included forming part of the IOC Young Leader and Young Reporters programmes.
Dawn Harper-Nelson During her highly successful athletics career, Harper-Nelson won four global medals in the 100m hurdles, including the Olympic title in Beijing in 2008. She also secured Olympic silver in 2012, as well as world silver in 2017 and world bronze in 2011. She is now an Emmy Award-winning broadcaster, speaker and recently served as the infield host for the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest.
Pascal Rondeau Rondeau started his sports photography career in London for the prestigious Allsport photography agency. He then led the photo department of L’Equipe newspaper in Paris. Over the past 30 years, he has covered eight Summer Olympic Games and a range of other major sports events. He was appointed Venue Photo Manager at the Tokyo 2020 Olympic and Paralympic Games and Photo Chief at Paris 2024.
Dan Vernon Vernon has been an athletics photographer and filmmaker for more than a decade, capturing many of the most iconic moments in the sport. He creates athlete documentaries and has covered two Olympic Games and numerous major athletics championships and one-day meetings, frequently capturing the action for World Athletics channels. He has documented the careers of athletes including marathon great Eliud Kipchoge.

articles.title_orig: He’s Played It Safe. But He Could Make California History as Governor.
articles.title_zh: He’s Played It Safe. But He Could Make California History as Governor.
articles.content_orig:
This story was reported for K Onda KQED, a monthly newsletter focused on the Bay Area’s Latinx community. Click here to subscribe.
The upcoming gubernatorial election in California has been characterized as “quiet” and “sleepy” because the frontrunner, Xavier Becerra , has a very high chance of winning.
But for Latines, this election is slated to be one of the most historic and monumental elections ever: The largest state in the nation with the largest Latine population is about to elect a Latino governor for the first time. Becerra’s election is a big deal.
“Having someone in this highest office signals a potential turning point, a potential watershed moment, for which the future will tell whether this is a one-time thing or whether this opens the door for many more folks,” said G. Cristina Mora, sociology professor and co-director of the Institute of Governmental Studies at the University of California, Berkeley. “The historical significance, the symbolism of it is incredibly important.”
The likelihood that Becerra will become the next governor of California comes at a time when Latines have made gains in the state’s political landscape, but also when the state faces major challenges — from standing up to President Donald Trump’s attacks, to more people struggling with the rising cost of living and increased risks of wildfires.
In America’s history, only 11 Latines have served as governor — ever. There have been three Black and Asian governors each, and women have only served as governor 44 times. Those numbers are quite paltry when considering that more than 2,300 white men have served as governor since our nation was founded. (Romualdo Pacheco served as governor of California for less than a year in 1875, but was elevated from lieutenant governor to finish out a term and was not elected.)
The 68-year-old Becerra came into the race with more than three decades of experience, serving in the California State Assembly, Congress, as California’s attorney general, and as the United States Secretary of Health and Human Services under the Biden Administration.
He highlights his upbringing as a working-class child of Mexican immigrants who forged a reputation in politics as a policy nerd, Mora said.
“Should the voters of California elect Xavier Becerra, he would be the first Latino governor in over a century — that within itself is monumental,” said Christian Arana, vice president of civic power and policy with the San Francisco-based Latino Community Foundation.
Latinos, Arana said, making up 40% of California’s population, comprise the second largest voting block in the state with nearly 9 million eligible voters — and contribute more than a trillion dollars to the state’s GDP. And, let’s not forget that half of the children in California are Latine.
“To have somebody potentially look like you and also share the experiences that you might have is pretty significant,” Arana told me.
Becerra’s ascent to frontrunner seemed unlikely before he won the June primary, beating out a crowded field of Democratic candidates. Former East Bay Rep. Eric Swalwell was considered the top contender, but he suspended his campaign in April amid allegations of sexual assault.
Many of Swalwell’s supporters moved to line up behind Becerra, propelling him from a long shot into a position to make history.
“Imagine the positive impact that will have on the identities and aspirations of Latino/a kids throughout the State of California,” Hayward Mayor Mark Salinas wrote in an April Facebook post.
Becerra’s rise happens at a time when three other Latines currently hold prominent roles: Monique Limón serves as the Senate President pro Tempore, Robert Rivas is speaker of the state Assembly and Alex Padilla serves as U.S. senator.
That doesn’t necessarily mean that Latinos have collectively arrived in state politics, said Sonja Díaz, a civil rights attorney, policy adviser and political expert. But it does show that we are not sitting on the sidelines.
On her Substack, “Unseen Fortitude,” Díaz wrote, “Representation matters. But representation without any accountability for doing (hacer) and delivering (cumplir) is merely symbolism. Democracies need more than symbolism, and Latino leaders are tired of being calm, quiet and told to wait.”
In the 1990s, California voters passed Proposition 187, a law that would have denied public services to undocumented immigrants.
It was ultimately ruled unconstitutional and never implemented, but that experience sparked a surge of Latino participation in politics in California, Díaz said. Still, the Democratic Party has depended on Latino voters in California without doing enough to elevate Latino candidates.
For Becerra to become the likely winner is “a historical feat because of the willful neglect of both major parties to integrate Latino candidates and Latino interest in places like California,” Díaz told me. “It is because of the infrastructure and the systemic decision-making that Latino leaders made in the ’80s and ’90s, we are where we are today. And, I think that that is huge.”
Political parties and candidates need to do a better job engaging with Latino voters, Arana said. A recent LCF survey of Latino voters in California found that 40% had not been contacted by any candidate or party for the upcoming election.
At the same time, Latine voters in California tend to have lower turnout than other groups — 47% of Latinos are considered likely voters compared with 54% of Asian Americans, 54% of African Americans and 65% of whites, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Arana said many voters don’t show up at the polls because they don’t feel like their vote will make a difference or that politicians care about them.
The three experts I talked to all agreed that for Becerra to not just represent Latinos, but actually deliver results, he needs to address issues that affect Californians of all backgrounds — namely the lack of affordability and rising cost of living, but also concerns about climate change and the threat of AI eliminating jobs.
Becerra has been criticized for not making specific promises, but has talked about the need to build more housing, make healthcare more accessible, reduce homelessness, prepare for natural disasters and fight the current presidential administration that has been hostile toward California and immigrant communities.
“There is an expectation that he is going to deliver, right? Because he’s one of us,” Arana said.
“At the end of the day, the governor of California has to operate in a system. He’s one of many actors in California. The other thing to consider is the final two years of the Trump presidency. We have yet to see what else may be coming down the pipeline.”
California governors propose a state budget, Díaz said, which is the principal way to influence policy and programs that can directly impact the cost of living and quality of life issues that many Latinos care about.
“There needs to be rebudgeting that ensures that the material conditions, the social, economic and cultural material conditions of households on the ground are improved,” she said. “There’s a myriad of things where the next governor can and will make a difference.”

articles.title_orig: Katie Zacharia's debut shows the pitfalls and possibilities of White House press secretary's role
articles.title_zh: Katie Zacharia's debut shows the pitfalls and possibilities of White House press secretary's role
articles.content_orig:
A version of this story appeared in CNN’s What Matters newsletter. To get it in your inbox, sign up for free here .
The press secretary is supposed to spin the news, not be the news.
On that most essential qualification, the new lead White House spokeswoman, Katie Zacharia, is struggling.
She has presented herself as a lawyer but does not meet the requirements in her home state to use that title.
It’s a development made even more awkward after Republicans mercilessly attacked the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor, though he went to medical school and made his career in public health.
Zacharia has a law degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, but there’s no evidence she ever passed a bar exam. She does claim to have obtained a credential in China, but it’s not at all clear what credential she’s talking about.
Squabbles over who can call themselves a lawyer or a doctor probably seem beside the point to a large portion of the country.
This issue here is not that a law degree is required to be White House press secretary — it isn’t.
The issue is that Zacharia has presented herself repeatedly on TV, including on CNN, as a lawyer, something the independent journalist Judd Legum first documented . Trump used the term “attorney” to describe her when he announced she would be his press secretary.
A review by CNN’s K-File found at least six instances when she referred to herself as either a lawyer or a corporate lawyer in her own words and multiple other instances in which she posted or reposted to social media using the term attorney or “legal strategist.”
Washington, DC, is filled to the brim with people who have law degrees but do not practice law. And it does not appear that Zacharia inappropriately tried to represent anyone in a court.
But all of this does suggest the vetting operation at the White House is, to be charitable, not very thorough.
When reporters asked Trump at the White House where Zacharia passed the bar, she chimed in from behind him that she was when she moved to China. Even Trump did a double take.
Zacharia later told Politico she had “practiced international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials.”
It’s not clear — and the White House has not clarified — what certification Zacharia obtained in China, but it’s not the Chinese version of the bar exam. Only citizens can become licensed to practice law in China, according to the Ministry of Justice .
Questions about Zacharia’s CV are also an awkward development since Republicans in Michigan have attacked the Democrat running for Senate there, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor despite having gone to medical school.
At a debate this month, the Republican in the Senate race, former Rep. Mike Rogers, went so far as to say El-Sayed was a “con man.”
As CNN has reported , El-Sayed earned a Doctor of Medicine from Columbia University, but he does not practice clinical medicine.
El-Sayed has held public health positions in the Detroit area. His top policy issue is extending health insurance to all Americans.
Democratic boosters of El-Sayed have continued to call him a doctor.
“Abdul’s a doctor, and he’s taken on special interests to fight for good jobs, better healthcare, and lower costs,” former President Barack Obama said in an ad he cut for the Michigander.
In addition to saying on TV that she is a lawyer, Zacharia cites some legal-sounding work on her LinkedIn page; for example, she lists herself as “general counsel” for the activist group Fix California. In the nonprofit group’s tax filing for 2024, Zacharia’s name appears as having been a fundraiser.
She also lists herself as having worked as an “associate” in the international practice group at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing for nearly two years starting in 2011.
The White House press corps, obviously, has followed up on this mystery.
“Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law,” according to a White House official.
CNN’s White House team has found no evidence that Zacharia has passed the bar exam in the states where she has lived and worked since graduating from Pepperdine.
Here’s what California’s bar association told them:
California law lays out what’s required to be a lawyer.
There are requirements for college and law school, or their equivalents; for “good moral character”; passing an ethics exam; and passing the bar exam in California.
Zacharia, as a result, should not be considered a lawyer in California, the state where she has lived and worked.
A separate section of California law makes it a misdemeanor to pretend to be a lawyer.
Does presenting oneself as a lawyer on TV violate that piece of code?
Many other questions remain. What is the credential Zacharia obtained in China, if any? Did she try to take a bar exam and fail, or simply not take it? Why did no one at the White House, especially after questions arose about El-Sayed’s status as a doctor, think to follow up on this earlier?
None of that really matters to anyone who is more concerned with how the White House is handling the war Trump launched on Iran or the related inflation that continues to hit Americans in the wallet. Questions about whether Zacharia can call herself a lawyer, or not, mostly distract from those other, larger issues.
Ultimately, Trump is the person who speaks for his administration in the long, often rambling appearances he frequently makes in the Oval Office.
But those appearances may become less enjoyable for him in the future, especially if Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress and, as expected, launch a series of investigations into his administration, the money his family has made during his presidency, and much more.
He will, at that point, need a press secretary he can trust.
CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Starlink restrictions affecting Ukraine's front line operations, Kyiv says
articles.title_zh: Starlink restrictions affecting Ukraine's front line operations, Kyiv says
articles.content_orig:
New restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to the Starlink internet network have disrupted Ukraine's battlefield "missions", President Volodymyr Zelensky's adviser has warned.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said Ukraine had not been told about speed limits set overnight at 100mph (160km/h) by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to effectively guide drones to Russian targets and also protect Ukrainian skies.
Beskrestnov said SpaceX's move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation". The firm has not commented.
In Wednesday's post on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that SpaceX had "implemented overnight a speed limit on Starlink terminals" and this had already resulted in "the disruption of a number of missions".
In a follow-up post, the adviser stressed that Starlink was the most effective tool for enabling interceptors to shoot down Russia's newly developed jet-propelled drones.
It comes as at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, Zelensky said. Pictures from Kyiv showed residents, some dressed in their pajamas, with bloodied faces.
He added that "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region, and in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv – despite US President Donald Trump's claim on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.
Three people were killed in Kyiv, local officials reported. Russia said its "massive" strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
Later on Wednesday, at least six people were killed in a Russian drone strike on a warehouse in the north-western city of Lutsk, local officials said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
A source in the Ukrainian defence ministry later told the BBC: "Last night, we detected restrictions affecting Starlink connectivity at speeds above 160 km/h." The source added that the "root cause" of the issue was being investigated.
Defence ministry sources later explained that "once a vehicle or asset exceeds this [160km/h] threshold speed, the terminal loses its connection".
They told the BBC that this made it more difficult to carry out drone operations, "specifically interceptors and middle-strike drones", and also degraded "capabilities for front line logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relaying".
In February, Musk's decision to deny Russian forces access to Starlink blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.
Musk's SpaceX has not commented on the reported speed restrictions.
Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire. On Tuesday, Trump denied that Washington was withholding intelligence.
Ukraine relies on US satellite systems to track Russian missiles in order to issue alerts and to try to shoot them down. But over the past two nights, missiles have struck targets in the Ukrainian capital without any warning, before air raid sirens could be sounded.
According to Ukraine's air force, Russia launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones overnight. Four of those missiles and 115 drones were shot down, it said.
It was the second night in a row that Kyiv was hit by Russian missiles, and came as Zelensky prepared to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv.
Meanwhile, the Russian defence ministry said 902 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight over a number of Russian regions, including the capital Moscow and Crimea - Ukraine's southern peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014.
On Sunday, Trump wrote on Truth Social: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Zelensky has since repeatedly said that Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow does the same.
But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Under any truce, he added, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons", enabling it to continue the war.
For residents of Kyiv, the past two nights have been frightening.
Tetiana Storozhyk, 54, said a late night blast on Tuesday at her apartment block blew her from the kitchen into the hallway. The sirens sounded just as the missile hit the building, giving her no time to evacuate.
"It all happened in a fraction of a second. In that moment I lost everything" she said.
Storozhyk told the BBC that Ukraine needs weapons to protect its people, "but from the other side we need peace".
Without peace Ukraine is reliant on its air defences, but this wrecked neighbourhood is evidence of how ineffective they are without the right data.

articles.title_orig: Mike Tomlin’s Minecraft World Is the Talk of the Internet, but How Good Is It Really?
articles.title_zh: Mike Tomlin’s Minecraft World Is the Talk of the Internet, but How Good Is It Really?
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
Football coaches have the freedom to create their own worlds on the playing field. But retired Steelers legend Mike Tomlin took a different route — manifesting his vision block by block within a massive Minecraft city. What started as a shared family project with his children evolved into a solitary, 12-year labor of love. Now, the sheer depth of Tomlin’s digital city is capturing widespread attention online.
Tomlin served as the Steelers’ head coach for 19 seasons before resigning in January, having never finished with a losing record.
His video was released Oct. 1 and received more than 3 million views in less than two weeks. In the video, Tomlin shows off an expansive Minecraft city, complete with sports stadiums, high-rise apartments, homes and other buildings. He began working on the city about 12 years ago after watching his kids and their friends play Minecraft when they were in middle school, building it in the game’s creative mode with their help.
“I was mesmerized by what could occupy their attention for such large periods of time,” Tomlin says in the video. “I’m certainly not skilled enough in video game play or have the stick control to [play the game’s survival mode], so I got interested in this creative mode. I like to build, I’ve always had an interest in architecture, and so I started doing this creative city as a means to spend time with them.”
His kids eventually outgrew the game and moved on to different ones, high school and eventually college. That left Tomlin to work on the city by himself, which he did off and on for years while still coaching the Steelers.
“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me, some mindless entertainment,” Tomlin says. “I’m not a big TV watcher. It allowed me to detach from the realities and pressures of life.”
Tomlin spends the rest of the video showing viewers around the place, focusing on his basic, early-days architecture, penthouses, apartments and how he tried to design a solid urban space. He plans to release more videos to discuss different buildings, the city’s design and other elements of his sprawling city.
Leading up to the video’s release, there was no indication whatsoever that Mike Tomlin played computer games. That helped make his big Minecraft debut all the more delightful. The 54-year-old coach showed off thousands of hours of playtime in a 19-minute video, and no one could believe it.
“12 years of Minecraft? Didn’t you know this? Did nobody know this?” asked a shocked Ty Schmidt, producer and on-air personality of the Pat McAfee show, on an episode of the show.
The sports world finally saw what some Minecraft fans already knew: Tomlin’s dedication to the game is unmatched.
“We’re talking block by block,” McAfee said. “He had 14 30-story buildings around a body of water that he wanted to build his city around — one block at a time! They all got patios! He had a penthouse with a shark aquarium. It was unbelievable.”
Minecraft fans, too, showed up to explore the coach’s dazzling feat. Many were surprised to learn that he built this on the Bedrock edition of the game using a video game console, beginning with PlayStation 3 before moving on to PlayStation 4 and 5. That means Tomlin didn’t have access to the mods that many builders use in the Java version of the game on PC, or the freedom that a mouse and keyboard provide. He built his city one brick at a time on a PlayStation controller.
Tomlin was initially unaware of his viral fame. In an interview on Late Night with Seth Meyers, Tomlin said he was at a gala with his phone off when the video went live, and it wasn’t until later that his kids told him about the massive response. Tomlin had caught up by the time he appeared on Football Night in America with NBC on Sunday night.
“I’m appreciating all of this, to be quite honest with you,” Tomlin said during the broadcast.
The spectacle of Tomlin’s Minecraft city is one of those wholesome events that had viewers smiling all weekend, except a few Steelers fans who were probably already pretty mad about losing to the Cleveland Browns less than 24 hours after the video was released. That didn’t stop a lot of people from wondering whether Tomlin’s city is actually as good as it looks. It turns out that most of the Internet agrees that it lives up to the hype.
“From my understanding, [it’s a] phenomenal Minecraft city,” McAfee said. “Like, as I was watching it, I was like, man, the attention to detail [is outstanding].”
Noted Minecraft city builder Alpine1 was one of the first to create his own video on the topic, and he was impressed. He had some suggestions for Tomlin, recommending that the coach consider using glass panes instead of glass blocks and more sophisticated floor designs, such as installing tile floors in showers. But Alpine1 did note that Tomlin likely started building the city before many modern building tools were available to Minecraft players.
“This is really awesome to see,” Alpine1 said in the video. “I’ve been advocating for people to build Minecraft cities for years because there’s so much you can do… and I think Mike has really captured this.”
Zach Nagel, an architecture student from the University of Cincinnati’s School of Architecture and Interior Design, also took a stab at analyzing Tomlin’s city in a separate video . He noted that Tomlin used some concepts that are actually practiced in architecture, specifically adding a penthouse with an aquarium right across the street from a full-sized aquarium.
“Now, what Coach Tomlin is talking about here, having a central theme to the building, is a term that we use in architecture as well, the parti ,” Nagel says. “If you talk to 20 architects and ask them to give a definition of a parti, you might get 20 pretty different answers. At its [simplest], a parti is a single idea or scheme that drives all of the decisions you make in a building.”
Nagel goes on to praise Tomlin for not only considering the building’s exterior appearance but also its interior design and the functional needs of the city’s fictional residents. He says that a lot of Tomlin’s design choices and approach are in line with what some architects use.
“In another world, he could’ve totally gone down this career path had he wanted to,” Nagel says. “And I’m glad to see that Minecraft remains such an accessible tool for those who want to shape the environment around them.”

articles.title_orig: The Ocarina of Time remake feels remarkably modern — and surprisingly terrifying
articles.title_zh: The Ocarina of Time remake feels remarkably modern — and surprisingly terrifying
articles.content_orig:
New tech and gameplay improvements make it easier to get into Nintendo’s defining title.
New tech and gameplay improvements make it easier to get into Nintendo’s defining title.
With its upcoming remake for the Switch 2, Nintendo might have nailed the best thing about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time : its timelessness. The 1998 3D action adventure game for the Nintendo 64 that pioneered so much — 3D graphics, movement, exploration, openness — has been reengineered with changes that make it feel more modern, and surprisingly terrifying at times. Based on my early hands-on time with the game, it’s shaping up to be the best-looking, best-playing version of the game that addresses the most frustrating aspects of playing the original.
More than just sanding off its roughest edges, Nintendo also fitted Ocarina of Time with modern trappings to make it more welcoming to those who were introduced to Zelda through more modern releases, like Breath of the Wild . The remake has a new progression marker, called Threads of Time, that’s viewable when you pause. It also has Zelda Notes integration within the Nintendo Switch app to let you view game maps and other info on your phone. Oh, it also has a dedicated jump button.
I spent around 90 minutes during a recent preview event in New York City playing through some chunks of the game, including when you first take control of Child Link, and later on after you yank the Master Sword in the Temple of Time to become Adult Link. Its story still makes it a standout Zelda title, and the improvements make it even easier to get immersed in.
In some ways, the remake feels similar to modern Zelda games. Link is snappy to control, and lock-on combat is engaging. Swapping between items and weapons no longer requires hopping into the pause menu, as it did in the original. Holding a shoulder button halts the action, and you can navigate with an analog stick to find what you want in near-realtime. However, it’s an adventure on a much smaller scale; the complexity of your quests, and the tools at your disposal for combat and getting around are simpler, but no less fun.
All of the sections I played were truncated, though I left feeling confident that Nintendo nailed this remake. My favorite section was the Forest Temple, which really shows off the more realistic art style. It can finally portray the game’s horror themes in ways that weren’t possible 28 years ago. For example, Link traverses rooms in the dungeon that have red stained glass windows, and as he passes through beams of light, he is cast in the color of blood. It really looks and feels like he’s on an adventure to stave off cataclysm, and the visual evolution frequently made me stop playing for a second while I took in the changes. Also, being able to use the right stick to control the camera lets you create cinematic moments on-the-fly, which is great if, like me, you like taking a lot of screenshots.
Ocarina of Time is one of Nintendo’s most influential games, and playing it is a rite of passage for any Zelda fan, but it can be tough to go back to the original. As accessible as it is considering it was one of Nintendo’s earliest fully-3D titles, the remake makes it so much easier to get into. And it’s launching at a time when the Zelda franchise is bigger than ever. Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom were big sellers, and they continue to attract new players years after launch, while fans will be able to dig into the live-action movie in April 2027 . Even sooner, though, Switch 2 owners will get to feast on the best way to play through a defining Zelda classic.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches for the Nintendo Switch 2 on Thursday, November 5th.
