articles.title_orig: Bloomfield Students Get an Inside Look at the World of Game Development
articles.title_zh: Bloomfield Students Get an Inside Look at the World of Game Development
articles.content_orig:
From playtesting games to connecting with the people who create them, Bloomfield students get a glimpse of the opportunities available in the world of game development.
For Bloomfield College of Montclair State University students passionate about video games, a recent trip to the 2026 Game Devs of Color Expo NYC Watch Party offered a chance to explore the industry beyond the classroom. Open to students across all Creative Arts and Technology (CAT) majors, the field trip gave attendees the opportunity to experience the world of game development firsthand.
The Game Devs of Color Expo is a virtual conference that brings together game creators to showcase their work, share their experiences and celebrate the creativity and diversity of the gaming community. For the first time, the NYC Watch Party gave Bloomfield students the opportunity to experience the online event in person alongside local developers, fellow students and gaming enthusiasts.
Throughout the event, students explored game stations featuring independent titles, tried out games created by developers and watched presentations highlighting different perspectives and experiences in the industry. The Watch Party also provided opportunities to speak with attendees about their work and learn more about the creative process behind developing games.
“So much of game design is about community, and meeting developers means our students can start building those connections on their own terms." — GJ Lee, associate professor of Creative Arts and Technology
The virtual conference gave students a chance to learn more about the gaming industry from the people working in it. Through presentations and discussions, they heard different perspectives on game development, from the creative decisions behind a game to the experiences of those building careers in the field.
For Game Programming major Tim Fuentes, the Expo offered a closer look at the industry he hopes to one day be part of.
“I’ve always been into video games since I was very young, and I want to become a game programmer,” Fuentes says. “I thought this field trip would be a good opportunity to meet professional game programmers and see how the space works.”
One of the highlights of the conference was seeing the variety of ideas being brought to life by independent creators. Games can take many different forms, and the presentations offered a look at how developers use storytelling, technology and their own experiences to create something unique.
GJ Lee , associate professor in Bloomfield's Creative Arts and Technology program, accompanied the students to the Watch Party, also sees value in introducing students to the community surrounding game development.
“So much of game design is about community, and meeting developers means our students can start building those connections on their own terms,” says Lee.
By bringing the virtual conference and in-person Watch Party together, the event gave Bloomfield students a chance to learn about the industry while experiencing the community that makes it all possible.
Bloomfield Faculty in the Gaming Industry
Bloomfield's involvement in the Game Devs of Color Expo goes beyond the student field trip. Professor G.J. Lee helped open the virtual conference alongside its directors, while fellow faculty member Hatim Benhsain had his game, coalescent || tidal rapture , featured at the event.
Benhsain is developing the 3D swimming adventure game through his studio, Games for my Computer. The game follows a society of merpeople undergoing evolution and explores themes of queer relationships and connection.
“It was a huge honor to have our game featured,” Benhsain says. “We are so excited to share coalescent with the whole wide world, and this helped us get closer to that goal.”
Having faculty members involved in events like the Expo gives students another way to see how the work happening in their classrooms connects to the gaming industry. For aspiring developers, it's a chance to learn from professors who are also contributing their own creative work to the field.
With opportunities to learn from industry professionals, discover independent projects and see their own professors' work represented at the conference, students left with a broader picture of the possibilities ahead of them in game development.

articles.title_orig: World Lung Day 2026 activities from Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients
articles.title_zh: World Lung Day 2026 activities from Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients
articles.content_orig:
Home » World Lung Day 2026 activities from Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients
Catch up on World Lung Day activities from Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients around the world.
From schools in Pakistan to communities in Ethiopia, the United Kingdom and Ukraine, organisations supported through Healthy Lungs for Life grants marked World Lung Day on 25 September with lung health awareness, screening and support activities.
World Lung Day is an annual global awareness day that highlights the importance of lung health and encourages people to take action to prevent lung conditions and protect their lungs.
The grants help organisations deliver projects tailored to local needs and many of this year’s activities focused on communities facing barriers to accessing health services because of geography, displacement or limited resources.
In southern Ethiopia, READIO Ethiopia worked with Community Health Workers and healthcare professionals to bring lung health checks (spirometry) and education directly to Chukare Kebele, a rural community with limited access to healthcare services.
The initiative reached 266 households and more than 1,300 people, including over 180 children under five. It also trained 27 Community Health Workers to recognise warning signs of lung disease, promote early care-seeking and support referrals. Education sessions covered topics including pneumonia, tuberculosis, clean air, smoke-free living, vaccination and recognising when to seek medical advice, helping build local knowledge that will benefit the community beyond World Lung Day.
In Sheffield, United Kingdom, SOAR Community hosted a “Breathe Better, Move More” event in Burngreave, one of Sheffield’s most diverse communities. The event brought together around 80 local residents to learn more about lung health and wellbeing.
Residents could access lung health checks (spirometry), smoking cessation advice, pulmonary rehabilitation information, breathing and singing exercises, and support from local charities and healthcare professionals. The event also brought together local health and community organisations, helping residents learn more about the support available in their area.
The Helping Hand Foundation in Multan, Pakistan, delivered 10 days of activities across schools, healthcare facilities and underserved communities.
More than 1,300 students took part in lung health checks (spirometry) and over 1,200 received structured lung health education. Community outreach activities focused on air pollution, tobacco exposure, vaccination and lung disease prevention, while people needing further assessment were referred for follow-up care. The project also encouraged young people to become ambassadors for lung health within their schools and communities.
In Ukraine, Dnipro State Medical University delivered educational activities and lung health checks (spirometry), despite the ongoing challenges facing the region.
The project also expanded support for internally displaced people living in university accommodation, including access to specialist lung health consultations for those whose healthcare had been disrupted by the conflict. The work demonstrated the determination and commitment of local teams to maintain access to care despite difficult circumstances.
Although each project responded to different local needs, all shared the same goal: helping more people understand their lung health and access the information and services they need.
The European Lung Foundation thanks all Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients, volunteers, healthcare professionals and community partners whose commitment and hard work helped make World Lung Day 2026 a success.
Healthy Lungs for Life grant recipients featured in this article included:
Healthy Lungs for Life is the European Lung Foundation (ELF) and European Respiratory Society (ERS) campaign that raises awareness of lung health and encourages people to take action to protect their lungs. Each year, the campaign supports organisations around the world to deliver activities that respond to the needs of their communities, whether through education, screening, prevention or public awareness.
Earlier this year, the European Lung Foundation (ELF) awarded Healthy Lungs for Life grants to organisations across Europe, Africa and Asia. The grants support local activities that raise awareness of lung health, encourage prevention and help people access information and support where they live.

double quotation mark Gaza has been levelled. There are Palestinians trying to hold on to their homes in the West Bank. Imagine trying to put a polling station in that circumstance.
The issue is, trying to make sure you have a election process that you can be confident in, that is held in a time that that can occur, and I don’t think it can be, not with those current circumstances …

double quotation mark I think the time for inquiries is over … But having said that, if we are going to do an inquiry, the expectation is it’s done thoroughly. So, you know, I can understand why there would be some discomfort about, you know, a letter being put forward in the way that it was done. If you’re going to do it, do it right.
Greens deputy leader hopes to be in government in ‘not too distant future’
The Greens’ new deputy leader, Steph Hodgins-May , says she wants the minor party to form government and hopefully soon.
Hodgins-May was on the ABC just now, discussing her objections to the government’s planned reform to its minimum 30% tax rate on discretionary trusts.
She said the Greens still wanted the reforms to happen “this year” but wanted an inquiry to find and close any loopholes in the proposed system:
double quotation mark We’re saying what the government’s dished up at present isn’t good enough. They’ve watered down something to the point where we’re uncomfortable with it. We think that it’s going to create further inequity in the taxation system and benefit the 1% …
Even if it’s not perfect, well, we’re going to fight for it to be better than it is.
Asked whether she accepted that the Greens could not make the laws “perfect,” Hodgins-May said:
double quotation mark Well, until the Greens are in government, which I do hope happens in the not too distant future – when we can put up legislation that we are incredibly proud of and that we think Australians would also get behind – yes, there’s a level of compromise. But let’s be clear, we are sending this to inquiry. We will interrogate it.
US is repeatedly warning Labor on algorithm reforms, says trade minister
Don Farrell has said the US representatives to Australia have repeatedly complained about Labor’s planned algorithm laws but made no direct threats.
The digital duty of care laws are expected to be introduced to parliament this week. Farrell told the ABC:
double quotation mark They’ve been raised with me every time I’ve met with the Americans. We obviously have a difference of opinion. We certainly don’t believe anything we are doing is contrary to our free trade agreement … I’ve tried to explain to the Americans that our objective is to protect our citizens, particularly young people. And so far, there hasn’t been a direct response.
He said the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer , has raised a range of social media issues but there had never been a threat of a consequence for the laws.
double quotation mark In a few minutes, I’m meeting the new American ambassador. He may or he may not [mention the laws]. I don’t know. But if he does, I will explain to him, as I’ve explained to Jamieson Greer, our job as an Australian government is to protect our citizens, and this is one of the ways we’re doing it.
The trade minister says Coalition representatives have walked out of meetings on the European Union trade deal but some of its members might still be interested in getting the deal done.
Don Farrell has told the ABC that Ted O’Brien had walked out on him while he was explaining the deal, along with the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, who protested the trade deal while holding a pineapple earlier today.
But Farrell told Patricia Karvelas the Coalition’s and Greens’ objections to the deal did not mean it could not proceed, adding:
double quotation mark I have to find nine sensible senators beyond the 30 that I’ve got. I’m discussing it with everybody. And don’t think for one moment, Patricia, that the opposition is united in their position against this agreement …
I’m hopeful, in fact, I’m perhaps even confident that there are enough senators in the Australian Senate right now who understand just how important this agreement is for Australia to get through.
The Reserve Bank of Australia has told its staff they will miss out on their pay rise if they don’t support a disputed wage deal.
RBA staff rejected a 9.5% increase over three years in July and have fought management for a better offer but the bank will put a roughly similar offer to a vote tomorrow.
Susan Woods , the RBA’s chief operating officer, told staff in an email today the 9.5% offer was competitive. She said:
double quotation mark We have genuinely negotiated to arrive at this position and are at the limit of what we can responsibly offer while meeting our obligations as a public institution and Australia’s central bank.
Staff have already missed six weeks of pay rise as their deal would have started in September. Woods told staff the RBA would not offer any back pay, adding:
double quotation mark This is the Bank’s best offer for the 2026 EA. A further “no” vote will not recover the salary already forgone, and the proposed 3.7 per cent increase will not proceed … Bargaining would continue, with no guarantee that this would result in a higher wage outcome.

articles.title_orig: Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband
articles.title_zh: Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband
articles.content_orig:
UK foreign secretary will call for World Bank and others to help governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , will claim the global financial system is failing developing countries, as he calls for a “new deal” for governments struggling under the burden of debt.
Promising to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind urgent reform, he will evoke the example of the Gleneagles summit under the last Labour government in 2005 – the culmination of the Make Poverty History campaign.
“The global financial system and indeed the global order is failing to serve developing countries on debt, on resilience and on climate. This is not just against our values but against our national interest,” Miliband is expected to say.
“In the interconnected world we live in, more than ever, the opportunities and challenges we confront are collective.”
Speaking in Bangkok on Wednesday, he will call for the World Bank and other multilateral development banks (MDBs) to use the resources they have available to lighten the load for governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs.
“We need action on developing country debt through the MDBs,” he is expected to say. “Action that leverages the balance sheets of the international financial institutions to support these countries to repay over longer time horizons, and crucially, refinancing, with better rates, to give them precious fiscal space.”
The foreign secretary will be in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings.
He opted to take up the UK’s seat on the bank’s board himself instead of leaving it to the development minister, Kirsty McNeill.
Labour’s manifesto in 2024 promised to restore the UK’s international reputation on development issues – but Keir Starmer subsequently slashed the aid budget to pay for defence.
Campaigners have long claimed the high interest rates paid by many developing countries mean the repayments crowd out vital public spending – including on tackling the climate emergency. In sub-Saharan Africa, more than three times as much is spent on debt servicing as on education.
Miliband will argue that making the global financial system work better for emerging economies will also help to attract more private investment – a key aim of the World Bank under the current president, Ajay Banga.
The UK is due to take up the presidency of the G20 group of nations next year – a key global forum for discussing global financial issues, including sovereign debt, which includes emerging economies such as China, India, South Africa and Brazil.
The chancellor, John Healey , will set out his own G20 priorities in Bangkok later this week, including mobilising more resources from the balance sheets of the IMF and the World Bank.
after newsletter promotion
When the UK held the chair of the narrower G8 group in 2005, at the leaders’ summit at the Gleneagles hotel the UK secured agreements that eventually resulted in more than 30 countries receiving large-scale debt write-downs.
Miliband will say resources are now more constrained – but as well as debt refinancing for a large number of countries, he will demand an overhaul of the “common framework” for restructuring the debts of countries unable to pay.
The framework is widely criticised as too slow and cumbersome. Among other reforms, the UK wants to see changes to ensure private creditors cannot hold up negotiations – as has happened in recent cases including that of Ethiopia.
The foreign secretary will also call for overhauls to allow help to be made available more rapidly to countries in trouble. “We need finance teed up in advance of crises, so that governments get support in days, not months,” he will say.
Miliband will be speaking at the launch of a report by the Rockefeller Foundation that calls for a “surge” in affordable financing from the IMF and the World Bank to debt-burdened countries.
Tim Jones, the policy director of the campaign group Debt Justice, welcomed Miliband’s focus on the issue but said a litmus test of any plan would be whether private sector creditors bear some of the costs. “Action on debt relief is urgently needed. That must include private lenders sharing in the cost. Otherwise public money will just bail out private lenders rather than be used for investment.”

articles.title_orig: How technology is changing the detection of breast cancer
articles.title_zh: How technology is changing the detection of breast cancer
articles.content_orig:
Dr. Rachel Brem decided at age 12 that she wanted to cure cancer after her mom was diagnosed with breast cancer. It was early detection that led to her mother living way past her prognosis of six months. Now, Brem is working to improve breast cancer screening for all women.
Brem is a board-certified diagnostic radiologist and director of Breast Imaging and Intervention at George Washington University. She created the Brem Foundation to help prevent breast cancer from taking more lives.
On this week's episode of "Healthful," she discussed the innovation that makes her hopeful.
"AI is going to change everything in medicine, and certainly breast cancer detection," Brem said.
In addition to her work with George Washington University's Breast Imaging and Intervention unit, Brem collaborates with ScreenPoint Medical to develop Transpara, an AI breast cancer screening software.
Already there is significant scientific research showing mammograms paired with AI evaluations "can find cancer up to five years earlier," she said, by detecting warning signs in women that might be missed with just mammograms alone. The software can also predict future risk of breast cancer even when none is detected in a mammogram.
"Imagine what the impact of that is going to be on survival therapy," Brem said.
If women begin getting screened at age 35 with AI-enhanced readings, she noted the software will constantly teach itself how to improve in detecting breast cancer with each analysis. That's younger than the starting age recommended by several major medical organizations.
At George Washington University, Brem said, "we've been using AI for over four years in every mammogram," adding that using the software does not cost extra.
However, nationwide, just 20% of practices use AI with their mammogram procedures. Often, the AI readings cost extra, which may make the option inaccessible for some.
"There is nothing you can do to absolutely prevent breast cancer," Brem acknowledged.
But she said, "One of the things AI can do is really equalize the inequalities," referring to the racial disparities that affect diagnosis and treatment for many women.
"Black women die at a 40% higher rate [from breast cancer] than White women," Brem noted, and women with fewer resources have less access to mammograms.
Brem wants to change this with her foundation , which for the past 20 years has championed early detection  through innovative screening, increased education and awareness, and equitable access.
"I look forward to the more wide-reaching implementation of AI to help not only find more cancers, but with healthcare," she said.
Brem is helping to develop a breath test that could detect breast cancer. Diseased tissues give off a chemical compound that becomes gas and, scientists believe, could be used as a noninvasive way to assess who needs further screening.
"It's not available yet, but I'm really excited about having no pain, no compression, and no injection way of diagnosing if you're accurately diagnosed," Brem said.
And there's hope it could someday help beyond breast cancer. "The next step on our roadmap is not just breast cancer but a women's health panel where you could do one breath and get all these tests done," Brem said.
The guidelines from the American College of Physicians stated in 2026 that women over the age of 50 should get a mammogram every other year. The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends that women should start screening every other year at the age of 40.
To Brem, "This is a travesty."
"Women will die if they listen to that."
From her research, women should get checked for breast cancer annually starting at the age of 40. For those with a history of breast cancer in their family, they should start at 35.
This is all easier said than done. Women often cite anxiety as a reason they delay or skip getting screened. The thought of receiving a positive test result understandably makes women nervous, but as Brem notes, "We don't get rid of the disease by not knowing we have it."
Early detection of breast cancer leads to significantly better outcomes compared to cases where breast cancer is found in its later stages.
"Ninety-nine percent of women with early breast cancer survive and thrive," Brem said, but this outcome can only be possible if women screen for it early and regularly.
In addition to the recommended mammograms, Brem also believes "you absolutely, unequivocally definitely need more exams" if you have dense breasts . Half of women have dense breasts, and mammograms might not be able to pick up potentially deadly tumors hiding behind the tissue. Ultrasounds, MRIs or contrast-enhanced mammograms are necessary for those with dense breasts to get a complete view of their risks.
Supplemental screening isn't always standard with some doctors. Brem advised that it is "really important" for women to insist that their doctors order these extra exams. The mammograms are not enough.
Brem is adamant in her belief that women can be proactive now to better their health and improve their breast cancer outcomes. If you have dense breasts, demand additional screening.
For those under 40 who think they have time until they need to start screening for breast cancer, think again.
"You're not too young to have breast cancer," Brem warns.
Having the conversation now about your plan for breast cancer screenings and seeking out additional exams is essential in early detection and better prognosis. "If you find it early, even if you're young, it's curable," Brem said.
Rates of cancer are rising in younger women and awareness is the first step to being proactive about your health. Her foundation provides resources to educate women.
But what do you do with this information? Brem urges you to advocate for yourself at the doctor's office.
"We tell women to be badass," she said. "You need to advocate for yourself. It is a fundamental principle. It's your right. It's what you deserve, and it's not a maybe."

articles.title_orig: Cousins make mark in art world
articles.title_zh: Cousins make mark in art world
articles.content_orig:
Cousins and artists Shelley Elser, left, and Kevin Davenport, right, live on one of the more recognizable properties along South Park Loop Road, adorned with their own art and collected works from artists across the world.
Artistic duo Shelley Elser and Kevin Davenport share an art compound — a well-known landmark for South Park Loop travelers. The cousins are part creators, part archivists, and 100% community members.
As doves move from tree to tree, Davenport and Elser hold space not just for traditional trades and craft work but for the evolution of art. The property is unmistakeable, outlined by gigantic metal daisies and dotted with work by John Simms, a former neighbor and mentor.
Davenport was nominated to complete Terry Chambers’ unfinished golden bear sculpture, which stands on its hind legs outside the two-floor studio on the property. The studio itself is clearly highly functional — blacksmith shop on the bottom floor, countless creative materials and other tools on the top. And yet, being filled with everything from partially constructed, unfinished pieces to photography, glass and Elsner’s foraged items and vignettes, the space feels a bit like a Victorian-era curiosity cabinet on steroids.
“Did you know mourning doves mate for life and everyone hangs out together, all the generations?” Davenport said while walking between his fence made of vertical mufflers and a shed adorned with beehive patterns.
The cousins are eight years apart; Elsner was born in 1966, and Davenport in ’74, and are avid bird fans, monitoring the nesting pair of osprey on the property, known to them as “ShelleyStone Park.” The “park” is filled with birds and art in every direction.
The duo is behind many creative projects in Jackson, including clubhouse fireplaces and staircase railings. Elsner has a background in jewelry making; she worked with former husband and business partner Dan Harrison at Dan Shelley Jewelers, once located in Gaslight Alley. Elsner moved to Jackson in the mid-1970s, and her family members soon joined. She and Harrison built their business of Teton- and totem-infused designs and men’s rings, among their silversmithing.
Davenport unapologetically said his cousin told him to move here to make art, so he did. Fover 25 years, he has curated an atelier spanning glasswork and bronze casting to metalwork, welding and milling. He’s created fireplace doors, railings, gates, lighting, signs and sculpture (with details like a Hardy fishing rod and reel, cutthroat trout and the Tetons etched in fireplace tools).
Davenport’s shop pays homage to those who have passed through. A garage door doubles as a white wall for sentiments and signatures. Along another wall hangs American sculptor David Smith’s entire collection of tools. Smith was known for abstract and Impressionist designs.
“Right now,” Davenport said, “I am working on a bespoke metal sheetwork that’s flat and 20-gauge thin (to) make it three-dimensional form. And so I’m making queen bees that walk across there and then the idea is that they’ll be freestanding.”
A member of the California Blacksmith Association, Davenport said he travels around the world about every two years to teach with other members.
Both artists love bones and history, but repairing an elk mount and making it a bronze took nearly a year and a half. Davenport had to find a mold maker in Cody and worked with a foundry in Oregon to find the right patinas.
Elser suggested doing mounts of grizzlies. While grizzly skulls are illegal in Wyoming, the Alaska Department of Game and Fish worked with Davenport to obtain a Kodiak bear skull — one that he’s been able to cast into new line of sculpture.
Some sculpture, on the other hand, has ancient origins. Before leaving his shop, Davenport pulls out a 75-million-year-old ammolite gemstone for which he’s designing a stand.
Elser has been running support for her younger cousin and has lately been spending more time prioritizing self-care, including taking classes at the Senior Center.
“We’re not married,” she said. “Being relatives is so much easier.”
Visit Davenport’s website at MetalByKevin.com .
Contact Tibby Plasse via valley@jhnewsandguide.com .

articles.title_orig: New chief for DP World Americas
articles.title_zh: New chief for DP World Americas
articles.content_orig:
DP World has appointed Morten Johansen as chief executive officer of its Americas region, placing a longtime ports and logistics executive in charge of the company’s operations across North America, South America, and the Caribbean.
Johansen made the announcement in a LinkedIn post Oct. 13. He succeeds Brian Enright, who served in the dual positions since Oct. 22.
Johansen has more than 25 years of experience in integrated port and logistics businesses. He joined Dubai-based DP World in 2011 and previously served as CEO of DP World Dominicana.
He later became chief operating officer of DP World Americas, with responsibility for ports and terminals, logistics services, economic zones, and maritime operations throughout the Western Hemisphere.
In that role, he has emphasized integrating physical infrastructure with ports, inland transport, customs processes, economic zones, and digital platforms.
The appointment comes as DP World continues to expand its Americas footprint.
The company entered exclusive negotiations with the Port of Corpus Christi in June 2026 to design, build, and operate a container terminal under a long-term lease. If completed, it would be DP World’s first container-terminal development on the U.S. Gulf Coast and its first U.S. container-terminal development in roughly two decades.
The proposed facility could ultimately handle about 1 million TEUs annually. No construction start date, final capital commitment, or definitive lease terms have been announced.
Other Americas initiatives include a $760 million port and free-trade-zone development in the Dominican Republic , which the company says is intended to increase cargo capacity and support nearshoring-related investment.
Prior to DP World, Johansen’s background includes senior roles at APM Terminals, Maersk, and Sociedade Gestora de Terminais. A native of Denmark, he has been based in Charlotte, N.C., in his Americas leadership role.

articles.title_orig: As Ebola spreads in eastern Congo, mothers and children shun vital care
articles.title_zh: As Ebola spreads in eastern Congo, mothers and children shun vital care
articles.content_orig:
The latest numbers from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) show the Ebola outbreak now stands at 9,066 cases 4,381 deaths. This is the second largest Ebola outbreak in history, following the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people across Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone.
The West Africa outbreak was caused by the more common Zaire strain of the virus. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, which has no approved treatments or vaccines. The outbreak’s current case-fatality rate is 48.2%.
Today CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, announced preparations are under way for a phase 2/3 trial called Tumaini, which will evaluate the safety, immunogenicity and efficacy of vaccine candidates against Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), including Ervebo, the Zaire-targeting vaccine.
“Tumaini is designed as an adaptive platform trial, subject to ethical and regulatory approval,” CEPI said . “This allows several vaccine candidates to be evaluated in parallel within a single trial framework, which saves valuable time during an outbreak.” In addition to Ervebo, the trial will include at least two Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates.
Currently the Bravo study, a research project coordinated by Doctors Without Borders (Medecins sans Frontieres) is evaluating the effectiveness of the Ervebo vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain in North Kivu and Ituri province. Teams have vaccinated 857 frontline workers.
Late last week the US Department of Agriculture’s National Veterinary Services Laboratory confirmed the detection of H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) on two Yakima County dairy farms in Washington.
“This marks the first known case of HPAI in cattle in Washington state,” state officials said. Since March 2024 dairy cattle herds in 19 states have documented H5N1 infections, including neighboring Idaho.
“Washington State Department of Agriculture conducted on-farm investigations, testing, and gathered additional epidemiological information to better understand this detection and limit further disease spread,” officials said. “The two farms are under quarantine and have employed strict biosecurity measures. Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows.”
Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows.
In the past 30 days four dairy herds have had H5N1 detections, including herds in Kansas and Texas. So far in 2026, US officials have confirmed avian flu in 93 dairy herds, compared to 917 in 2024 and 171 last year.
“We appreciate how difficult this is for our dairy families, farmworkers, and veterinarians that are working hard to keep animals safe and healthy,” said Washington State Veterinarian Amber Itle, VMD. “The most important thing you can do is implement enhanced biosecurity and report symptoms immediately if animals show signs of illness.”
Unannounced drills to assess healthcare facility readiness to manage infectious disease outbreaks in three areas of the United States revealed variable adherence to containment protocols, according to a new study published in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report .
Using a simulated avian flu scenario involving an A(H5) strain with professional actors as patients, local and national public health authorities conducted 73 drills in 69 emergency departments, urgent care centers, and outpatient clinics in New Jersey, New York, and the US Virgin Islands from January to June 2026. The aim was to assess facilities’ ability to rapidly identify and isolate patients with suspected high-consequence infectious diseases.
“Successive recent outbreaks of viral hemorrhagic fevers, novel coronaviruses (e.g., COVID-19), monkeypox [mpox] virus disease, measles, and avian influenza A(H5) have reinforced the importance of rapidly recognizing and safely managing patients with potentially severe transmissible infections at health care facility points of entry, to protect health care workers, patients, and surrounding communities,” the authors wrote.
Facilities conducted symptom screening in 93.2% of the drills, documented travel history on patient arrival in 79.5%, and asked about exposure to avian flu in 9.6%. In 82.2% of drills during which the patient was appropriately masked, the median time from arrival to masking was two minutes, one minute short of the target.
Findings identified opportunities to support these outpatient settings in implementing more robust screening, isolation and notification processes, and IPC training.
Of 71.2% of drills that included patient isolation, the median time to isolation was 11 minutes, one minute shy of the 10-minute goal. A combination of masking and isolation took place in 60.3% of exercises. Patient actors were identified as being at risk for avian flu in 63.4% of cases.
Infection prevention-and-control (IPC) teams were notified or scheduled to be notified in 54.8% of drills, and staff wore all recommended personal protective equipment (PPE) in just 25.0% but wore none in 5.9%.
“These drills identified needs for health care workers and health care facility staff member training to achieve earlier identification, masking, and isolation of potentially infectious febrile patients,” the researchers wrote. “Findings identified opportunities to support these outpatient settings in implementing more robust screening, isolation and notification processes, and IPC training.”
Russia has yet to confirm what caused the lab worker’s death.
A Danish university has approved a CDC-funded study in African newborns, in which only half of babies will receive the hepatitis B vaccine.
The oral microbiota is significantly less diverse in people with severe persistent symptoms than in those with mild symptoms.
A study in blood cancer patients found that intake of foods with high sugar content was linked to less bacterial diversity in the gut.
No other state has reported that many measles cases in 35 years.
Undercover GAO staff were able to acquire four pieces from the HHS and USDA that experts said could have been resold to countries of concern.
Florida has tracked more than 250 locally acquired dengue cases this year.
The US now has 4,080 confirmed cases, more than a quarter of which are in hard-hit Pennsylvania.
The most recent from the DRC shows 8,665 confirmed and 4,178 deaths, with a case-fatality rate of 48%.

articles.title_orig: The Geerlings Gaze Into Their Crystal Ball for Radio
articles.title_zh: The Geerlings Gaze Into Their Crystal Ball for Radio
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › News Makers
During Radio World’s late-summer conversation with Joe and Jeff Geerling, the dynamic father-and-son duo who combine broadcast engineering and software development expertise, a funny thing happened: An impromptu podcast broke out.
As we discussed with the Geerlings the convergence of traditional RF tools and IT management, we asked them about two topics on the minds of station managers and engineers this fall: cybersecurity and AI.
Finally, in such a competitive landscape, Joe and Jeff offer one simple piece of advice to radio station operators: Stay small.
And a reminder to check out our September story on what makes the Geerlings tick .
Joe’s grandfather was born in 1900. When he was 82, Joe recalled, he made a remark about the velocity of changes he saw over his lifetime following the industrial revolution.
“When he was born, there were really no cars. He saw streets pop up, buildings, airplanes, rockets, air conditioning. In his mind, how could anyone see as much change as he did?
“Well, I’ve seen a whole lot change too in my lifetime, and with the tools we have, I don’t think it’s going to slow down,” Joe said.
An engineering veteran, Joe has spent decades protecting physical transmitter buildings. He sees network security as a natural extension of the job.
“Every time you connect something to the internet, you should be thinking about security,” Joe said. “I think the majority of engineers always had that mindset, protecting the plant. So this requirement is welcome. You have to do something.”
But recent FCC mandates regulating IT and security in the audio chain have opened a window of concern for smaller stations.
“You’re never going to get high-end Cisco gear at a small tower site,” Joe explained. “By protecting the EAS first, everybody is going to make sure they have a router with a complicated password and that’s probably going to solve 95% of the problem.”
Jeff, meanwhile, grew up in the dawn of the internet age. It would be a delight to shop with him at a certain computer retail outlet.
Taking advantage of the conveniences that running audio over IP offers requires configuration ahead of time. Network security has become a fundamental part of most businesses.
Jeff pointed out that the engineers who built the legacy systems still running today were RF experts, not IT professionals. Thinking about digital security requires a different mindset.
“There is still gear running from the early 1990s that doesn’t use encryption,” Jeff warned. “If they get physical access or into your network remotely, it’s game over.”
Even today’s broadcast software carries baggage. Joe observed how some on-air automation systems still demand administrative privileges to run simply because that is how they were coded 20 years ago.
Then there is the elephant in today’s tech room. AI.
Both Geerlings view the AI boom through a nuanced lens. For Joe, it brings back memories of broadcasters relying entirely on the AP teletype wire.
“When I first started, it wasn’t unusual for stations to ‘rip and read’ off the AP teletype,” he recalled. “They would tear off the story and read it on air without thinking about relating it to their audience.
“For me, AI is the same thing. You need to make sure you are using it and that it isn’t using you.”
Joe sees potential for AI as an internal tech support knowledge base. But he draws a hard line at replacing on-air talent.
Jeff uses AI as a sounding board for his software development but he is wary of large-language models that slurp up creator content and summarize it without attribution.
He’s seen fluctuations in visits to his blog and realizes the proliferation of AI slop plays a part.
“And worse, these AI tools take the things I write, summarize them and just give people the little nugget they want,” Jeff said.
Still, he admits the tech is impossible to ignore. He describes it with a clever analogy.
“I think of it like a drill,” Jeff said. “I have a manual hand drill where you crank the chuck. Now, you have battery drills you only have to charge once every six months. AI is similar for me.”
Jeff does not perform as much software development as he used to. He looks at AI from a content creator perspective. But he knows other developers who will burn as many as two million AI tokens a minute — tokenmaxxing as it is known in some circles — spending around $500 a day.
“I think it goes back to what my dad said,” Jeff explained, “you work with it and check, rather than saying, ‘give me this thing’ and immediately shipping it. It’s like the news. Grabbing a summary and pasting it directly only on your website is much different from helping to identify themes within an article.”
Our chat could have gone on for much longer. The pair offered well-spoken, articulate takes on all the topics we covered. Nothing was off limits. Midterm general election predictions, anyone?
But with their uniquely different perspectives looking at radio, it felt like the most opportune time to ask the Geerlings to gaze into their crystal ball: What is over-the-air radio’s path to stay relevant?
A desire for genuine human connection tied directly into Joe’s primary advice for smaller broadcasters.
“Stay small. Small is cool,” Joe advised. “Nobody was going to sit there and say, ‘I’m going to play the same thing as St. Louis’s big rock station, won’t that be cool?’ Listeners could already hear the big stations. Small stations had to be local and if they stopped, they would die.”
As we’ve heard previously, operating a small-town radio station might offer the chance to run a “boutique” style business . Despite his busy schedule with video creation, Jeff has those feelings. He even told us that running a small station would be a dream gig.
But the barrier to entry, he said, ends up a detriment.
“When I look at the licensing fees and the companies that you’d compete with just to get a tiny slice of the pie, it’s just discouraging,” Jeff said.
But despite the red tape and the uncertain future of the AM band, the Geerlings are optimistic about the underlying technology and the medium itself.
“I think that there’s always room for broadcasting with RF just like in TV,” Jeff concluded. “The only way it can die is if the industry kills it, not if people stop listening. People stop caring if the industry doesn’t care.”
If the father-and-son duo in St. Louis are still infatuated with the medium, that feels like the best vote of confidence we could have.

articles.title_orig: Namibia takes step towards nuclear power
articles.title_zh: Namibia takes step towards nuclear power
articles.content_orig:
In an announcement from the Office of the Prime Minister, John Titus, a Director in the Department of Energy in the Ministry of Industries, Mines and Energy, has been named as Namibia's Nuclear Commissioner. As well as coordinating the technical programme of the Nuclear Energy Programme Implementing Organisation (NEPIO) and heading its Secretariat, Titus's appointment establishes a central focal point for coordinating the country's nuclear energy preparatory work.
"The decision to support a long-term nuclear power programme is a decision to invest in the institutional, technical and human capacity required to prepare Namibia for its future energy needs," Prime Minister Tjitunga Elijah Ngurare said.
Ngurare has also constituted the NEPIO Management Committee to provide "high-level policy coordination and strategic oversight". Made up of executive directors from the Office of the Prime Minister, the Ministry of Industries, Mines and Energy, the Ministry of International Relations and Trade, the Ministry of Health and Social Services, and the National Planning Commission, and guided by the International Atomic Energy Agency, the NEPIO Management Committee will assess issues ranging from nuclear safety and security to financing, radioactive waste management, environmental protection, human resource capacity, nuclear power and public engagement.
Namibia holds about 7% of the world's uranium reserves, and has a long history of uranium mining: the Rössing uranium mine has marked 50 years of production this year. The country's 2024 uranium production of 7333 tU made it the world's third largest producer behind Kazakhstan and Canada.
Namibia's domestic electricity production is currently dominated by hydro, and the country relies heavily on imports of electricity, mainly from South Africa.
The Namibian government approved its first Nuclear Industry Strategy in October 2025, and earlier this year a draft nuclear bill - replacing the 2005 Atomic Energy and Radiation Protection Act and establishing a nuclear commission, a nuclear institute and an independent regulatory authority - underwent nationwide public consultation.
"Namibia's substantial uranium resources have strengthened the case for exploring nuclear energy as part of efforts to secure the country's long-term energy needs, promote local mineral beneficiation and value addition, and unlock greater economic value from its natural resources," according to the Office of the Prime Minister.

articles.content_orig:
Chairman and CEO Letter to Shareholders
Creating thriving communities together

Veteran’s Unconventional Path to Landing her Dream Job in Tech
U.S. Army Veteran Ashley Wigfall transitioned to a civilian role and charted her path to technologist through mentorship and skills training at the JPMorgan Chase tech hub in Plano, Texas.
Chairman and CEO Letter to Shareholders
Why we built our Center for Energy and the Environment
The world needs more energy. That energy will help power factories, deploy AI, electrify the economy, and expand energy access. Meeting that demand while balancing affordability, security, reliability, and sustainability, what we call the "Four Forces,” is one of the defining economic opportunities of our era.
In 2021, JPMorganChase set ambitious targets to help us seize that opportunity: our portfolio-level carbon intensity targets and our $2.5 trillion Sustainable Development Target. We are helping increase supply by facilitating nearly $100 billion each year to add new energy from all sources. We are also helping decarbonize: our tax-oriented investing team alone has helped finance one in four gigawatts of U.S. renewables and storage. For more than 125 years, we have banked companies that help build and power the global economy, and we intend to bank companies that help power the world for the next one hundred and twenty five.
We are proud to have helped shape the banking industry’s approach to climate, including as the first U.S. bank to publish detailed financed-emissions targets and an Energy Supply Financing Ratio. Since we set targets, we said that our approach would evolve as conditions changed and better information became available, so we continue to test our approach against experience and evolve as appropriate. We believe that is part of disciplined management.
Based on that belief, we also continue to evolve how we approach energy and environmental issues more broadly. This includes the launch of the JPMorganChase Center for Energy and the Environment (CE&E). CE&E is JPMorganChase's hub for expertise on the Four Forces shaping energy and environmental outcomes. One of the things my team is focused on is our environmental targets, which we have evolved to better reflect how we support low-carbon energy and to reflect updated decarbonization pathways.
Meeting energy demand while balancing affordability, security, reliability, and sustainability, what we call the 'Four Forces,' is one of the defining economic opportunities of our era.
Head of Center for Energy and the Environment and Global Head of Sustainability
The changes to our environmental targets are rooted in the lessons we have learned during the prior five years. And we believe these evolutions sharpen our strategy: helping to mobilize more capital, address the energy system as a whole, and use our platform to help address barriers that financing alone cannot solve.
Here are a few of the lessons we have learned:
Based on these lessons and our belief in the opportunities ahead, we have developed the following principles to guide our approach.
These principles are already changing how we organize, engage, and measure progress.
These principles reflect how we intend to lead: with pragmatism, candor about the trade-offs, and clear focus on helping our clients succeed in a complex and rapidly evolving world. The opportunity in front of us is enormous. Let’s get to work.
For more information on our targets and approach, please refer to Carbon Compass and to our 2025 Sustainability Report .

articles.title_orig: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying
articles.title_zh: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying
articles.content_orig:
FSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defences
Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of spying, in the latest sign of rising tensions between Moscow and Tokyo.
Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai, from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, adding that he had been accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Japan’s foreign ministry summoned the Russian ambassador in Tokyo, Nikolay Nozdrev, over the arrest later on Wednesday.
Imai, a reporter at the newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin, was reportedly preparing to return to Japan when he was arrested for allegedly collecting information on Russia’s defence capabilities, according to Russia’s Tass news agency.
Russia’s FSB security agency claimed the journalist had intended to pass the information on to Japanese intelligence.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Japan’s foreign ministry urged Moscow to extend “fair and impartial treatment” to the detained journalist. “The Japanese embassy … in Moscow and the consulate general in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk lodged a request with the Russian authorities for the prompt provision of information, as well as for humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” an official told Agence France-Presse.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said in a statement that it was aware of the announcement by Russian authorities but it was “still confirming the details”.
“Ensuring the safety of the journalist is our top priority, and we are responding accordingly,” it said.
Imai’s arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over sovereignty of islands belonging to the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido.
Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war ⁠in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap .
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kurils have been under Russian control since the end of the second world war, when Soviet forces seized the islands in the final days of the conflict, forcing about 17,000 Japanese citizens to leave and, over time, replacing them with a similar number of Russians.
In 2022, Moscow scrapped a programme that allowed former residents to travel to the islands to visit the graves of their ancestors in protest at Japan’s support for Ukraine.
Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an ​uproar in Japan . Tokyo has ‌said it would continue ​implementing sanctions against ​Russia and supporting Ukraine.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

At the beginning of Q3, in Week 27, prices were relatively low at NOK 65.93 (USD, 6.91, EUR 6.18) and volumes sat at 58 metric tons (MT). articles.title_orig: The Iran war's unexpected impact on US defenses against China threat downplayed by top Army leader
articles.title_zh: The Iran war's unexpected impact on US defenses against China threat downplayed by top Army leader
articles.content_orig:
Gatestone Institute senior fellow Gordon Chang warns that Beijing's military buildup and cyberattacks on Taiwan are designed for intimidation. Chang explains that leadership vacancies within the Chinese Communist Party's Central Military Commission leave the military unready for a full-scale invasion of the main island. These aggressive actions from China are stiffening Taiwanese opposition rather than forcing submission.
Amid growing concerns that the Iran war is drawing away critical U.S. defenses from China's doorstep, the Army's top commander in the Pacific says the forces are using this unexpected opportunity to modernize.
Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific, provided his assessment that diverting Patriot missile defenses to the Iran war has not increased risk to forces in the Indo-Pacific despite concerns about deployments impacting America's readiness for potential conflict with China.
"Actually, it's given us an opportunity to modernize our systems here," Clark told Fox News Digital during a small-group interview at the Association of the United States Army's annual conference in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday.
Patriot systems have been redeployed from the Indo-Pacific to support operations in the Middle East, while U.S. forces in South Korea have also sent Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors to the region.
U.S. Army Gen. Ronald Clark, commanding general of U.S. Army Pacific, speaks with NSS guests during National Security Seminar Week at the U.S. Army War College in Carlisle, Pa., June 4, 2026. (Elizabeth Bukowski/US Army War College)
An October Congressional Research Service report cited estimates that U.S. forces had expended roughly 1,700 Patriot and 200 THAAD interceptors during the conflict, while the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the military had used between half and two-thirds of certain interceptor inventories. The Pentagon's inspector general has cited strategic inventory shortfalls and manufacturing bottlenecks stemming from the conflict, raising questions about how quickly the U.S. could replenish its defenses in the event of another major confrontation.
Clark said the deployments are giving Patriot crews firsthand experience defending against enemy attacks, while equipment upgrades are expanding what individual batteries can accomplish.
He said an upgraded Patriot battery can now provide coverage that previously required an entire battalion, though he did not specify whether he was referring to geographic coverage or the number of threats the system can engage.
Asked whether recent diplomatic progress between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping had changed his assessment of the threat from China, Clark said he believes the People's Liberation Army (PLA) is continuing its build-up.
"Well, I believe they're continuing to prepare," Clark said.
XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT
U.S. President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of a bilateral meeting at Gimhae Air Base on October 30, 2025 in Busan, South Korea. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
The assessment comes weeks after Trump welcomed Xi to Washington for a high-profile state visit that produced new trade agreements and commitments to improve military communications. But the diplomatic progress has not resolved tensions over Taiwan and China's growing military reach across the Indo-Pacific, where American commanders continue preparing for a potential conflict.
Clark did not say whether China's military preparations had accelerated or whether diplomatic outreach had changed Beijing's intentions. He emphasized that the U.S. military's responsibility is to remain ready for a potential conflict while working to prevent one.
TAIWAN ANALYSTS SAY TRUMP-XI SUMMIT PRODUCED NO POLICY SHIFT BUT REAL TEST LIES AHEAD
"Hopefully my legacy in this job is that when we walk away from command of USARPAC, that the deterrent posture of our command is such that we have not just prevented war, but we're preventing war in the future," Clark said.
Clark said Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, recently discussed reviving disaster-management exchanges between the U.S. Army and China's PLA during talks with his Chinese counterpart.
The exchanges would provide an opportunity for American and Chinese military personnel to work together on disaster response, restoring a channel of direct engagement that Clark said he hoped to see revived.
"If you're able to have a conversation with your adversaries, you're able to share information with them in a way that makes them not want to fight," Clark said.
A Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel, labeled DA-BFAR MMOV 3015, navigates in close proximity to another ship during a maritime encounter. (Chinese Coast Guard)
He said U.S. Army Pacific would be responsible for coordinating the exchanges with its Chinese counterparts if the effort moves forward. He did not announce a date or say that Beijing had formally agreed to resume the program.
The U.S. and Chinese militaries have periodically conducted disaster-management exchanges in the past, including an event hosted by the Army at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state in 2017.
"The cost of going to war is just so high that it's our duty to, one, be absolutely prepared for that eventuality, but two, to prevent that from happening," Clark said.
The diplomatic outreach comes amid continued confrontations between Chinese and Philippine forces in the South China Sea. As Fox News Digital previously reported, the Philippines tracked 101 Chinese navy and coast guard vessels around disputed waters in September, nearly double the number recorded in August. More recently, Philippine authorities accused Chinese forces of obstructing maritime operations and carrying out dangerous maneuvers near Philippine aircraft.
CHINESE MILITARY ACTIVITY NEARLY DOUBLES AROUND KEY US ALLY IN DISPUTED WATERS
Meanwhile, the Army has been expanding its capabilities across the Indo-Pacific, positioning additional forces and equipment closer to potential flashpoints as part of its effort to deter Chinese aggression.
China launched rockets near Taiwan during massive live-fire drills, surrounding the island with warships, aircraft and military pressure as tensions rise. (PLA Eastern Theater Command via Reuters)
Clark said the Army now has more resources committed to the region than at any previous point in his career, including additional divisions, a corps headquarters and specialized formations designed to conduct long-range strikes and operations across multiple domains.
"The Army is now better resourced in the Pacific than I've ever seen it," he said.
He pointed to the Army's growing ability to support naval and air operations, including land-based weapons capable of striking targets at sea.

Clark said recent military war games have demonstrated the importance of those capabilities, including one maritime scenario in which the addition of Army forces changed an unfavorable outcome.
"It's really tied to existing capabilities we have," Clark said, citing the Army's ability to detect targets, conduct strikes, protect military assets and sustain operations from land.

articles.title_orig: Apple's new hardware strategy capitalizes on trust — just in time for the AI era
articles.title_zh: Apple's new hardware strategy capitalizes on trust — just in time for the AI era
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Apple household just got a new lineup. On Tuesday, the company unveiled several new smart home devices , including the HomeView hub, the HomePod Mini 2, and Apple TV 4K.
The company's new releases are a clear pivot in its corporate strategy. Not only is it trying its hand at smart home products once again after its HomePod failure, but Apple and its accelerating hardware releases show new CEO John Ternus's ambitious strategy as a company meeting the AI era head-on.
Tim Cook was Mr. Services, growing that business massively. But Ternus is clearly saying, why not both?
Finally, it seems, Apple has figured out a new way to take its "walled garden" design philosophy — a closed, safe ecosystem that favors trust, its signature design language, and vetted partners — and apply it to the home, putting its customers literally inside it.
You can see how this is low-hanging fruit for the company. Securing your home and your physical safety is already a big business that involves iPhones and Apple Watches. Why not directly capitalize on it, further monetizing its seamlessness and trust?
After all, its privacy record looks very different than , say, the Amazon Ring privacy record . One can only imagine Apple has thought of that, even if trumpeting the contrast would be too low a blow for the company's advertising style.
It's clear also that Apple's smart home strategy echoes its approach to AI, which we argued recently positions its brand of trust front and center . At the heart of both experiences is your iPhone, the quarterback for your AI-enabled smart assistant, but also all your domestic gadgets: the new indoor and outdoor cameras, thermostats, temperature sensors, the video doorbell, and the door lock.
The new lineup gives people more reasons to put Apple's hardware in their home and their routines. The other side of this is more subtle: For every app integration and product purchase, customers might find it harder to leave the pleasures of Apple's garden. There isn't any AI-first alternative to an iPhone just yet. But if one emerges, it'll have to pry Apple's consumers out of a deeper hole — which could buy time for Cupertino to come up with an answer.
All this shows that while other tech companies are busy expounding on their LLMs, Apple is clearly in a totally different conversation. Superintelligence and everything else in the AI debate might as well be unfolding on another planet. The company's vision, in its marketing of new hardware and its design ethos, is selling relief from home-based chaos and is ready to harness whatever AI capabilities emerge to tame and smooth our lives.
Apple isn't strictly selling AI hardware, but rather touting its ecosystem, its walled garden. Won't you step inside?
Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban .

articles.title_orig: Your Galaxy Watch is about to become a whole lot better
articles.title_zh: Your Galaxy Watch is about to become a whole lot better
articles.content_orig:
It will then build a tailored four- to eight-week program based on your goals and habits.
Samsung Health has offered Sleep Coaching for several years, but using it required a full week of consecutive sleep data in a month. With this new update, the app will let users start Sleep Coaching faster and provide more personalized sleep guidance. The update also brings a few new features for runners.
With the new version, anyone using a Galaxy Watch 4 series or later model (or the Galaxy Fit 3 or Galaxy Ring) can start Sleep Coaching with just three days of sleep data from the past two weeks.
When setting it up, you need to fill out a survey around your sleep regularity and interruptions, along with alcohol and caffeine intake. It will also ask you to rate how satisfied you are with your sleep. Using your survey responses and three days of data, Health will assign you a personalized Sleep Animal symbol and tailor a four- to eight-week coaching program to your goals.
As you progress, the app will adjust its weekly recommendations to your changing sleep patterns, while tracking your daily sleep satisfaction. It will also provide daily habit checklists and sleep tips, like avoiding screens and caffeine before bed or stretching outdoors after waking up—all based on behavioral sleep science.
Users will get more intuitive, detailed analysis reports, with a five-sided Sleep Balance graph showing sleep time, sleep regularity, nighttime wakefulness, sleep satisfaction and an "Energy Score" to highlight areas needing attention. It also provides daily morning insight messages that review your previous night's sleep and offer helpful tips.
Samsung is also boosting its Running Coach app for a more "dynamic and connected training experience." Tiers have expanded from 10 to 12 levels to better support intermediate and advanced runners, allowing them to set higher benchmarks and challenge themselves.
The app is also adding enhanced social media sharing for milestones, personal records and route highlights, along with a new partnership with the fitness platform Strava. "Users can import their favorite Strava Routes for running, trail running, and cycling directly into Samsung Health," the company said. The new features will begin rolling out this month.

articles.title_zh: Amazon rainforest wrecker and world’s biggest meat company JBS is now expanding into Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:

TL;DR: JBS – the global meat empire linked to widespread Amazon deforestation – is planning a massive US $5 billion expansion into Southeast Asia, which could threaten the climate, fragile ecosystems and Indigenous lands in Indonesia. Greenpeace Netherlands is taking JBS to court to block the company’s nature destroying expansion – and we need your support to stop them. When you think of global warming, you probably picture smoke billowing from coal power plants or tailpipes of gas-guzzling cars. But behind closed doors, one of the biggest drivers of the climate crisis isn’t an oil company – it’s a global meat dynasty.
You might not know its name, but JBS is the largest meat processor on Earth . JBS has capacity to slaughter tens of thousands of cattle and pigs, and millions of chickens every single day. In doing so, Greenpeace Nordic estimates it pumps out more superheating methane gas than fossil fuel giants ExxonMobil and Shell combined .
For years, investigative reports have linked JBS’s supply chain to massive deforestation in the Amazon rainforest , Indigenous rights violations , and brutal labour conditions . Now, evidence suggests the company is planning the biggest meat sector expansion we know of, setting its sights on new frontiers in Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa .
To understand where JBS is headed, we have to look at the trail it has already left behind.
JBS isn’t just a dominant force in the Americas – it is also Australia’s largest beef processing company .
A recent investigation by the Australian Conservation Foundation (ACF) reports a startling fact: agriculture in Australia now drives more land clearing than palm oil in Indonesia in recent years . Bulldozers routinely flatten native Australian forests to create cattle pastures, the report finds, destroying critical habitats for native wildlife like koalas and washing sediment onto the fragile Great Barrier Reef.
Australia is the world’s second largest beef and bovine meat exporter, after Brazil – and the top one when looking at fresh or chilled beef . About two thirds of Australian beef and veal are exported. If you buy a beef burger at a fast-food chain in Japan, South Korea, or anywhere across East Asia, there is a chance that meal is connected to lost koala habitat in Australia.
Over three quarters of Australian live cattle are exported to Indonesia . Now, JBS wants to take its model even further into Southeast Asia.
JBS plans to combine its entire Australian and New Zealand operations into a new joint-venture with Danantara, Indonesia’s newly formed sovereign wealth fund . Together, they aim to supersize industrial meat production across Southeast Asia.
The proposed joint venture would establish a holding company registered in the Netherlands – a country frequently used as a tax haven and JBS’s corporate headquarters since 2025. The venture aims to raise US $5 billion for further JBS expansion. This almost doubles JBS’s previous known expansion plans, which was already the largest identified industrial meat expansion in the world.
The answer may be connected to Indonesia’s deeply controversial Food and Energy Estate program.
In regions like South Papua, the Indonesian government has reportedly been using state pressure and even its military to terrorise and intimidate Papuans, as it advanced a project to clear millions of hectares of Indigenous land. Officially launched under the banner of “national food security,” the project sparked resistance from Indigenous communities whose ancestral forests, wetlands, and savannahs are threatened by mega-farms for sugarcane, rice, palm oil, and cattle ranching. This was documented by the powerful new documentary ‘ Pig Feast ’, co-produced by Greenpeace Indonesia, which was widely viewed across the country despite reported efforts by Indonesian authorities to prevent it being screened .
A 2025 Greenpeace Indonesia report calculated that clearing just 560,000 hectares for planned sugarcane plantations in South Papua would release 221 million tonnes of CO₂ – the equivalent of driving 48 million cars for a full year. Rapid industrial land clearing also increases the risk of severe droughts, forest fires, water pollution, and widespread flooding.
While official documents have not explicitly named JBS as a direct partner in the Papua project, the timing raises serious questions. Danantara oversees key state enterprises involved in the Food and Energy state program , and JBS’s new joint venture aims to fund and expand multi-protein production through acquisitions and greenfield investments across the region, reportedly initially focused in Indonesia and likely to involve beef, poultry and possibly aquaculture. While Indonesian officials have indicated that the government will stop clearing forests for rice fields – a testament to the courageous resistance of local people – officials have clarified that they are not confirming that all projects in the food estate will be stopped .
Reacting to this, my colleague Kiki Taufik, Global Head of the Indonesian Forest Campaign, stated that “Papua is not a wasteland or a new land bank for industrial expansion; its forests are home to Indigenous Peoples, a source of food and water, a stronghold of biodiversity, and the foundation of Papua’s future.” Kiki went on to call for the government to “halt projects that threaten natural forests, critical ecosystems, and customary territories” and restore so-called “degraded lands”, centering local communities in decision making, instead of imposing extractive activities on these lands, affirming that “there is no path to food sovereignty and sustainable development at the expense of forests, Indigenous Peoples’ rights, and Papua’s future.”
Connecting all these dots reveals a troubling picture: a global meat giant linked to rampant rainforest destruction and Indigenous and labour rights violations partnering with a state fund that is reportedly connected to tropical forest clearance on Indigenous lands with military backing.
Big agricultural corporations often claim that massive industrial farms are necessary to feed growing populations – and that is, predictably, the headline in JBS’s PR about the deal.
However, independent research from groups like IPES-Food and the Alliance for Food Sovereignty in Africa shows that global corporate farming actually threatens food security rather than protecting it.
Why global conglomerates create vulnerability:
Rebuilding our food systems gives us a practical, real-world toolkit for survival in times of increasing instability. True food security and nature resilience do not come from building massive industrial factory farms or handing control of local land and ecosystems to foreign corporations.
When we invest in traditional and nature-friendly farming methods, we can massively cut methane emissions and actively heal the land to prote
