articles.title_orig: Houthi Strike Hits Building at Saudi Aramco Headquarters
articles.title_zh: Houthi Strike Hits Building at Saudi Aramco Headquarters
articles.content_orig:
Missiles and drones have been intercepted over Riyadh after the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.
Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said projectiles targeting the Saudi capital and other cities were intercepted. No casualties have been reported however fires broke out at Saudi oil company Aramco's building in Dhahran after the strike, officials said.
It comes after the coalition struck the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday night.
The latest tit-for-tat attacks in the conflict "have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere", the chief of the the International Monetary Fund said.
The Houthis warned they would target the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.
It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.
Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.
On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.
The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.
A correspondent for AFP news agency reported that queues formed at petrol stations in Sanaa on Tuesday afternoon following the coalition's warning of an impending operation against the al-Sabaha oil facility, with many residents worried about shortages.
The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products".
The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner".
After al-Maliki confirmed the strike, first reported by Houthi media, explosions were heard over Riyadh and other Saudi cities, with al-Maliki reporting four missiles and two drones had been intercepted near the capital.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday the Houthis were "behaving very badly... and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices".
Speaking to reporters, he did not answer a question on whether he'd made a decision to help the Saudis retaliate against them, but said he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children.
More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy adviser: Starlink operations restricted in Ukraine overnight
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy adviser: Starlink operations restricted in Ukraine overnight
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian forces reported restrictions on the military use of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system on Wednesday, saying an overnight change disrupted several drone missions amid escalating tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
The restrictions appear to affect StarShield, the military-grade version of the satellite communications service, with connectivity reportedly cut when terminals move at speeds exceeding approximately 160 kilometres per hour.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on military technology, known as "Flash", said SpaceX had introduced the speed limit overnight without notifying Ukrainian forces.
"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation and this led to the disruption of several missions," Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
Ukrainian volunteer Serhiy Sternenko also reported the disruption, suggesting that SpaceX might have introduced the restrictions at the request of US President Donald Trump's administration.
There is, however, no independent evidence that the White House ordered the change, and the reason for the reported restrictions remains unclear.
The development has raised concerns that access to critical American satellite communications could become another source of leverage over Kyiv, alongside reported US threats to suspend intelligence-sharing unless Ukraine halts its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
According to media reports the Trump administration warned that intelligence cooperation could be curtailed, although Washington has denied suspending intelligence-sharing and Ukrainian officials maintain that cooperation continues.
The timing has also attracted attention following public criticism of Zelenskyy by Elon Musk, the billionaire owner of SpaceX, which operates Starlink.
On Saturday Musk responded to a White House video of Trump criticising Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities, writing on X: "Zelenskyy has gone too far."
The comment came amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Washington and Kyiv, following Trump's agreement with Moscow to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and his demands that Ukraine suspend attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
No connection has been established, however, between the reported Starlink restrictions and the diplomatic dispute.
The reports come amid fresh questions over the reliability of advance intelligence-sharing after Zelenskyy said Ukraine had received no warning from its partners ahead of Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv for a second consecutive night.
The attacks continued despite Trump's declaration of an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv says Moscow has failed to observe.
According to Zelenskyy Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against Kyiv, the surrounding region and Kharkiv overnight, damaging 26 electricity facilities and four oil and gas installations and leaving at least 600,000 people without power.
"Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy wrote on X, accusing Moscow of deliberately targeting infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by Trump.
Despite the growing tensions with Washington Zelenskyy appealed directly to the US president to impose tougher sanctions on Russia and provide additional Patriot missile interceptors.
"We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond and to respond forcefully," he wrote.
The latest developments underscore Ukraine's continued dependence on American intelligence, military technology and air defence support at a time when relations with Washington have become increasingly uncertain.

articles.title_orig: Residents in Saudi Arabia’s capital say they have heard new explosions in Riyadh.
articles.title_zh: Residents in Saudi Arabia’s capital say they have heard new explosions in Riyadh.
articles.content_orig:
A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces said Wednesday they had intercepted an attack from the Iran-backed Houthi militia.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a post on X a ballistic missile "launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh has been intercepted and destroyed."
Earlier, residents in the Saudi capital had reported hearing explosions.
Residents in Saudi Arabia's capital say they have heard new explosions in Riyadh.
The residents spoke on condition of anonymity for their safety. One lives in northern Riyadh, where King Khalid International Airport is located.
The source of the explosions wasn't immediately clear. The Saudi civil defense reported air raid alerts in Riyadh and Kharj province southeast of the capital. Kharj is home to the state-owned Military Industries Corporation and Prince Sultan Air Base.
The airport in Riyadh has been targeted several times in the past week with deadly attacks. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen have claimed responsibility.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi missiles fell on residential areas in Riyadh on Tuesday, injuring four people and damaging 15 homes.
State-run Saudi Press Agency reported the injured included two women, a man and a child. Images released by Saudi's Civil Defense showed broken windows caused by what it said was fallen shrapnel.
The Saudi Ministry of Energy said Tuesday a limited fire broke out in an administrative building in Aramco, one of the world's largest oil facilities, that was targeted in the country's Eastern Province. The ministry said no injuries were reported.
The attack comes as the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi coalition exchanged attacks Tuesday night. It marks a fresh escalation in the widening Middle East crisis and came shortly after the Saudi coalition reported a series of alerts for incoming missiles heading for the country's Eastern Province, a major oil-producing region and the capital Riyadh.
The Saudi-led coalition battling the Iran-backed Houthis confirmed it struck oil sites across western Yemen on Tuesday, including in the capital Sanaa, in response to the deadliest attack on the kingdom's soil in years.
Blasts were heard shortly after in Saudi capital Riyadh and at an oil giant Aramco facility in eastern Saudi Arabia, witnesses and journalists told AFP.
Tuesday's coalition strikes in Yemen's Sanaa and the western provinces of Dhamar and Saada targeted facilities used to "supply the war effort" by the Houthis to "threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and waterways," coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X.
An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said earlier that "Saudi aggression" targeted the oil firm.

articles.title_orig: Russian strikes leave 600,000 without power in Ukraine, Zelensky says
articles.title_zh: Russian strikes leave 600,000 without power in Ukraine, Zelensky says
articles.content_orig:
Watch: What we know about Russia's overnight strikes on Ukraine
Speed restrictions on the key Starlink communications network have disrupted Ukraine's battlefield "missions", President Volodymyr Zelensky's adviser has warned.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said Ukrainian troops had not been informed about the speed limits set overnight at 100mph (160km/h) by Elon Musk's SpaceX company. A source in the Ukrainian defence ministry later confirmed this to the BBC.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to effectively guide drones to Russian targets and also protect Ukrainian skies. SpaceX has not publicly commented.
This comes as at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, Zelensky said.
He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region, and in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv – despite US President Donald Trump's claim on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.
Three people were killed in Kyiv, local officials said. Russia said its "massive" strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
In Wednesday's post on Telegram, Beskrestnov said SpaceX had "implemented overnight a speed limit on Starlink terminals" and this had already resulted in "the disruption of a number of missions".
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," he added.
In the follow-up post, Zelensky's adviser stressed that Starlink was the most effective tool for enabling interceptors to shoot down Russia's newly developed jet-propelled drones.
The Starlink system has become a vital tool to give troops in Ukraine internet access [Reuters]
A source in the Ukrainian defence ministry later told the BBC: "Last night, we detected restrictions affecting Starlink connectivity at speeds above 160 km/h. The source added that the "root cause" of the issue was being investigated.
Defence ministry sources later explained that "once a vehicle or asset exceeds this [160km/h] threshold speed, the terminal loses its connection".
They told the BBC that this made it more difficult to carry out drone operations, "specifically interceptors and middle-strike drones", and also degraded "capabilities for front line logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relaying".
In February, Musk's decision to deny Russian forces access to Starlink blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.
Musk's SpaceX has not commented on the reported speed restrictions.
Zelensky has said the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire. Trump on Tuesday denied that Washington was withholding intelligence.
Overnight, Russia had launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones, and that four of those missiles and 115 drones had been shot down, according to Ukraine's air force.
It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and came as Zelensky prepared to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv.
During the past two nights, ballistic missiles have struck targets in the Ukrainian capital without any warning, before air raid sirens could be sounded.
Ukraine relies on US satellite systems to track Russian missiles in order to issue alerts and to try to shoot them down.
People watched the emergency services at work at the scene of the strikes in Ukraine [Getty Images]
Meanwhile, the Russian defence ministry said 902 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight over a number of Russian regions, including the capital Moscow and Crimea – Ukraine's southern peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014.
On Sunday, Trump wrote in a post on social media: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Zelensky has since repeatedly said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same.
But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Under any truce, he added, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons", enabling it to continue the war.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title_orig: CNBC Daily Open: Zelenskyy heads to UK for talks on fresh support
articles.title_zh: CNBC Daily Open: Zelenskyy heads to UK for talks on fresh support
articles.content_orig:
Hello, this is Justina Lee writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open.
Taiwan has agreed to purchase 30% of gas sourced from a proposed liquefied natural gas project in Alaska, according to U.S. President Donald Trump.
The latest economic data coming out of Asia on Wednesday offers clues to the region's growth outlook, with China's producer prices rising at its fastest pace in over four years.
Meanwhile, over in Europe, the U.K. is set to host Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
U.S. President Trump said at a rally that Taiwan has agreed to purchase 30% of gas sourced from a proposed liquefied natural gas project in Alaska, adding that the deal "guarantees a success."
Trump has been increasing pressure on South Korea to participate in the project, cautioning earlier that he would charge the country more and threaten to double charges if Seoul failed to sign soon. South Korean media outlets speculated that Trump was referring to higher tariffs.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to host Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as European leaders rally to show support for the country. Zelenskyy will reportedly meet with EU leaders on Friday, on the second day of the European Council summit.
Burnham is expected to tell Zelenskyy that he has asked his ministers to draw up further sanctions, military support and fiscal packages to provide urgent support in the coming weeks.
It comes after Russia unleashed an attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions.
ASML , a bellwether for the global chip industry, posted its third-quarter results on Wednesday. The Dutch semiconductor equipment maker said that some of its customers are expressing interest in placing orders for its critical semiconductor tools for 2029 and 2030 as AI demand remains buoyant.
The comments will likely comfort investors who have been looking to assess the longer-term demand outlook for ASML's lithography machines.
On Wednesday, traders continue to digest the latest economic data coming out of Asia, as they look for clues about the region's economic outlook.
China's producer prices in September rose at its fastest pace in over four years, due to higher fuel prices driving costs up for businesses.
Data out of Singapore on Wednesday showed that GDP growth softened to 5.4% in the third quarter, after hitting a four-year high in the prior quarter. A decline in the city-state's manufacturing sector contributed to the slowdown, though this was offset by an expansion in the construction sector.
Over in the Philippines, the country's central bank is bracing itself for a "Godzilla" El Niño , which is exacerbating the effects of a prolonged oil shock, as it tries to tame inflation from three-year highs.
Meanwhile, Korean automaker Hyundai Motor revealed it is planning a "strategic" $15.5 billion investment in the country by 2032. The company said India is a strategic core market to the firm's emerging-market growth and expansion plans.
In the oil markets, Brent and WTI prices rose Wednesday amid concerns over supply disruptions as tensions in the Middle East continue to heat up between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
Judge indefinitely blocks Trump White House from banning 3 media outlets
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., late Tuesday night issued an order indefinitely blocking the White House from enforcing the ban on three media outlets announced by President Donald Trump in mid-September.
The preliminary injunction by Judge Timothy Kelly extends his existing block on Trump's ban of MS NOW , CNN and Politico from the White House complex.
Kelly, in a written opinion, said the three outlets were likely to succeed on a claim in their lawsuit challenging the ban that they were denied due process by Trump having summarily ordered them barred from the White House without a chance to argue against that action first.

Charles is a writer for Oilprice.com
A surge in energy costs is expected to drive overall U.S. consumer inflation higher, with September numbers seen at 0.6% on a monthly basis by economists polled by Reuters. The official CPI data for September is due out later today.
Gasoline prices in the United States went up by 7.1% last month, with the latest daily average national price at $4.3413 per gallon, according to AAA . This is close to what the average was a month ago, with the difference at $0.028 per gallon. Diesel prices, however, remain stubbornly high, at above $6 per gallon, although they are off their all-time high of over $6.50 per gallon.
Another Reuters poll suggested that well over two-thirds of Americans, or 78%, are blaming Trump policies for the rise in the cost of living. Among specific policies, respondents in the poll noted the war in Iran and tariffs on imports.
“People care about food and energy. That's what they feel every day,” according to Sung Won Sohn, professor of finance and economics at Loyola Marymount University, who spoke to Reuters. “Many voters are at the lower leg of the K-shaped economy. They are suffering because of higher energy and food prices, and I assume that will have an impact on the election results, as a lot of people seem to think.”
The K-shaped economy concept describes a situation where one part of the economy grows while another shrinks, with the different parts essentially moving in opposite directions.
In further data on U.S. inflation, Reuters reported that the reading for the 12 months to September stood at 3.6%, significantly higher than the Fed’s 2% target. Core inflation, which excludes energy and food prices, was also higher than the Fed’s target for the 12 months to September, but at a much more moderate 2.4%.

articles.title_orig: NEURA Robotics Introduces Neuron AI: The Brain of the Physical World
articles.title_zh: NEURA Robotics Introduces Neuron AI: The Brain of the Physical World
articles.content_orig:
NEURA Robotics (“NEURA”) today introduced Neuron AI, its multimodal foundation model for Physical AI. Combining 3D vision, touch, audio, robot state and language with memory, Neuron AI enables robots to act on information beyond what cameras alone can capture, as well as retain relevant context when objects disappear from view. Its Perception-Language-Action (PLA) architecture connects what a robot sees, hears and feels with what it has already done, turning multisensory information into physical action.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261013482085/en/
Neuron AI: The Brain of the Physical World
“An intelligent robot needs a brain that brings its senses together and remembers what happened,” said David Reger, Founder and CEO of NEURA Robotics . “With Neuron AI, we are building the brain of the physical world: Physical AI that turns human expertise and physical experience into capabilities robots can learn and apply. Developed in Germany, built for the world.”
Multimodal by design: how Neuron AI perceives the physical world
Cameras capture geometry, color and position, but provide no information about contact, force or sound. Humans also rely on more than sight: they feel whether a screw has caught and hear when a connector clicks into place. Neuron AI applies this principle to robots. Rather than treating each sensor as a separate input, the model encodes 3D vision, tactile and force data, audio, robot state and language, aligns them in one shared space over time, and turns them into a single stream of action.
Multisensory perception matters most for tasks that cameras cannot solve on their own. When a robot opens a lock, only sound and touch confirm that it is really open. With touch, a robot can grasp objects it cannot see. The additional senses also improve tasks that vision can already handle: in welding, for example, the quality of a seam can be judged from the sound of the process.
In addition, Neuron AI has a memory function. To act in the physical world, a robot needs a sense of cause and effect and object permanence, the ability to remember objects when they are out of sight, which humans acquire in their first two years of life. Unlike purely digital AI, a robot acts in a continuous physical world and must keep track of objects and the consequences of its own actions over time, often without seeing them. NEURA adapted the model’s architecture specifically to introduce memory and trains it on dedicated datasets that make use of it.
Three data pillars, one model for every embodiment
Neuron AI is trained on three complementary sources of physical experience:
Together, these pillars combine real physical interactions, simulated variation and human know-how to train a shared foundation across five NEURA robot embodiments, with different grippers and hands.
From learning a skill to deploying it across a fleet
The NEURA Gyms connect data collection, skill training and benchmarking before deployment. Training data and skills developed in the Gyms inform subsequent model releases.
The Neuraverse provides the platform for deploying and updating these capabilities across robot fleets. It also gives customers tools to fine-tune the model for their own tasks, turning process expertise into robot skills. Customers can keep their skills private. Where they choose to share skills or deployment data, those contributions can support the wider ecosystem and future model development. This makes Time-to-Skill a central measure of progress: how quickly a robot can learn a new task and perform it reliably. For industrial customers, shortening that time is essential to bringing Physical AI into more processes and adapting it as requirements change.
Physical AI built in Germany
Neuron AI was developed and trained in-house in Metzingen, Germany. NEURA brings together the robots, hands, sensing technology, data infrastructure and AI development needed to connect model training with physical performance. Germany’s industrial base provides an important setting for this work: complex manufacturing processes, specialized expertise and demanding operating environments. Data partnerships with industrial companies including Schaeffler and Bosch complement training in the NEURA Gyms. For NEURA, this proximity connects the development of Physical AI with the knowledge and practical requirements of the industries it is intended to serve.
Live demonstration at NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026
At NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026, NEURA will demonstrate its humanoid robot 4NE1 (“For Anyone”) performing an eleven-minute laundry-handling sequence with the current version of Neuron AI. The sequence includes sorting laundry, loading a washing machine, closing and reopening it, unloading it and transferring the laundry to a dryer, without human intervention. The demonstration focuses on handling and task coordination within the laundry process. The challenge extends beyond any individual movement. The robot must carry relevant context through the sequence, complete each step and transition to the next. It brings NEURA’s architecture into one tangible example: planning, multisensory perception, memory and physical action working together. Visitors can see the demonstration at Station-Berlin, Hall 3, Booth #3031, from October 20 to 22.
More information on Neuron AI: https://neura-robotics.com/neuron-ai
NEURA was founded on the conviction that the next great technological revolution will not take place on screens, but in the physical world. As aging societies, labor shortages and the growing demand for skilled work reshape economies worldwide, Physical AI is becoming indispensable to safeguarding productivity, prosperity and quality of life.
Founded in 2019 and headquartered in Metzingen, Germany, NEURA Robotics is a global Physical AI company developing the technologies that enable intelligent machines to learn, adapt and work side by side with people in the real world. The company develops cognitive robots that can see, hear, feel and learn, as well as the software, AI and data infrastructure required to deploy them at scale.
A large share of global gross domestic product is generated today through physical work. NEURA's mission is to make physical work scalable, drastically shortening the time it takes to teach machines new skills and deploy them worldwide. With its cognitive robots, the NEURA Gyms and the Neuraverse , an open ecosystem in which robots continuously learn and share skills, the company is building the foundation for a future in which intelligent machines help to solve some of humanity's greatest challenges. NEURA Robotics builds Physical AI from Europe, together for the world.

articles.title_orig: Initiative seeks wider water access and UN votes on new world map | D+C - Development + Cooperation
articles.title_zh: Initiative seeks wider water access and UN votes on new world map | D+C - Development + Cooperation
articles.content_orig:
Between 2015 and 2024, more than 960 million people gained access to safe drinking water and 1.2 billion to safe sanitation. This is undoubtedly a success. Nevertheless, according to the World Bank, 2.1 billion people still lack access to safe drinking water – a situation made even worse due to the water scarcity associated with climate change.
During World Water Week in Stockholm at the end of August, one campaign attracted particular attention: Water Forward, a World Bank-led initiative that aims to improve access to water for 1 billion people by 2030. Described as the most promising initiative in decades for attracting financing and political attention to the WASH (water, sanitation and hygiene) sector, the programme was launched in April and frames water as an economic asset.
The UN General Assembly has adopted a resolution calling for the introduction of a world map that more accurately reflects the actual proportions of the continents. The resolution, introduced by Togo and other member states of the African Union, is aimed in particular at depicting the size of the African continent more accurately. The widely used Mercator projection, developed in the 16th century for European navigators, distorts the proportions because of the way the curved surface of the Earth is transferred onto a flat map: regions near the poles consequently appear oversised, while regions close to the equator appear smaller than they actually are. Now that Africa appears larger on the map, it might be easier for the US Department of State (or rather, the AI it uses) to correctly assign African territories to the right countries on presentation slides in future. At the AIDS 2026 Conference in Rio de Janeiro in July, it used a heavily distorted, AI-generated map of Africa on which all the highlighted countries were incorrectly labelled and positioned. That optimism is tempered, however, by the fact that the United States was the only nation to vote against the non-binding resolution.

articles.title_orig: Ebara Elliott Energy secures world’s first type approval for liquid hydrogen cargo pumps
articles.title_zh: Ebara Elliott Energy secures world’s first type approval for liquid hydrogen cargo pumps
articles.content_orig:
By Energy Connects Brand Studio
The global transition toward a low‑carbon energy economy is no longer a distant vision; it is an active engineering imperative. As industries worldwide scale up green hydrogen infrastructure to decarbonise heavy transport, power generation, and manufacturing, maritime transport remains a vital link in the global energy supply chain. Transporting liquid hydrogen (LH 2 ) across oceans requires maintaining extreme cryogenic conditions at -253°C, presenting unmatched technical and operational challenges for maritime developers.
Ebara Elliott Energy (EEE) has secured the world’s first Type Approval certification for liquid hydrogen cargo pumps designed for maritime carriers. This landmark achievement shifts global supply chain standards away from unverified equipment testing on active vessels toward globally certified, pre‑validated infrastructure solutions.
Type approval vs. individual approval
To grasp the magnitude of this achievement, it is essential to compare type approval with the traditional maritime benchmark, individual approval. Under individual approval, a marine inspector must physically witness and certify every manufactured unit upon shipboard installation. Until now, conventional cargo pumps installed on pioneering liquid hydrogen carriers relied on individual approvals due to a lack of land‑based, real‑liquid test facilities. Their true performance and reliability were only discovered after the ship entered active service.
If an unproven pump malfunctions at sea, operators face severe consequences: disrupted schedules, costly downtime, and financial losses caused by unexpected boil‑off gas. In contrast, type approval certifies the fundamental design, structural integrity and performance specifications through comprehensive advance testing. Acquiring type approval proves that the engineering design itself is safe, robust, and reliable before equipment reaches a shipyard. For developers and operators, this pre‑validation eliminates shipboard risks, guarantees consistent manufacturing quality, simplifies inspections, and shortens delivery timelines.
Engineering breakthroughs at -253°C
Securing the world’s first type approval required exhaustive, long‑term performance, and durability trials using actual liquid hydrogen at extreme cryogenic temperatures. Historically, obtaining type approval for LH 2 cargo pumps was impossible because no facility could perform long‑term liquid hydrogen pump testing. EEE overcame this barrier by utilising a newly established, large‑scale liquid hydrogen test facility at EEE’s facility in Futtsu, Japan. Through rigorous real‑world condition testing, EEE proved its pump capabilities under extreme conditions, a ground-breaking achievement.
“Acquiring the world’s first type approval for an LH 2 cargo pump completely eliminates a critical risk for the global hydrogen transport economy,” said Shane Reph, Deputy Chief Executive Officer and Chief Operating Officer at Ebara Elliott Energy. “By validating our technology on land under real‑world operating conditions, we give maritime developers complete confidence from the design stage onward. This upfront proof guarantees equipment reliability while eliminating costly rework and operational risks that typically plague shipboard pre‑commissioning.”
Accelerating the global hydrogen roadmap
This breakthrough provides EEE with a decisive competitive advantage in the energy transition. By mitigating maritime risks and guaranteeing equipment performance prior to installation, EEE offers clean energy supply chain operators unprecedented peace of mind and operational security. The achievement is expected to accelerate infrastructure deployment across regions aggressively building liquefied hydrogen trade routes, including Japan, South Korea, Australia, the Middle East, and the European Union.
Moving forward, EEE will expand its certified portfolio to cover a wider range of flow rates and differential heads, ensuring the company maintains technical leadership across global maritime requirements. By setting a new industry standard, EEE not only strengthens its position in turbomachinery but also advances the broader hydrogen economy, enabling safe, reliable, and scalable maritime transport of liquid hydrogen.

articles.title_orig: How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state
articles.title_zh: How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state
articles.content_orig:
Drawing on dozens of interviews with intelligence and police officers across two continents, a Guardian investigation reveals the murderous cost of our insatiable appetite for cocaine
Read more: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’ Explainer: What is state capture and why does it matter?
As abductions go, few have been more brazen. Alan Jalloh was with two friends outside Goodies supermarket, frantic as usual with late afternoon shoppers. Rush hour in downtown Freetown, Sierra Leone’s capital, was under way with familiar gusto.
A black Toyota Rav4 forced its way through the Peninsula highway traffic. Witnesses describe burly white men leaping out, yanking on balaclavas. Jalloh, 40, seemed to freeze. As did his two friends, one a famous Freetown footballer. All three were dragged into the waiting SUV. None of them have been seen since.
Two days later, on 25 October 2025, another three men disappeared. Within a week, nine people had been seized from the city’s streets, most in broad daylight. They were dismembered, police sources were told. At least one was beheaded. An officer investigating Jalloh’s abduction, says: “They were exterminated to hide the truth.”
No bodies have been found.
Five months after Jalloh disappeared, an ageing cargo ship, the Arconian , left Freetown. By May, it was navigating savage seas 100 miles off the coast of Morocco when Spanish civil guards boarded. Lucas Fernández*, clutching his assault rifle on the ship’s lower deck, stumbled across figures in the Arconian’s darkened cargo hold.
Fernández raised his gun, finger on the trigger. A man pointed an assault rifle back at him. Time stood still. Fernández says the man became agitated, yelling in English, incomprehensible above the storm outside. “It was crazy,” Fernández says.
Within minutes, he and his fellow officers had disarmed six gunmen found hiding in the bowels of the ship. Nearby, were 1,279 bales of cocaine wrapped in plastic; weighing between 30 and 45 tonnes, it is the largest amount of the drug ever seized.
Seventeen days later, the audience at Oxford University rose to applaud the guest speaker. Julius Maada Bio had nailed it once again. His address – eulogising robust leadership – was the latest in a whirlwind year for the president of Sierra Leone.
The chair of Ecowas – the Economic Union of West African States , a region home to more than 400 million people, Bio is among the most influential African voices in the UN. The EU sees Bio as one of its most reliable allies in Africa and has a long history of showering the impoverished country with aid stretching back more than 45 years .
But the most important figure in Sierra Leone is not this ambitious politician, but the man who ordered the abduction of Jalloh; the man responsible for the Arconian’s monumental cocaine stash. A man called Jos Leijdekkers . He also happens to be Bio’s son-in-law.
At 35, Leijdekkers is Europe’s pre-eminent cocaine baron . Intelligence assessments credit the Dutchman with importing volumes vast enough to repeatedly crash Europe’s cocaine market. Last year, he halved the drug’s wholesale price. Multiple intelligence sources confirm he has also transformed Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state.
“It is state capture by a criminal network on a scale never seen,” says a western official.
At least 14 people have been killed inside Sierra Leone on Leidjekkers’ orders. High-ranking police are believed to have been murdered on his say-so. Officers have fled the country fearing they will be next.
“If you get in his way, he wipes you out,” says an intelligence source.
Like most, they spoke on condition of anonymity, aware of Leidjekkers’ capacity to reach those who cross him.
Sierra Leone’s fate is a tale of western duplicity. Despite detailed intelligence of the extraordinary volumes of cocaine being exported to Europe , the EU continued to woo Bio and his government. The UN did the same: overlooking its own evidence.
And intelligence sources warn that Leijdekkers’ network is rapidly expanding. “The entire west Africa region is at risk,” says a Dutch official.
Leijdekkers’ prodigious transcontinental network brings deadly violence.
Dozens of his gunmen descended on a sleepy Dutch village last month intent on retribution. A European police source said: “We’ve had cocaine disputes before, but nothing like this. We’ve entered a new era.”
The first recorded sighting of Leijdekkers in west Africa came in October 2022. A six-vehicle convoy thundered down Aberdeen Road, towards Lumley beach, leaving Freetown traffic police baffled. No one had briefed they were expecting VIPs. “‘The convoy was bigger than our president’s,” says one officer.
Unaware of Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker, Freetown police were sufficiently concerned to begin surveillance on the mysterious convoy, which had stopped outside the Sky Bar , a nightlife institution in the city.
At 4am, the group were trailed to a waterfront house near Hamilton beach. There, the covert surveillance team were stunned: revellers included their own bosses.
At the time, western intelligence agencies had no idea of Leijdekkers’ whereabouts. One of Europe’s most wanted men had simply vanished. For years, authorities had tracked his rise in the Dutch underworld, watching how the local hitman from the well-heeled town of Prinsenbeek accrued key contacts for transatlantic cocaine shipments.
When Dutch intelligence traced Leijdekkers to Sierra Leone in 2024, he had created something remarkable: a sprawling cocaine empire from scratch.
“He’s very adept at adaptation, cultivating ties,” says an official. “A new country, but he won over its most influential people.”
That included marrying the president’s daughter, Agnes Bio, and starting a family. Sierra Leone’s top officials partied with the moneyed new guy. Immigration chiefs secured him a diplomatic passport. The person whose job it was to investigate cocaine traffickers became a drinking buddy.
Leijdekkers’ wealth corrupted. According to intelligence, he was generating a $150m (£113m) monthly profit – greater than the running cost of Sierra Leone’s entire state.
Hundreds of people were on his payroll, say sources, including senior military and police figures. But what Leijdekkers coveted most was Freetown’s seaport: the Queen Elizabeth II Quay, perfectly sited between cocaine-producing South America and Europe’s booming markets.
In August 2023, his wife’s uncle, Yankuba Bio, became head of the port. Yankuba Bio denies a close relationship with “any individual called or identified as Jos Leijdekkers”. Sources, though, say port officials on Leijdekkers’s payroll make $2,000 a month – more than 30 times the national average .
In January 2025, the Dutch sent an extradition request to Sierra Leone for the fugitive, who had been sentenced in absentia to more than 100 years in prison for crimes including attempted murder.
Sierra Leone denied knowing the man. For Leijdekkers, it was a defining moment: he had state protection. His confidence culminated in the arrival into Freetown’s port on 18 April of the Arconian, a green cargo vessel the length of a football pitch. Over the next four days, about 30 tonnes of cocaine were hauled onboard, according to western intelligence.
“From experience, the maximum you can hide is eight tonnes. Thirty tonnes says you’re operating in plain sight,” says a UN agent. Yankuba Bio says such claims are “false, completely untrue and without foundation” adding that the port “does not engage in or facilitate the export” of cocaine.
On 26 April, a cryptic tip-off electrified European investigators. An unidentified vessel had left west Africa carrying 18 tonnes of cocaine, the second-largest such cargo identified in Europe.
Within 70 hours, the Arconian had been identified. At 8pm on 1 May, with the vessel pitching in brutal, black seas, Fernández, of Spain’s civil guard central operational unit , was first onboard.

articles.title_orig: Trump says "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is "getting ready to begin"
articles.title_zh: Trump says "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is "getting ready to begin"
articles.content_orig:
President Trump said Wednesday that "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration is preparing to begin in Greenland.
In a statement posted on his Truth Social platform, Mr. Trump said "Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland," but did not give more details.
The president added that "there are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World."
Mr. Trump also touted Greenland's role in the defense of the United States in Europe, saying that "any future attack" on the U.S. would have to come across the semi-autonomous island, "where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet conceived."
"It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!" Mr. Trump added.
The announcement comes more than four weeks after the U.S., Greenland and Denmark, which oversees the territory, signed a new security agreement to bolster American military and security presence on the island.
That agreement, which gives the U.S. broad access to the island's airspace and territory, largely focuses on using Greenland for military purposes, but also mentions resource extraction and "minerals cooperation" between the two countries, without specifying any details.
The plan allows the U.S. to expand the existing Pituffik Space Base, the northernmost U.S. military installation which serves as an early-warning system for incoming missiles. The agreement also says the U.S. can establish additional bases at the sites known as Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, which are roughly 950 miles apart. Any of the three parties can propose more "defense areas" as needed, subject to approval by the others.
The deal, which has no expiration date, also blocks non-NATO countries from establishing bases on the island without agreement from the parties.
Since his first term, Mr. Trump had cited Greenland's strategic location as one of the reasons for greater U.S. control over the semi-autonomous island, and even suggested purchasing the island from Denmark or using military force.
Some industry experts believe mineral resources in Greenland have only been lightly explored and up until now the cost of extraction has not made economic sense for private companies.
Kathryn  Watson contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: The leap second is on the chopping block — and timekeeping could change forever
articles.title_zh: The leap second is on the chopping block — and timekeeping could change forever
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — When the sun hits its highest point over the meridian line that travels north and south from the 351-year-old Royal Observatory Greenwich in London, it's noon Greenwich Mean Time, a tangible and physical reference point that helped establish the world's time zone system.
Timekeeping has long relied on Earth's spin and location of the sun or moon in the sky. Before observatories such as Greenwich, humans used sundials — essentially a stick in the ground that casts shadows as the sun moves overhead. But this ancient link between Mother Earth and today's clocks looks set to be severed.
International timekeepers are on track to vote Thursday on a proposal to eliminate what's known as a leap second — a tiny, but many say important, link between Earth's rotation and the world's time standard used in critical infrastructure such as telecommunications, power grids and computers.
Inserted into global clocks 27 times since 1972, the leap second essentially allows two time systems to run in sync: astronomical time, long anchored by Earth's rotation and measured by observatories, and Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, the global standard that's set by ultraprecise atomic clocks first developed in the 1950s. These cutting-edge, lab-based clocks rely on tracking the natural vibrations — or ticks — of atoms.
The two time-telling methods differ because Earth does not rotate at a steady pace but wobbles, essentially making it a "lousy" clock, said Jeff Sherman, a group leader of the National Institute of Standards and Technology's Time and Frequency Division in Boulder, Colorado.
This wobbling stems from various factors, such as the moon's gravitational pull, shifts deep in the planetary core and the movement of water and ice on Earth's surface, an effect that's exacerbated by the melting of the polar ice caps due to the climate crisis.
"We have to make a choice on whether or not the most important thing is a sense of time given by objects in the sky directly above, say, the Greenwich longitude," he said referring to the Greenwich meridian that marks 0 degrees longitude. "Or you decide to follow what you believe are more stable, laboratory, man-made clocks," Sherman added.
Leap seconds have served as the compromise between the two time-telling systems. Most people never notice them — unlike a leap year, which adds an extra day to February every four years to account for the discrepancy between the Gregorian calendar used in most parts of the world and the time it takes Earth to complete one orbit around the sun.
But the addition of leap seconds, which happens at irregular intervals and is announced with only six months' notice, creates problems for operators of data servers, high-frequency financial trading systems and other infrastructure that rely on precise timekeeping to work properly.
The extra second crashed Reddit and LinkedIn and knocked out Qantas' booking system in 2012. And when the most recent leap second was added at the end of 2016, customers of cloud computing provider Cloudflare briefly experienced outages or delays after its servers failed to handle the introduction of a leap second properly. Big tech players such as Meta have been calling for its demise, describing the leap second as "a major source of pain."
The 69 member states of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, an intergovernmental organization that determines measurement standards, will meet this week in Versailles near Paris. The group, known by its French acronym BIPM, will vote on a resolution to ditch the leap second, a move that would take effect in May 2027. A majority needs to support the proposal, said Patrizia Tavella, director of the time department at BIPM.
When atomic time was first introduced, Tavella said, it was important to keep it tethered to astronomical time because navigational tools still relied on traditional celestial methods and timekeeping. With the advent of GPS, however, that was no longer the case.
"This correction in time has become a serious issue for modern applications," she added.
Members of BIPM have discussed the switch to what Tavella called Continuous Coordinated Universal Time for more than 20 years, she noted. At the group's last meeting in 2022, member countries voted in favor of a resolution that called for a plan to phase out the leap second on or before 2035.
In the past, some countries, such as Russia and the United Kingdom, have opposed ditching the leap second, she noted. Russia's 2022 opposition stemmed from the fact that its Global Navigation Satellite System, or GLONASS, incorporates leap seconds, unlike other satellite navigation systems, such as the United States' GPS and the European Union's Galileo, that do not. The United Kingdom was once opposed because of its cultural attachment to the foundational role that Greenwich played in the history of time, but its stance has since changed, she added.
Since the world's timekeepers last met in 2022, the debate over whether to abolish the leap second has taken on an urgency because of the prospect of something unprecedented: It will soon be necessary to subtract rather than add one second, known as a negative leap second, according to experts.
The long-term trend of Earth's rotation is slowing, but in the near term it appears to be speeding up, potentially requiring a subtraction of a second from Coordinated Universal Time to keep astronomical and atomic time matching.
A 2025 report by the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, a consortium headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany, tasked with tracking Earth's rotation, estimated that the likelihood of a negative leap second would rise sharply in the coming years — hitting a probability of 30% by 2035, according to BIPM.
Deleting a second has never previously been attempted and could create havoc in today's digitally time-stamped world. BIPM said the operators of critical infrastructure are "largely unprepared" for such a move.
"The preparation would create, for the industries that rely on time synchronization, a need for financial investment, whose amount is estimated to be similar to their preparations for the millennium bug," the organization said, referring to Y2K, a computer flaw that programmers thought might cause severe systemic problems after Dec. 31, 1999.
However, not everyone agrees that it's necessary to ditch the leap second.
The technical challenges of incorporating leap seconds, whether negative or positive, into digital systems were overstated, according to Marek Ziebart, a professor of space geodesy at University College London who said there was value in keeping the world's fundamental timescale aligned with Earth's rotation.
"We have a system in place that uses leap seconds. It works. It maintains the timescale that all of us use on a day-to-day basis," Ziebart said. "If you abolish the leap second, a lot of things will have to change. People will have to check their software, redesign it, fix it."
He added that it was also "intellectually comforting" to maintain a timescale tied to Earth's rotation.
"There's an intrinsic relationship for human beings between rotation and time," he said. "It relates to us as animals. We're driven by these periodicities of the sun rising, the sun setting."
Instead of juggling positive and negative leap seconds, the BIPM resolution essentially proposes that atomic time would be allowed to drift gradually away from astronomical time. Doing so means official timekeeping would become independent of Earth's rotation, and another leap second would never be added to clocks.
However, the proposal does recommend that the maximum difference between atomic and astronomical time should not exceed 3,600 seconds or one hour. It would take more than 3,000 years for such a difference to occur, BIPM's Tavella said.
The move essentially punts the problem to future generations, and they would have to decide whether or not to take a "leap hour," said Louise Devoy, senior cu

articles.title_orig: How Winnie-the-Pooh became the world’s most controversial bear
articles.title_zh: How Winnie-the-Pooh became the world’s most controversial bear
articles.content_orig:
Patrick Kidd began his career working in Westminster as a researcher and has been a journalist for more than 25 years. He now writes political sketches and features for the Telegraph. An anthology of his sketches covering the Brexit referendum and its aftermath was published in 2019 under the title The Weak Are A Long Time in Politics.
Now we are 100. Winnie-the-Pooh, to give AA Milne’s amiable bear of very little brain the correct hyphenation, has reached his centenary. Clearly, an optimistic outlook on life, a talent for tiddly-pomming and a health regimen that runs to a game of Poohsticks before eating a little smackerel of something must be good for longevity. Just so long as the heffalumps don’t get you.
Christopher Robin’s teddy bear appeared in a poem in Punch in 1924, under the name of Edward, but he was rechristened as Winnie after a bear at London Zoo. Milne’s first collection of stories about Pooh and his friends of disparate personality types, from the gloomily depressive to the manically bouncy, was published on October 14, 1926.
The honey-addict has since become the world’s most popular bear. Yet in some places he is also the most controversial. Here are seven times when Pooh has been banned, cancelled or cruelly mocked and exploited. Paddington doesn’t have to put up with this.
One of the most important rules of being a politician is not to let on when the satirists wound: it only encourages them. China’s President Xi was reportedly unamused in 2013 when an image of him walking with the leaner, more upbeat Barack Obama was compared to Winnie-the-Pooh and Tigger. It quickly spread on Weibo, the Chinese micro-blogging site, leading to a social media ban by the censors, though the South China Morning Post pointed out that, while chubby, Pooh was very popular and it might have been good PR for XI.
Realising that the president hated to be winnified, dissidents made further images copying his meetings with Japan’s Shinzo Abe (Eeyore) and Carrie Lam, the chief executive of Hong Kong (Piglet). These memes were also taken down, while Pooh’s Chinese name was censored from video games. The 2018 film Christopher Robin was not granted a release in China.
This sensitivity has only encouraged Xi’s opponents. Pro-democracy campaigners in Hong Kong took to wearing Pooh face masks at protests, while Taiwanese pilots have worn patches on their uniforms showing a Formosan black bear, a native species, punching Pooh in the face. Or perhaps they were just protesting about his twee poetry?
In 2006, Turkey’s public television station TRT banned the Walt Disney cartoon Winnie the Pooh because one of its main characters was a pig – an unclean animal for a Muslim audience. Turkish press reported that the station had considered just cutting out Piglet’s scenes but he appeared too often.
They were not the only ones to chop the little porker. In the first Disney animation since it acquired the rights, Winnie-the-Pooh and the Honey Tree (1966), Piglet does not appear. He was replaced by a Gopher to appeal to American audiences. Disney also gave Christopher Robin a Midwest accent. Ernest Shepard, who had illustrated the books, called the Disney Pooh “a complete travesty”. Piglet returned for the next one.
Many children’s books have come under attack from hyper-sensitive American parents, including Harry Potter and Where’s Wally . In 2006, a Christian group in Kansas came for Winnie-the-Pooh and Charlotte’s Web , the 1952 book by the American author EB White, because they featured talking animals.
“Humans are the highest level of God’s creation and are the only creatures that can communicate vocally,” they argued, calling for a ban from school libraries. “Showing lower life forms with human abilities is sacrilegious and disrespectful to God.” Only humans should tie themselves to a balloon in order to get honey from a tree.
Russian audiences were less bothered by talking animals, though Fyodor Khitruk did cut Christopher Robin from the three animated films he made of the books from 1969-72. His version won a state prize and was chosen to appear on Soviet postage stamps. Forty years later, however, the Moscow Times reported on a more sinister rendition. The Justice Ministry had listed the depiction of Winnie-the-Pooh wearing a T-shirt featuring a swastika among 414 items of extremist material that could be punished by a 3,000 rubles fine and 15 days in prison. This came about after such an image was found at the home of a man in the state of Bashkortostan who had been sentenced on extremist charges in 2006. Images of Vladimir Putin in Nazi uniform were also banned.
When the Polish town of Tuszyn sought a role model to be a statue in a children’s playground in 2014, Pooh’s name was put forward. Some councillors were concerned, however, with his casual attire. “The problem is it doesn’t have a complete wardrobe,” councillor Ryszard Cichy said. “It is half-naked which is wholly inappropriate for children.”
An official explained that Pooh had a bare (and a bear) behind because he was a hermaphrodite. Another said he was sexless. They decided it was safer to go for another mascot – and obviously not Donald Duck, who exposes his parson’s nose for all to see. Perhaps they should have considered Rupert Bear, another ursine Brit who sensibly covers his hindquarters in yellow checked trousers?
While most loved Milne’s adventures, the American critic Dorothy Parker loathed its mawkish tone. In a review, she described the scene where Pooh composes an ode about snow and explains to Piglet that he added the word “pom” to “make it more hummy”. This adjective was too much for Parker, who wrote her column in The New Yorker under the pen name Constant Reader. “It is that word ‘hummy,’ my darlings,” she wrote, “that marks the first place… at which Tonstant Weader fwowed up.”
Parker already had a beef with Pooh’s creator because her publisher had advertised her poetry collection, Enough Rope , as being by “America’s AA Milne”. This provoked her into writing a parody called When We Were Very Sore , mocking Milne’s poem about John and his waterproof boots, that went: “Dotty had great big visions of quietude./ Dotty saw an ad. and it left her Flat./ Dotty had a Great Big Snifter of Cyanide./ And that (said Dotty) is that.”
When Milne’s US copyright expired in 2022, one of the first to take advantage was Rhys Frake-Waterfield, who made a horror film called Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey . It features the animals, abandoned by Christopher Robin, deciding to eat Eeyore and then take their bloody revenge on the human who left them and all his friends. Panned as one of the worst films ever made, it grossed (in so many ways) almost £6m at the box office on a budget of less than £40,000. A sequel in 2024 also did well and a third film is in the works. Not such a silly old bear now, eh?

articles.title_orig: New knee arthritis treatment delivers lasting pain relief without surgery
articles.title_zh: New knee arthritis treatment delivers lasting pain relief without surgery
articles.content_orig:
A minimally invasive procedure that targets abnormal blood vessels in the knee could provide lasting relief for people struggling with osteoarthritis, offering a potential alternative to joint replacement surgery.
In a study involving 194 patients, researchers found that a treatment using tiny particles that dissolve within hours was associated with substantial reductions in knee pain and improvements in mobility. The benefits persisted for at least 12 months, with 80% of patients assessed at the one-year follow-up reporting clinically meaningful pain relief.
The approach, known as genicular artery embolization, aims to interrupt the inflammation and abnormal blood vessel growth that contribute to chronic knee pain. Rather than replacing the damaged joint, doctors use a thin catheter to deliver microscopic particles directly into specific blood vessels.
The findings, published in the journal Radiology , suggest that this technique could provide another option for patients who have exhausted conventional treatments but cannot or do not want to undergo knee replacement surgery.
Why Knee Arthritis Is So Difficult To Treat
Osteoarthritis is the world's most common form of arthritis and a major cause of disability. According to the World Health Organization, knee osteoarthritis affects more than 365 million adults worldwide.
The condition develops as cartilage, the protective tissue that cushions the ends of bones, gradually deteriorates. But osteoarthritis involves more than cartilage damage. Inflammation within the joint, changes in surrounding tissues, and increased sensitivity of pain signaling nerves can all contribute to persistent discomfort.
For many people, the consequences extend far beyond occasional knee pain. Everyday activities such as walking, climbing stairs, exercising, or standing for extended periods can become increasingly difficult.
Treatments typically begin with physical therapy, medication, and injections into the affected joint. When these approaches stop providing adequate relief, knee replacement surgery may eventually be considered. However, surgery is not appropriate or desirable for everyone.
"For many patients with knee osteoarthritis, there is a real treatment gap today," said Florian Nima Fleckenstein, M.D., deputy head of Interventional Radiology Campus Mitte, Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin. "Conservative measures such as intra-articular injections no longer provide sufficient relief, but joint replacement is not an option for medical or personal reasons."
A Different Way To Fight Knee Arthritis Pain
The treatment being investigated, genicular artery embolization (GAE), approaches knee arthritis from an unusual direction. Instead of focusing directly on damaged cartilage, it targets the abnormal blood vessels that develop around an inflamed joint.
These vessels can form within and around the synovium, a thin membrane lining the inside of the joint. As the vessels multiply, they can contribute to inflammation and encourage the growth of sensory nerves involved in transmitting pain.
GAE is designed to interrupt this process by reducing blood flow through the abnormal vessels while preserving the knee's normal circulation.
During the procedure, an interventional radiologist inserts a thin catheter into an artery and carefully guides it toward the affected blood vessels. Tiny particles are then injected to block selected vessels, with the goal of reducing inflammation and pain.
The technique is called superselective embolization because doctors target specific small arteries rather than blocking circulation throughout the joint. It does not require an open surgical incision or replacement of the knee.
Researchers have previously investigated both temporary blocking agents and permanent microscopic particles. Each approach has potential drawbacks, including differences in how precisely the particles can be delivered and how long they remain inside the blood vessels.
For this study, the team examined rapidly resorbable, gelatin-based microspheres. These precisely sized, spherical particles are engineered to dissolve within hours, potentially combining the advantages of temporary agents with the controlled delivery of permanent microspheres.
"GAE is a whole new treatment regimen that targets abnormal hypervascularity around the joint and, in turn, modulates the pathological neurovascular environment," Dr. Fleckenstein said.
Hypervascularity refers to an unusually high concentration of blood vessels. The pathological neurovascular environment describes the abnormal interactions between those vessels and pain signaling nerves in the affected tissue.
"By reducing both inflammation and pain, GAE with resorbable microspheres may be the first procedure that alters the course of the disease, slowing its progression."
Whether the procedure can actually slow osteoarthritis progression remains an open question. Although reducing inflammation could theoretically influence the disease, the study did not demonstrate that GAE prevents cartilage deterioration or reverses existing joint damage.
Nearly 200 Patients Underwent the Procedure
To evaluate the approach, researchers conducted a prospective single-center study involving 194 patients with osteoarthritis-related knee pain. The participants included 114 women and 80 men, with a median age of 69 years and a median body mass index of 28.4.
All had continued to experience symptoms despite at least three months of conventional care, including physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medications, and injections into the knee.
"We believe these results carry real weight because they come from real-world data," Dr. Fleckenstein said. "With this broad, inclusive study design, our participants are exactly the patients that physicians encounter every day in their practices."
The procedures took place between July and November 2024. Forty-five participants (23%) had osteoarthritis affecting both knees and received two separate treatments, with the second performed within four weeks of the first.
Altogether, the researchers carried out 239 GAE procedures.
Doctors used real-time X-ray imaging, known as fluoroscopy, to guide the catheter and deliver the particles to the targeted arteries. All 239 procedures were technically successful, meaning the intended blood vessels were successfully treated.
The safety findings were also encouraging. No moderate or severe adverse events were recorded, and mild, temporary complications occurred in 6.7% of procedures.
These included brief skin discoloration near the treated area and one superficial collection of blood near the catheter insertion site. All resolved without lasting complications.
Knee Arthritis Pain Dropped and Stayed Lower for a Year
The researchers monitored pain, movement, and quality of life before treatment and at several intervals afterward. Assessments were conducted at six weeks, three months, six months, and 12 months. An orthopedic surgeon also examined patients in person at the six-month follow-up.
Participant retention remained relatively high throughout the study. Follow-up rates were 94% at six weeks (183/194), 89% at three months (172/194), 89% at six months (171/194), and 79% at 12 months (154/194).
The most striking finding was the sustained reduction in knee pain.
Using the Numeric Rating Scale (a 0-to-10 measure of pain intensity), median pain scores fell from 7 before treatment to 4 after six weeks. By six months, the median score had declined to 3, and it remained at that level at the 12-month follow-up.
That represents a reduction of more than half from the original median pain score, with benefits that were still apparent a full year after treatment.
"In our cohort, we saw a significant drop in pain and a significant increase in function, including sports and recreation and daily activity," Dr. Fleckenstein said. "Most importantly, their quality of life significantly increased."

articles.title_zh: U.S. probe of Rep. Ilhan Omar focuses on birth date, citizenship papers, people familiar say
articles.content_orig:
Dem Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar's husband, Tim Mynett, appears at Washington, D.C., home after a raid by HSI agents amid a criminal fraud investigation into the congresswoman's immigration paperwork. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
The husband of Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn., was captured on camera by Fox News Digital entering their shared Washington, D.C., residence the day after it was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents.
Tim Mynett, a political consultant, was walking with a yellow Labrador dog on a leash Tuesday afternoon before entering the home that was searched early Monday morning amid a federal investigation into Omar's immigration status.
His outing came the same day U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro announced her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures about reporting of the couple's shared worth.
Two sources close to HSI’s investigation say the raid was part of a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman's immigration paperwork , which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)
Omar’s husband is at the center of one of the congresswoman's most prominent controversies after her financial disclosure filings decreased significantly in reported worth within the span of one filing period.
Pirro revealed her office is now investigating Omar's financial disclosures after the Office of Congressional Conduct in September dropped its misconduct investigation into the congresswoman. Tuesday's announcement opens a new chapter of investigations into the Minnesota Democrat.
The controversy surrounding Omar’s finances began when a 2024 financial report estimated that Omar and Mynett possessed between $6 million and $30 million in assets, all while the Minnesota fraud scandal within the Somali community was beginning to come to fruition.
The largest change in the documents was from Mynett’s assets. His reported ownership interests in both his winery and venture capital advisory firm, which were previously valued in the millions of dollars, are listed with no value now.
In Omar’s 2024 financial disclosure records, Mynett’s share in his winery was valued between $1 million and $5 million, and his share at the venture capital advisory firm was valued between $5 million and $25 million. Now, his equity interests are both listed at $0.
OMAR DUCKS QUESTIONS AS SCRUTINY GROWS OVER FILINGS THAT SLASHED HER REPORTED WEALTH BY MILLIONS
Omar's office previously told Fox News Digital that Mynett has partners in both businesses and said the earlier disclosure mistakenly reflected the businesses' total equity rather than his ownership interest. The office also said the original filing listed assets without accounting for liabilities.
Mynett was a partner of a firm that worked on Omar’s 2020 re-election campaign. The two announced their marriage in March 2020.
This is Omar’s third marriage, but not her most controversial. The "Squad" Democrat has also come under fire for her first marriage to a man many alleged to be her brother. Critics and skeptics claim the two married as part of an immigration scheme .
WATCH: ILHAN OMAR DENIES FEDS HAVE CONTACTED HER AFTER BORDER CZAR HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION
When White House border czar Tom Homan first announced a criminal investigation into Omar, many speculated it would be related to the allegations that she married her brother to evade United States immigration laws. But a former federal prosecutor recently confirmed to Fox News Digital that the statute of limitations would make opening an investigation into the matter difficult.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A Department of Justice (DOJ) spokesperson told Fox News Digital that the judicially authorized search warrant for the raid of Omar’s house Monday was obtained by the DOJ as part of an ongoing federal investigation.
Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca and Amanda Macias contributed to this report.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.
