articles.title_orig: Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture
articles.title_zh: Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture
articles.content_orig:
Fraternities on Cornell's campus will not be allowed to host parties or events for the rest of the academic year. Jeongyoon Han for NPR hide caption
Cornell University has banned parties and social events at fraternities for the rest of the school year and will bring sexual assault investigators into its police unit, in response to a former student's allegation of gang rape in 2024.
The changes came on Tuesday as the university said it is committed to addressing a "deeply disturbing" culture of drug and alcohol abuse, and a rise in sexual violence on campus following a civil lawsuit filed by a former student, Jane Doe, which set off national outrage and a crisis at Cornell.
"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," Michael I. Kotlikoff, who is Cornell's president, wrote in a letter addressed to the campus on Tuesday. "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action."
The lawsuit, which Doe filed nearly one month ago, alleges that Doe was plied with ketamine and was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity during a party in October of 2024. The details of the allegations, which disclosed how fraternity members used a Snapchat group chat to discuss the woman and events at the party with openly crude language, sparked fury across the nation.
Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told news outlets that Doe has been sent death threats and police swarmed her family's home since she filed the lawsuit.
The administration's changes come after student groups organized protests last week on campus.
"The administration is clearly feeling the heat and needed to make a move," says John Hartnett, a sophomore at Cornell who has helped organize protests. He called the changes a "half measure," and said that banning frats was not a long term solution to systematic issues at the university.
The faculty senate is considering a vote of no confidence in the university administration at a meeting scheduled for Wednesday. It's a rare move that demonstrates the deep seated frustration and distrust stemming from the 2024 case.
"Trust is still eroded on campus — that hasn't changed," says Julia Chang, an associate professor of Hispanic studies in the Department of Romance Studies. "The fact that these changes are coming about now — two years later — is a testament to the power of the student movement and the global conversation it has sparked; not the integrity of the administration."
The moratorium on events at fraternities is expected to have a reverberating effect on campus, where about one-third of all students participate in fraternities and sororities. The university's ties to Greek life, Kotlikoff said, has in part created a toxic culture on campus that requires serious course correction.
"While this is not a problem unique to Cornell, we are committed to setting a higher standard for education, oversight, and enforcement of safe social behavior and citizenship," Kotlikoff wrote.
Ray Epstein, who works with a consent education company, and is one of the organizers of a rally planned just steps away from Cornell's campus on Tuesday, said that while the measures from Cornell are "overall a win," they also serve as an "effort to save face."
"What I think they should be doing, is operating first instead of as a business, the way that they are now, as institutions that are meant to educate and keep their students safe," Epstein said.
Kotlikoff said that in addition to enhancing bystander training programming, the university will also improve its services to survivors of sexual assault by increasing staffing in its civil rights office, which would help individuals navigate the reporting process for incidents.
Additionally, the university will work with the New York State Police's criminal investigators on campus sexual assault investigations. The move allows the investigators, who are independent from the university, to take on cases in which survivors pursue criminal charges.
The university plans to bring in faculty who are experts in sexual assault and rape culture to help reform the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault through listening events with the Cornell community.
Kotlikoff's letter did not explain why these events are only being issued now — two years after administrators at Cornell learned about the allegations in 2024.
Although the district attorney did not prosecute the case in 2024, Cornell's Title IX office conducted an investigation in 2025. In March 2025, a panel of staff and faculty at Cornell moved to expel or suspend some of the men. The panel required the remaining men to write "essays" in addition to other sanctions.
Cornell also barred the Chi Phi fraternity chapter, which was closed in 2024.

articles.title_orig: One of the World’s Largest Chinstrap Penguin Colonies Is Shrinking Fast
articles.title_zh: One of the World’s Largest Chinstrap Penguin Colonies Is Shrinking Fast
articles.content_orig:
Scientists are sounding the alarm after discovering that one of the world’s largest chinstrap penguin populations has collapsed.
Zavodovski Island, a remote, uninhabited volcanic island between South America and Antarctica, lost 63 percent of its chinstrap penguins between 2011 and 2025, according to a new study published October 7 in the journal Current Biology .
Researchers attribute the losses—which amount to half a million breeding individuals—to climate change, which they say is disrupting the birds’ food supply.
“Imagine losing 60 percent of a country’s entire population in that timeframe,” Lucas Krüger García , an ecologist with the Chilean Antarctic Institute who was not involved with the research, tells National Geographic ’s Avery Schuyler Nunn. “It’s really concerning. The fact that this single colony represented 30 percent of the global chinstrap population makes it even more concerning.”
Zavodovski Island, part of the South Sandwich Islands , was once home to the largest penguin colony on the planet, a combination of chinstrap and macaroni penguins. But, since 2011, as chinstrap numbers have plummeted, the island has lost more than a quarter of its total penguin population. Because of the declines, scientists say the island has now lost its world’s largest penguin colony title to the Adélie penguins living at Cape Adare in Antarctica’s Ross Sea.
Chinstrap penguins have been declining across the Antarctic Peninsula and surrounding islands since the 1980s. But, for years, the birds living on Zavodovski Island, located some 1,240 miles from the nearest permanent human settlement, appeared to be holding their own.
In December 2023, scientists decided to check in on the Zavodovski chinstraps. They were in for a shock: Their analysis—conducted using a combination of drone surveys, aerial photography and satellite tracking data from individual birds—revealed that the island now has the highest rate of chinstrap population decline in the world.
In 2011, scientists counted nearly 543,000 breeding pairs of chinstrap penguins on the island. By 2025, that number had plummeted to roughly 201,000 breeding pairs, according to the paper.
The team ruled out a variety of explanations for the birds’ demise. The island has plenty of breeding habitat, so the chinstraps likely weren’t competing with their macaroni neighbors for space. Krill harvesting is banned in the waters surrounding the island, which eliminated local overfishing as a culprit. The March 2016 eruption of the island's Mount Curry might have killed some of the birds, but it doesn’t explain the chinstrap population’s steady decline since 2011.
Instead, the evidence points to climate-driven changes to the Southern Ocean that are affecting krill , the tiny crustaceans that make up the bulk of the chinstrap penguins’ diet. As the ocean warms and sea ice shrinks, krill are becoming increasingly scarce around Zavodovski—and chinstrap penguins are paying the price.
Tracking data shows the birds prefer to forage in the cooler waters northwest of the island, where they would normally find abundant krill. However, as ocean temperatures rise, the krill are increasingly moving south into the Weddell Sea .
Since chinstrap penguins rely so heavily on krill, even small changes in its availability can have significant consequences for their survival. The chinstrap penguin is “quite a specialist species that’s got a very limited global range, and that range is getting squeezed,” lead author Norman Ratcliffe , an ecologist with the British Antarctic Survey, tells CNN ’s Laura Paddison.
Did you know? Emperor penguins are also in trouble
Earlier this year, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) listed emperor penguins as “endangered.” Projections suggest the birds’ population could shrink by as much as half by the 2080s.
Meanwhile, the island’s macaroni penguins are holding steady. The birds’ numbers increased by 28 percent between 2011 and 2016, and have remained stable at roughly 217,000 breeding pairs since then. Zavodovski Island now has a combined chinstrap and macaroni penguin population of roughly 419,000 pairs, per the paper.
Scientists think macaroni penguins are faring better than chinstraps because their diet is broader and more flexible. They also like to eat krill, but can supplement with or switch to other food sources, such as fish and crustaceans, when necessary. Tracking data suggests they’re doing just that, heading to the warmer waters northeast of the island to forage for alternate prey.
Overall, it’s good news that Zavodovski’s macaroni penguins are flourishing. But researchers worry that the decline of chinstrap penguins could have broader ripple effects.
“Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely,” Ratcliffe tells the Guardian ’s Jonathan Watts.
Sarah Kuta is a writer and editor based in Longmont, Colorado. She covers history, science, travel, food and beverage, sustainability, economics and other topics.

articles.title_orig: Bank earnings: Higher rates haven't hurt consumer spending or AI financing, yet
articles.title_zh: Bank earnings: Higher rates haven't hurt consumer spending or AI financing, yet
articles.content_orig:
Four of the largest U.S. banks reported third-quarter results on Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase , Wells Fargo , Goldman Sachs and Citigroup .
Bank of America and Morgan Stanley will post earnings on Wednesday.
The quarter was dominated by headlines around artificial intelligence, IPO uncertainty, high fuel prices and rising borrowing costs.
The banks that reported Tuesday put up mixed results . JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets and the largest in the world by market capitalization, posted a rare miss. Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, blew past estimates for revenue and earnings per share, led by strong equities trading.
Analyst calls for all four banks touched on the opportunities and risks associated with AI, citing robust financing demand and operational advantages, but also the threat of rogue agents.
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon also addressed recent reports of a CEO transition plan, and Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo joined CNBC to discuss the firm's growth and the state of the consumer.
Here's what you need to know:
Citi's analyst call is over, which means bank earnings reports for Tuesday are wrapped. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley report on Wednesday to round out third-quarter results for the major U.S. firms.
Wells Fargo's Santomassimo told CNBC that both consumers and businesses are doing "really well."
"I think despite higher gas prices, both sides of the equation have been able to really work through that," he said. "We're just not seeing any sort of cracks around delinquency trends that would lead you to believe you're going to see any near-term stress that come through, at least at least for now."
Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the company's underlying results are "really good" and that the bank is seeing "continued momentum" across all of its businesses.
"As you look at the net interest margin, what that really shows is sort of this good stabilization of the underlying trends," he said. "You see the higher rate environment starting to come through in terms of helping it as you look forward, and so for us, the opportunity we have ahead of us is just as big as it was last quarter."
Citi's Fraser said on the call with analysts that macro environment conditions softened during the third quarter and that the "global economy has held up remarkably well."
"In the U.S., while much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much of the growth," she said. "The labor market is stable, and companies remain active. Our near-term economic outlook remains positive."
She added that the bank's clients have remained "engaged" and "healthy."
Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser said on a call with analysts on Tuesday that the company is focused on reducing systemic risk while deploying AI firmwide.
"Our cyberdefense strategy is about being on the front foot, about moving fast and retaining trust," Fraser said. "We don't wait for risks to happen. We're constantly preparing and improving our defenses. We're in the business of managing risk everyday, and this is no different."
Investment banking fees at all four firms reporting on Tuesday largely held up during the third quarter, with most firms either matching or surpassing prior guidance. Still, the reports revealed declines on a quarter-over-quarter basis.
At JPMorgan, investment banking revenue was up 14% year over year but down 8% quarter over quarter. JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said the pipeline remains "very, very strong."
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon echoed that sentiment on his company's analyst call, while declining to say whether capital markets activity has peaked. That bank reported fees that were 21% higher from the prior year, but 5% lower than the second quarter.
"IPOs that came in September were really the result of conversations in May and June around valuation expectations. Things got a little bit softer in September," Solomon said. "The IPO market was wide open. It's just if you expected a valuation and you got something 10 %to 15% less, you might choose not to go forward, you might choose to wait."
Solomon added all the tech innovation and the AI infrastructure activity is a "real good ballast" for capital markets activity on a go-forward basis, noting that doesn't mean there won't be bumps.
Citi posted the largest quarter-over-quarter decline in the fees, at 13% down. Wells Fargo reported investment banking revenue that was down 5% from the prior quarter.
Solomon warned that the AI infrastructure boom could face a painful reset if higher borrowing costs or overbuilding undermine the economics of some data center projects.
"There is going to be a lot of financing to do, and we're going to be in the middle of that," Solomon said during the bank's third-quarter call.
"It may be that over time as the financing needs grow, that there's pressure on rates and that will affect the returns and the viability of certain projects," he said. "Not every project is going to be received as well."
For now, demand for computing power remains strong and supply has yet to catch up, Solomon said, meaning more infrastructure will be built and more financing from Goldman and others will be needed. It's impossible to predict when a reset might happen or how the technology would evolve and be deployed, he said, calling the dynamic "an unknown we have to live with."
"There will be a point in time when this recalibration resets, for sure," Solomon said. "When that does happen, of course there'll be some bumps."
Citigroup, the final bank of the morning, is beginning its conference call with executives and analysts to discuss its third-quarter earnings results.
Goldman Sachs CEO Solomon pushed back against reports of an impending transition to executive chairman, saying Tuesday that no succession process or timeline is underway at the investment bank.
Last month, news outlets cited anonymous sources that said Solomon would be replaced as CEO by Goldman President John Waldron as early as next year. The process would involve a vote by the bank's board that could happen in a matter of months, according to The Wall Street Journal.
"I just want to be clear, there is no succession transition or timeline underway at Goldman Sachs," Solomon said during the bank's earnings call.
"The board and I are singularly focused on our strategy to grow the firm and continue to serve our clients," he said.
The CEO also pointed to the firm's future growth prospects, saying his leadership team was focused on expanding the franchise and accelerating its earnings growth in the coming years.
"I have to say, at the point right now where we see the benefits of the effort that the broad team has made, I'm really enjoying the job," Solomon said.
Wells Fargo's Scharf said on the call with analysts that the AI investment cycle has become "a complicated macroeconomic force in its own right."
"Demand for semiconductors, networking equipment, power generation, data center infrastructure, cooling systems, storage, cybersecurity and advanced manufacturing equipment continue to surge," Scharf said.
"The scale of investment here increasingly resembles prior infrastructure booms, creating both significant opportunities but also risks given the significant leverage used to finance the build-out and the upward pressure on prices in selected industries and supply chains," he added.
Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company's customer base is "still strong."
"Our underwriting criteria recognize that at some point consumer credit conditions will weaken," Scharf said. "To be clear, we do not see signs of this yet, but we know that cycles are inevitable."
Wells Fargo's Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company is "devoting significant management time and resources" to building out its AI capabilities.

articles.title_orig: Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
articles.title_zh: Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
articles.content_orig:
Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets in a cyberattack that reportedly caused refrigerators and freezers to overheat, spoiling food and sparking fires.
Fridges at French supermarket chains Carrefour, Monoprix, the Les Mousquetaires-owned Intermarché, and Coopérative U, among others, all saw fridges heat up to as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, Reuters reported Monday.
Coopérative U's CEO, Dominique Schelcher, confirmed that cyberattacks had affected "refrigeration production facilities of several stores."
"Attacking equipment that is essential to the preservation of fresh products and the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and unprecedented. It is unacceptable," Schelcher said in a LinkedIn post .
CNBC has reached out to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché, Coopérative U and E Leclerc for comment but did not immediately hear back.
Felix Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said the attack affected several European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium, according to the Reuters article.
"I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at @intermarche @CooperativeU @Leclerc," European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said in a post on X on Monday.
"Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality."
Les Mousquetaires said it was expecting the damages, which affected around 180 stores, to reach "several million euros in losses," in an email to CNBC.
It said some fresh and frozen food displays have been out of service after the cyberattack affected one of its service providers responsible for managing refrigeration systems inside some stores.
"Intermarché and Netto have taken all necessary precautions to remove and dispose of any affected products as quickly as possible, to ensure consumer safety," the Les Mousquetaires spokesperson said. "In some stores, the overheating of equipment resulted in smoke, but no fires have been reported."
They're now awaiting findings from a court-appointed bailiff and insurance experts to get more precise figures on damages.
Stop & Shop parent Ahold Delhaize , which owns popular Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, said that it was experiencing a "security issue within its network," and that systems had been taken offline. It said its stores are still open.
This comes amid a broader wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes, which experts are warning are being enhanced by artificial intelligence. British online fashion retailer Asos experienced a cybersecurity breach last week which revealed some customers' personal information.
Meanwhile, a small power plant in the U.K. was shut down for four days in July after a cyberattack which was suspected to be linked to Iran.
Interpol's global chief information security officer, Bjorn R. Watne, recently told CNBC that AI can be used to target multiple victims at once, and is increasing the scale and speed of cyberattacks. "It's an evolution and not a revolution."
Correction: Bjorn R. Watne is global chief information security officer at Interpol. An earlier version misspelled his name.

articles.title_orig: World stocks slip as AI spending worries hit chipmakers
articles.title_zh: World stocks slip as AI spending worries hit chipmakers
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Sruthi Shankar and Chibuike Oguh
NEW YORK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - World stocks edged lower on Tuesday as concerns about AI spending weighed on chipmakers and investors looked ahead to more US corporate earnings for clues on whether big technology ‌firms can justify their heavy capital spending.
Brent crude futures also fell as traders assessed developments in the Middle East ‌conflict.
Investors have ridden the AI wave in the past four years as massive spending powered corporate profits and economic growth, but more recently, worries over concentration risks ​and whether a payoff will come soon enough have weighed.
On Wall Street, all three indexes finished lower with industrials, healthcare, and financials driving losses. Chip stocks lost more than 2%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.35%, the S&P 500 fell 0.02% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.15%.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 0.1%. MSCI's main world stocks index dipped 0.23%.
"The AI trade has been driving the market for the first ‌part of the year up until the third ⁠quarter and usually the Nvidias and AMDs trade down ahead of the hyperscalers' earnings announcements because of the uncertainty with regards to the capital spending cycle," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at ⁠Sparrow Capital Management.
Reported progress by Chinese memory chip maker CXMT has fueled concerns about increased competition from China's AI players, while Broadcom CEO Hock Tan likened some of the flows into the broader AI sector to "casino gambling."
Investors are turning their eyes to the US quarterly earnings season, which ​kicked off ​with results from big banks.
Shares in JPMorgan Chase dropped 0.86% after it ​reported a profit increase in the third quarter, driven ‌by investment banking and trading performances. Wells Fargo dropped 3.1% and Goldman Sachs fell 0.23% after their results.
AI heavyweights Alphabet, Amazon.com, Meta Platforms and Nvidia are yet to report their quarterly earnings.
"Until we get clarity on hyperscaler capital spending and revenue on the AI trade, you're going to see some very mixed results on the benchmarks: Dow, S&P 500 and the Nasdaq," Sparrow said.
The benchmark 10-year yield fell 2.72 basis points to 5.22%, inching away from the 24-year high of 5.364% it hit last week.
A toxic ‌mix of inflationary pressure from elevated energy prices and worries about ballooning ​government debt has triggered several bond selloffs in recent weeks, pushing borrowing costs to ​multi-decade highs across the globe.
Traders are awaiting US inflation data ​on Wednesday for clues on the Federal Reserve's policy path. They are pricing in an 80.6% chance ‌that it holds rates steady later this month, up ​from 51% a month earlier, the ​CME FedWatch tool showed.
Oil prices eased as traders assessed supply risks from attacks on Saudi Arabia while weighing the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia. Brent crude futures dipped 0.9% to $105.69 per barrel.
The dollar slipped from 18-month highs, along ​with a drop in yields and oil prices. ‌The euro was last up 0.01% at $1.1199, while the Japanese yen was at 158.31 per dollar. [FRX/]
The dollar index, which ​measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.34%.
(Reporting by Chibuike ​Oguh in New York; Editing by Will Dunham and Jamie Freed)

Former PGA Tour star Hunter Mahan talks about getting into posting golf content online and eyeing a return to professional golf.
Somehow, someway, life just got even better for Rory McIlroy.
The career grand slam winner, who has earned well over $200 million on the golf course alone, has entered into a global partnership with DP World. While athletes joining forces with a company is hardly ever newsworthy, McIlroy teaming up with the logistics company is an exception thanks to the perk that comes along with it.

Moving forward, DP World will be sending not one, but two fitness and recovery trailers to every tournament McIlroy tees it up in on both the DP World Tour and the PGA Tour.

"Rory McIlroy’s season takes him around the world, but his training and recovery environment doesn’t have to change with it," an announcement from DP World stated. "In a new multi-year global partnership announced today, DP World will take McIlroy’s personalised fitness and recovery environment from tournament to tournament, using its smart end-to-end global logistics network to give him and his team greater consistency wherever he competes."

While McIlroy is playing a more limited schedule than ever before in his career, he is still very much a global player, making starts across multiple countries and continents each year.

Sending two fitness trailers around the globe sounds like a nearly impossible challenge, but DP World directly addressed the potential hurdles it may face logistically.
"At the heart of the partnership are two personalised fitness and recovery trailers that will travel with McIlroy across his PGA Tour and DP World Tour schedules ," the statement continued. "DP World will manage every stage of their journeys, from collection and customs clearance to storage and delivery, so everything McIlroy needs to train and recover is ready when he arrives at each tournament."

McIlroy has long been one of the leading proponents of fitness in professional golf, and his hours in the gym have resulted in him being among the longest hitters in the game. He's also consistently remained healthy over the years, with his last significant injury taking place in 2017 when he suffered a hairline fracture to his rib cage.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 beta 4 no longer includes Apple’s overhauled Health app
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 beta 4 no longer includes Apple’s overhauled Health app
articles.content_orig:
An overhauled Apple Health app is coming, but it looks like iOS 27.2 won’t include it.
Apple first announced the upgraded Health app in September. The company still says to expect it to launch later this year.
iOS 27.2 developer beta 1 was the first iPhone software update to include the new Health app .
Apple added it to iOS 27.2 public beta 1 and public beta 2 as well. It features new data points like health age while adding the ability to schedule lab work through Quest Diagnostics.
However, it appears Apple plans to take a bit more time to get the new Health app ready for release.
Today’s iOS 27.2 developer beta 4 release no longer includes the new Health app. Instead, the prior version is restored. The longevity section is replaced with the previous sharing section.
iOS 27.2 beta 4 notes that Health data added during the beta testing period will be retained and viewing in the Settings app. It also adds that the release is still planned for this year.
This likely means that we’ll see iOS 27.3 beta in late October or early November with the Health app upgrade included.

articles.title_orig: ‘Super app’ aimed at UK students uses servers owned by Chinese firm on US blacklist
articles.title_zh: ‘Super app’ aimed at UK students uses servers owned by Chinese firm on US blacklist
articles.content_orig:
ZyMix platform has contract with Tencent, which US alleges has links to People’s Liberation Army
A new messaging and payment “super app” marketed at British students uses servers owned by a Chinese company that has been put on a US military blacklist for its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army.
ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen.
Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list.
The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.
The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes.
The DoD is prohibited from entering into, renewing or extending contracts for goods, services or technology with any entity on the list although wider sanctions are not automatic.
A Tencent spokesperson said: “Tencent’s inclusion on this list is clearly a mistake. We are not a military company or supplier. Unlike sanctions or export controls, this listing has no impact on our business. We will nonetheless work with the Department of Defense to address any misunderstanding.”
China’s footprint in higher education in the UK has become a controversial issue. MI5 recently warned British universities to cut ties with the China General Technology Research Institute.
The domestic intelligence service claimed it was secretly channelling funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to UK-linked academics to improve the technical espionage capabilities of China’s ministry of state security.
The link between the Chinese-owned infrastructure and ZyMix was initially disclosed in the company’s privacy policy at the time of its launch last week.
The document, which is legally required, said that Tencent (Frankfurt) stored user-generated content and messages. After the Guardian approached the company, the privacy policy was rewritten and mention of Tencent was removed.
The policy now states that users’ personal data is stored and processed primarily in the United Kingdom and the EU, adding that “some of our service providers are located in other countries, including the United States”.
It goes on to say that “auxiliary infrastructure providers, hosted in the EU, receive only encrypted user messages and limited technical data, such as technical statistics, licence validation when the app starts”.
A spokesperson said: “As a newly launched startup, we are updating our privacy notice as we develop our services, including clarifying that Tencent, Twilio and the other providers concerned are used solely for performance testing.”
The spokesperson added: “Our agreement is with Tencent Cloud Europe BV, which we use for auxiliary services, rather than as the provider that stores ZyMix user data. We take our obligations under UK data protection law seriously.”
The new privacy policy invites those who wish to know the identity of their suppliers to request the information from the company.
In response to a request from the Guardian, Tarique Ghaffur, a former assistant commissioner at the Metropolitan police, who described himself as a security consultant for ZyMix, responded.
He said: “We have reviewed your request as against our private privacy [sic] you mentioned. Unfortunately, at the present time for reasons of commercial confidentiality, contractual obligations and legal privileges, we are not able to provide you with the requested information.”
Fraser Sampson, a professor of security and national governance and formerly the UK’s biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, said he was “sceptical when ‘commercial confidentiality’ arguments are used to duck basic policy questions and amending policy on the fly is never reassuring”.
He added: “When companies ask us for our personal data, they should expect us to ask them where it’s being kept, for what purpose(s) and who they’re going to share it with – and be prepared to answer fully.”
Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency NGO, said: “There are serious questions about whether ZyMix have taken due care before launching this product.”
A spokesperson for ZyMix said: “Whilst still in its beta stage, the ZyMix app has been developed to fully comply with all UK data, privacy and financial regulations.”
ZyMix is heavily targeting the university market and is offering £200 to £400 a month to people who agree to be brand ambassadors on campuses. Staff roles have also been advertised in the UK by ZyMix for Mandarin-speaking applicants.
One advert on LinkedIn for the job of operations manager (Mandarin speaking) required “excellent written and verbal communication skills in both English and Mandarin (required for daily communication with the China team)”.
Separately, a distinct company appeared to be recruiting on behalf of ZyMix on WeChat, the Chinese instant messaging service, saying: “The product, R&D, design and testing team is in Greater China, with branch-company bases covering: Taipei / Shenzhen / Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Chengdu / Zhengzhou.”
Ghaffur said that Flicknmix, the UK company that publishes the ZyMix app, “does not have any subsidiaries or branch offices in China. Our aim is to create opportunities within the UK”. A spokesperson for ZyMix described it as “British born”.

articles.title_orig: The Forces Driving Up Bond Yields Take a Troubling Turn
articles.title_zh: The Forces Driving Up Bond Yields Take a Troubling Turn
articles.content_orig:
The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell on Thursday as traders digested comments from a top Federal Reserve official along with another long-dated bond auction.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was down more than 4 basis points at 5.229% after reaching its highest level since 2002 this week. The 30-year Treasury bond yield dropped more than 5 basis points to 5.602% after trading around a 24-year high recently.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Thursday that more hikes are needed to bring inflation down after around 5-and-a-half years above the central bank's 2% target, but suggested rates did not need to rise immediately.
"The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings," Waller told a Central Bank of Turkey forum in Istanbul. "But they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
His comments initially sent yields higher on the day. However, rates gave back those advances after President Donald Trump said the U.S. won't attack Iran until after the November midterm election . Yields also pulled back after a solid 30-year Treasury bond auction.
The department sold $22 billion in 30-year paper, with indirect bidders — which include central banks — scooping up 72.3% of the sale. That's above a 10-auction average of 68%. Direct bidders, including institutional investors, took 20.9% of the auction, just below an average of 22%. The yield at auction ease 5.618%.
That marks the final auction of the week. The department sold $58 billion in 3-year notes on Tuesday and another $39 billion in 10-year notes.
Thursday's sale "was decent but nowhere close to as good as the 10 yr auction yesterday," wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer of One Point BFG Wealth Partners.
— CNBC's Brianna Bernath contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: CCI Instructors Apply Real-World Experiences in Their Classrooms
articles.title_zh: CCI Instructors Apply Real-World Experiences in Their Classrooms
articles.content_orig:
Instructors at the Florida State University (FSU) College of Communication and Information (CCI) come from a variety of professional backgrounds. As they have transitioned into careers in academia, they have continued to draw on those experiences to strengthen their teaching. By bringing real-world knowledge and industry perspectives into the classroom, CCI instructors create meaningful learning opportunities that help students connect what they learn in class to their future careers.
One such professor is Rhonda Collins ( EdD, PMP) , who incorporates hands-on learning into her project management courses, preparing students to navigate challenges they may encounter in their future projects and careers.
“ My goal is to help students understand that project management is not just about following processes or using tools, but requires communication, leadership, problem-solving, adaptability, and sound judgment,” said Collins.
With the guidance of their professors, students have opportunities to gain valuable professional experience while still in the classroom. Experiences like these help prepare students for success beyond graduation, giving them the skills and confidence to navigate the workforce as they begin their careers.
“I help students bridge the gap between the classroom and their first professional job or internship by making the learning experience as practical and workplace-oriented as possible,” said Collins. “I want students to build confidence in their ability to think about projects like a project professional.”
Instructors use more than their curriculum to prepare students for their future professions. With a professional background in branding, marketing, and event coordination, Lauren Helm focuses on helping students build their personal brands and use their current jobs and internships to make themselves more competitive in the job market.
“Having that drive to do something that showcases your leadership skills, recognizes the responsibilities of college jobs that you’ve had, and showcases that to your employer is crucial,” said Helm. “Employers are looking for those opportunities where you are able to connect those dots.”
The implementation of hands-on experiences in the classroom is crucial to developing the skills students need to succeed in the professional world. As instructors, it is important to recognize the ever-changing job market and understand how these changes impact the way students learn, as well as the skills and qualifications they need to succeed after graduation.
“As a student, I had to figure out my way pretty much on my own. Textbooks are great, but they’re talking in past tense. They’re not talking about things that are happening now,” said Helm. “It’s important to be able to guide somebody through something that’s relatable, and actually applying this knowledge and these concepts to something that’s happening today.”
As students prepare to enter the workforce, professors ensure they are developing the professional skills and experiences that will help them stand out in a competitive job market.
“It’s a balance between teaching and transitioning students to practicing these skills,” said Collins. “Academic knowledge, practical experience, professional skills, and continuous learning are what provide graduates with a competitive edge in an ever-changing job market.”

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 is little changed as traders mull over bank earnings; chip stocks slide: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 is little changed as traders mull over bank earnings; chip stocks slide: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 traded near the flatline on Tuesday, with traders digesting a slew of corporate earnings reports from major banks along with a steep overnight decline in South Korea that put pressure on memory chip names.
The S&P 500 was little changed on the day, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 135 points, or 0.3%, lower, giving back an earlier gain. At its high of the day, the 30-stock index was up more than 460 points.
JPMorgan Chase reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that missed analyst expectations, but the bank raised its net interest income guidance for 2026. Shares were last little changed on the day. Wells Fargo shed 2% on mixed Q3 numbers, while Goldman Sachs rose slightly after its revenue for the third quarter surpassed expectations.
"These banks still reported strong numbers, it's just that expectations were high, and higher expectations is a risk for companies across the board during this current earnings season," said Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at Walser Wealth Management.
UnitedHealth , meanwhile, was marginally higher after the insurance giant's results exceeded analyst expectations.
The early reports could set the tone for an earnings season with lofty expectations. Analysts on average expect S&P 500 profits grew by nearly 30% from the year-earlier period, according to FactSet.
Memory stocks were under pressure after South Korea's Kospi benchmark dropped 5.5% — reaching its lowest level since July 31 — on valuation concerns in the space along with growing competition out of China. This week, China's CXMT said it plans to release a new, more powerful chip by year-end.
SK hynix slipped nearly 4%. Seagate Technology and Western Digital lost 2%. Micron Technology and Sandisk fell almost 5% and more than 2%, respectively.
Short sellers betting against JetBlue and Alaska Air are increasing their wagers against the airlines as energy prices remain elevated as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
Per estimates from S3 Partners, short interest in JetBlue has advanced to 30.5% of the company's publicly tradable float, up from 20.6% at the end of 2025. Alaska Air has seen an increase in short interest to 10.8% of the float from 6.4% at last year's end.
To be sure, active long interest has also been rising in the two names. For JetBlue, that's increased to 36.1% of shares outstanding from 25.2% at year-end 2025, while active long interest in Alaska Air has moved up to 36.7% of shares outstanding from 31.7%.
"These are crowded positions in small, volatile stocks," Sam Pierson, director of research at S3, told CNBC. "If oil prices ease, short sellers in JetBlue and Alaska could be forced to cover quickly, and that buying would push the shares higher."
Both stocks were down on Tuesday, with JetBlue and Alaska Air shedding nearly 6% and almost 1%, respectively. In 2026, the stocks have each fallen around 25%.
The outlook of retail estate agents is only getting worse, according to Wells Fargo.
The bank's survey of agents had a record-low share describing their market as friendly to sellers. It also showed an increasingly number of agents reporting negative sales growth compared with a year ago.
"August reads were bad, but conditions further deteriorated in September across all key metrics," Wells Fargo analyst Sam Reid wrote to clients on Tuesday.
But Reid said it's not all "doom" or "gloom," citing constructive early signals for next year.
Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading:
Read here for the full list.
— Darla Mercado and Fred Imbert
The iShares US Healthcare Providers ETF (IHF) hit its highest level since Sept. 2024 before pulling back.
It was up more than 2% at the high and was last up nearly 1%.
Leading the initial way higher was Veeva Systems , which was up 3%. Healthcare technology platform company HealthStream was up 1% too. Both hit new all-time highs, and remained in the green even as the broader ETF turned negative.
— Gina Francolla and Davis Giangiulio
HSBC downgraded software maker Adobe on concerns that "vibe-coded clones" of its products, aided by AI, may dent its sales.
Analyst Stephen Bersey at HSBC said he was cutting his adjusted EPS estimates by between 1% and 2% "to reflect risks that some amateur retail users may migrate out of Adobe."
"ArtCraft (apparently a firm of just a few people) has released what we believe to be an 'auto-coded' free open source clone of Adobe's Creative Cloud suite, including versions of Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, Acrobat, After Effects, and InDesign. ArtCraft said it hopes to reach '100% feature parity' with Adobe's software within a month," Bersey wrote.
The bank lowered its price target to $267 from $310, which still implies upside of 10%.
Piper Sandler upgraded VF Corp to overweight from neutral on Tuesday.
Piper Sandler's Fall Teen Survey of about 9,000 respondents found Vans ranked as a top footwear for male consumers.
"As a favorite footwear brand for all males (vast majority of customer base), Vans maintained its #7 spot vs. declining the past three surveys; for upper income guy, the brand moved up one spot," analyst Anna Andreeva wrote in a note to clients.
Vans web traffic performance for the fiscal second quarter of 2027 was strong while foot traffic signaled to be positive, she said. Andreeva also raised her target to $20 from $16, implying 26.7% upside from Monday's close.
Famous investor Paul Tudor Jones delivered some bearish pronouncements on market conditions in a Tuesday interview on CNBC's " Squawk Box ."
He compared current conditions to the period just before the dot com bubble popped in the early 2000s, tracing the similarities to increasingly debt-financed capital investments powering the artificial intelligence buildout and global sovereign debt levels.
He said that 2027 is going to be a very challenging year for the stock market and that he'll be short for the duration. He also sees oil prices rising between $20 and $25 dollars from their current levels.
"I'll be short the whole year. There just -- there's little value," Jones said. "You had all this issuance, all these IPOs in 98 and 99, and really 2000, 2001, 2002. Those were the easiest years to be short because you kept having these unlocks that just kept adding supply to the market."
Jones added that he expects another federal bailout to follow the crash he is anticipating.
"We're never going to fix these deficits until the market makes us to. It's going to be just like 2008 and TARP [Troubled Asset Relief Program]. So that's the reality. No politician is going to voluntarily raise taxes or cut spending. They're going to be forced to. And the only question is, are we now at that tipping point where the market's about to do that? And if you put a gun to my head, I'd say 60-40, we're down that path."
The S&P 500 began Tuesday's session slightly in the red.
The broad market index fell 0.1% shortly after the opening bell, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 0.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 359 points, or 0.7%, however.
Weakness in the AI trade continued Tuesday as memory stocks came under more pressure amid worries about Chinese competition.
Micron fell 5%, while others like SK hynix and Western Digital dropped 6% and 7%, respectively.
Meanwhile, comments from Broadcom CEO Hock Tan on AI investors' "extreme expectations" compared some of investment flow into the sector to "casino gambling."
His comments come amid the ongoing debates about open-weight model competition, new frontier models and concerns about financing.
Shares of Goldman Sachs gained more than 4% in the premarket on Tuesday after the bank's third-quarter revenue far exceeded analyst expectations.
The firm posted revenue of $18.68 billion for the quarter, while analysts surveyed by LSEG had penciled in $16.71 billion. Equities revenue for the period also beat estimates.
— Hugh Son and Sean Conlon

articles.title_orig: This grad helps runs the Amazon of the medical device world
articles.title_zh: This grad helps runs the Amazon of the medical device world
articles.content_orig:
In the medical device industry, time is often of the essence.
A critical component shortage could delay a project for weeks if not months, an all too common occurrence for many device startups. Ask Northeastern graduate Katie Karmelek.
A mechanical engineer in the health care industry, Karmelek experienced this firsthand early in her career while working in research and development.
“I’d have maybe up to 10 projects going at the time, innovating, developing and prototyping medical devices for a wide range of companies,” she said. “I was always having a hard time getting the parts I needed to innovate fast enough. I was even going to Home Depot to buy tubing because that’s what we could get to make a catheter prototype.”
That’s why in 2017, Karmelek co-founded Chamfr, a digital marketplace pegged as the Amazon for research and development engineers in the medical technology field. The company’s pitch was to offer an online store where medical device makers could go to purchase important components needed to make their products.
Today, the company has customers in 50 countries and partners with more than 100 suppliers to offer everything from medical balloons and catheters to batteries and electrodes, according to the company’s website .
For these efforts, Karmelek, who now focuses on product development engineering at Chamfr, has been named a Women Who Empower Innovator Award Fellow.
The honor, according to Northeastern University’s Women Who Empower Initiative, recognizes women “who have demonstrated extraordinary vision, impact and leadership.” And as part of the fellowship, Karmelek will participate in a nine-month program that will give her access to mentorship opportunities and workshops.
Karmelek described the recognition as a full circle moment. She credited Northeastern for leading her down this career path. Karmelek received her bachelor’s in mechanical engineering from Northeastern in 2006 and went on to obtain her master’s in the same subject in 2008.
It was actually her first co-op at Aspect Medical Systems, a brain monitoring device company, where she really fell in love with medical devices, she said.
The company, which in 2009 was acquired by a larger medical firm called Covidien, created a sensor device that measured the electronic activity of a patient’s brain to determine the right amount of anesthesia they should be administered during surgery.  At that co-op, Karmelek worked directly with the product development team to help improve the instrument’s capabilities.
“I’ve even seen the device on either ‘ER’ or ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ once while I was watching TV, and I was like, ‘Oh, I worked on that product,’” she said.
Subsequent co-ops at NMT Medical, a now defunct medical device supplier focused on the cardiovascular system and Boston Scientific, a biotechnology company based in Marlborough Massachusetts, were also critical for her development, she said.
During those co-ops, she got hands-on time with medical devices designed to fill holes in people’s hearts and helped create a loop system that allowed doctors to reposition and remove stents, tiny tubs placed inside blocked or narrow passages in the body, after they are already surgically placed.
The practical know-how Karmelek gained during these co-ops helped shape her career, giving her critical insights into how to develop and prototype a device and eventually take it to market, she said.
“These experiences helped me discover my passion for developing medical devices that improve patients’ lives,” she said.
One of Karmelek’ greatest skills as an engineering executive at Chamfr is her ability to connect and communicate with both people who are technically inclined and those who are not, said Steve Maxon, vice president of growth at Chamfr.
“There’s a lot of really good engineers out there, but she has a unique combination of having really strong technical skills and excellent communication and collaboration skills,” he said.
It’s those combination of skills that make her the perfect person to serve as a public representative for the company during shows and events, he added.
Maxon highlighted the fact that in June, Karmelek moderated a discussion held during one of the company’s medical processing conferences in Quincy, Massachusetts,  focused on catheter development and manufacturing  And during a conference last year held at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, she served as the official master of ceremonies.
“That’s how versatile she is,” Maxon said. “She can be in front of a highly technical group and talk about technology, but on the other hand, she can run a show and keep things in order.”
Karmelek plays a similar role as a board member of Northeastern University’s Galante Engineering Business Program, a graduate certificate program designed for students who have obtained their bachelor’s in engineering and are interested in sharpening their business and leadership management skills.
As a board member, Karmelek regularly comes back to campus to share her story and offer advice to students and graduates, who have careers in the health care industry or related engineering fields.
In December, Karmelek will host an event at the Egan Research Center, a multidisciplinary facility on the Boston campus, where she will speak about her career path, explained Hailey Bloch, a coordinator for the program.
“Within the Galente program, we have a lot of students who are getting their masters in bioengineering and mechanical engineering, and they are very interested in medical devices,” Bloch said. “That pairs nicely with Katie’s business and experience.”
Karmelek said having the opportunity to engage with fellow Huskies and offer advice has been extremely rewarding. It’s a way for her to give back to a community that has done so much for her, she explained.
She also just loves talking about the work she does and its positive – sometimes life-changing —  impact.
“Even though I’m not the doctor or the nurse at the bedside, I’m still a part of the process, ultimately helping that person feel better and sometimes saving their life,” she said.

articles.title_orig: More Republicans come out against Trump's diesel deal with Putin
articles.title_zh: More Republicans come out against Trump's diesel deal with Putin
articles.content_orig:
More Republicans are speaking out against President Donald Trump 's decision to let Vladimir Putin 's Russia temporarily export diesel fuel on the global market, expanding the bipartisan blowback over the deal.
Six GOP senators joined six of their Democratic colleagues in a letter Tuesday urging Trump to cancel the arrangement allowing Russia to supply 4.8 million metric tons, or nearly 36 million barrels, of diesel through mid-April.
"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," the lawmakers wrote.
Republican Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, Oklahoma's Alan Armstrong, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Kentucky's Mitch McConnell and John Cornyn of Texas signed on, adding to the list of of GOP Congress members who had earlier questioned the deal Trump announced Friday. Armstrong has roots in the energy industry, having been CEO of Williams Companies , the largest natural gas-focused company in the U.S.
They joined Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, New Hampshire's Jeanne Shaheen , Richard Durbin of Illinois, Delaware's Chris Coons and Rhode Island's Sheldon Whitehouse and Jack Reed .
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the letter.
Collins, Murkowski and Tillis had already spoken out, joining a statement with Democrats on Sunday that urged Trump not to "provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians."
Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah had also joined that statement.
Trump announced the Russia diesel deal after a call with Putin. The announcement quickly drew an unusually critical response from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who counts on continued U.S. support for his military. Trump, in turn, slammed Zelenskyy, saying Ukraine should get a new president .
Trump claimed in Friday's announcement that the deal will help quickly and sharply bring record-high diesel prices down. But oil analysts don't think the Russian supply will be nearly enough to make a meaningful impact on prices.
The 12 senators who signed Tuesday's letter to Trump agreed, writing that the deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans."
"Allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans," the senators told Trump.
"It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea," they wrote.
The senators also alleged, as other critics already have, that the diesel deal contradicts the bipartisan Russian sanctions law that Trump signed into law a few weeks before announcing the deal, which required lifting existing sanctions on Russia.
"These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," their letter read.
"Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," they wrote.
"Maintain our legacy – and the duty America holds – as leader of the free world."
Trump has doubled down on his decision . "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" he wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Wall Street Revenues Power Profit at Goldman and JPMorgan
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Wall Street Revenues Power Profit at Goldman and JPMorgan
articles.content_orig:
Four of the largest U.S. banks reported third-quarter results on Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase , Wells Fargo , Goldman Sachs and Citigroup .
Bank of America and Morgan Stanley will post earnings on Wednesday.
The quarter was dominated by headlines around artificial intelligence, IPO uncertainty, high fuel prices and rising borrowing costs.
The banks that reported Tuesday put up mixed results . JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets and the largest in the world by market capitalization, posted a rare miss. Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, blew past estimates for revenue and earnings per share, led by strong equities trading.
Analyst calls for all four banks touched on the opportunities and risks associated with AI, citing robust financing demand and operational advantages, but also the threat of rogue agents.
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon also addressed recent reports of a CEO transition plan, and Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo joined CNBC to discuss the firm's growth and the state of the consumer.
Here's what you need to know:
Citi's analyst call is over, which means bank earnings reports for Tuesday are wrapped. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley report on Wednesday to round out third-quarter results for the major U.S. firms.
Wells Fargo's Santomassimo told CNBC that both consumers and businesses are doing "really well."
"I think despite higher gas prices, both sides of the equation have been able to really work through that," he said. "We're just not seeing any sort of cracks around delinquency trends that would lead you to believe you're going to see any near-term stress that come through, at least at least for now."
Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the company's underlying results are "really good" and that the bank is seeing "continued momentum" across all of its businesses.
"As you look at the net interest margin, what that really shows is sort of this good stabilization of the underlying trends," he said. "You see the higher rate environment starting to come through in terms of helping it as you look forward, and so for us, the opportunity we have ahead of us is just as big as it was last quarter."
Citi's Fraser said on the call with analysts that macro environment conditions softened during the third quarter and that the "global economy has held up remarkably well."
"In the U.S., while much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much of the growth," she said. "The labor market is stable, and companies remain active. Our near-term economic outlook remains positive."
She added that the bank's clients have remained "engaged" and "healthy."
Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser said on a call with analysts on Tuesday that the company is focused on reducing systemic risk while deploying AI firm-wide.
"Our cyberdefense strategy is about being on the front foot, about moving fast and retaining trust," Fraser said. "We don't wait for risks to happen. We're constantly preparing and improving our defenses. We're in the business of managing risk everyday, and this is no different."
Investment banking fees at all four firms reporting on Tuesday largely held up during the third quarter, with most firms either matching or surpassing prior guidance. Still, the reports revealed declines on a quarter-over-quarter basis.
At JPMorgan, investment banking revenue was up 14% year over year but down 8% quarter over quarter. JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said the pipeline remains "very, very strong."
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon echoed that sentiment on his company's analyst call, while declining to say whether capital markets activity has peaked. That bank reported fees that were 21% higher from the prior year, but 5% lower than the second quarter.
"IPOs that came in September were really the result of conversations in May and June around valuation expectations. Things got a little bit softer in September," Solomon said. "The IPO market was wide open. It's just if you expected a valuation and you got something 10 %to 15% less, you might choose not to go forward, you might choose to wait."
Solomon added all the tech innovation and the AI infrastructure activity is a "real good ballast" for capital markets activity on a go-forward basis, noting that doesn't mean there won't be bumps.
Citi posted the largest quarter-over-quarter decline in the fees, at 13% down. Wells Fargo reported investment banking revenue that was down 5% from the prior quarter.
Solomon warned that the AI infrastructure boom could face a painful reset if higher borrowing costs or overbuilding undermine the economics of some data center projects.
"There is going to be a lot of financing to do, and we're going to be in the middle of that," Solomon said during the bank's third-quarter call.
"It may be that over time as the financing needs grow, that there's pressure on rates and that will affect the returns and the viability of certain projects," he said. "Not every project is going to be received as well."
For now, demand for computing power remains strong and supply has yet to catch up, Solomon said, meaning more infrastructure will be built and more financing from Goldman and others will be needed. It's impossible to predict when a reset might happen or how the technology would evolve and be deployed, he said, calling the dynamic "an unknown we have to live with."
"There will be a point in time when this recalibration resets, for sure," Solomon said. "When that does happen, of course there'll be some bumps."
Citigroup, the final bank of the morning, is beginning its conference call with executives and analysts to discuss its third-quarter earnings results.
Goldman Sachs CEO Solomon pushed back against reports of an impending transition to executive chairman, saying Tuesday that no succession process or timeline is underway at the investment bank.
Last month, news outlets cited anonymous sources that said Solomon would be replaced as CEO by Goldman President John Waldron as early as next year. The process would involve a vote by the bank's board that could happen in a matter of months, according to The Wall Street Journal.
"I just want to be clear, there is no succession transition or timeline underway at Goldman Sachs," Solomon said during the bank's earnings call.
"The board and I are singularly focused on our strategy to grow the firm and continue to serve our clients," he said.
The CEO also pointed to the firm's future growth prospects, saying his leadership team was focused on expanding the franchise and accelerating its earnings growth in the coming years.
"I have to say, at the point right now where we see the benefits of the effort that the broad team has made, I'm really enjoying the job," Solomon said.
Wells Fargo's Scharf said on the call with analysts that the AI investment cycle has become "a complicated macroeconomic force in its own right."
"Demand for semiconductors, networking equipment, power generation, data center infrastructure, cooling systems, storage, cybersecurity and advanced manufacturing equipment continue to surge," Scharf said.
"The scale of investment here increasingly resembles prior infrastructure booms, creating both significant opportunities but also risks given the significant leverage used to finance the build-out and the upward pressure on prices in selected industries and supply chains," he added.
Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company's customer base is "still strong."
"Our underwriting criteria recognize that at some point consumer credit conditions will weaken," Scharf said. "To be clear, we do not see signs of this yet, but we know that cycles are inevitable."
Wells Fargo's Scharf said on the call with analysts that the company is "devoting significant management time and resources" to building out its AI capabilities.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth wants a livestream execution. Here's how firing squads work
articles.title_zh: Hegseth wants a livestream execution. Here's how firing squads work
articles.content_orig:
The archbishop assigned to serve Catholics in the US military strongly condemned the Pentagon’s plan to livestream a firing squad execution and said Monday that Catholic personnel should not participate.
“As I would in the case of a procured abortion, I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Archbishop Timothy P. Broglio wrote in a statement , marking the latest dispute between the Trump administration and the Catholic Church .
His comments came after he met with Pope Leo on Monday. The pontiff himself strongly condemned the death penalty over the weekend, consistent with the church’s opposition to capital punishment but also coming after the relatively new pope has already clashed with US President Donald Trump over issues of war, immigration and press freedom.
Last week, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced in a podcast interview that the execution of the convicted Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan would be shown in public . A Pentagon official later said the execution “will be livestreamed.”
Army caught off guard by Hegseth’s order to make firing squad execution public
The decision to livestream a public firing squad execution was swiftly met with bipartisan concern and opposition — including from Republican members of Congress — as well as widespread condemnation from world leaders.
He also made clear he felt for the loved ones of those impacted by Hasan’s 2009 mass shooting that killed 13 people, adding that he presided at the funeral for one of the victims of the attack.
“I renew my expression of heartfelt sympathy to the families and friends of those who died in the attack at Fort Hood,” Broglio wrote. “It was an attack that disregarded the dignity of the human person.”
Broglio questioned the purpose of making such an event public, calling on “all men and women of good will” to “do what is possible to keep the exposure to the live-streaming of the proposed execution from the vision of the young and impressionable.”
“Will the exposure of a live-stream to the young and impressionable during the 250th anniversary year of our independence be able to be repaired?” Broglio asked in his statement. “The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world. Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheel chair to the whole world?”

articles.title_orig: Assessing the Impact of China-Russia Economic Coordination in Latin America and the Caribbean - CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies
articles.title_zh: Assessing the Impact of China-Russia Economic Coordination in Latin America and the Caribbean - CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies
articles.source: CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies
articles.content_orig:
Photo: Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV/POOL/ AFP/Getty Images
Report
                     by Henry Ziemer
Published October 13, 2026
Discussion of the so-called “no-limits partnership” between China and Russia has driven significant coverage from the perspective of U.S. national defense strategy in the Eurasian and Indo-Pacific theaters. But as the United states move to shore up its presence in the Western Hemisphere, it is worth considering the extent to which China and Russia may be coordinating their moves in the media, security, and economic domains in the region. For this reason, the CSIS Americas Program has designed a series of novel tabletop exercises (TTXs) to better understand the consequences of China-Russia cooperation across a range of sectors.
The findings from this latest exercise examine the economic and trade space. While China enjoys far greater economic clout in the region, Russia has been adept at leveraging its more limited presence to nevertheless wield substantial influence. Results from the exercise suggest that when China and Russia cooperate, they tend to pursue more coercive trade and economic measures. However, this same coercion tends to backfire in the region, a lesson that may also carry implications for how the United States calculates its own approach.
To address the challenges of rising Chinese and Russian economic coercion in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), the United States must leverage the current spate of U.S.-aligned governments in the region to build new architectures for economic and trade security, focus on creating enabling conditions for private sector investment, and prioritize competition in critical infrastructure, particularly ports, energy, digital communications, and artificial intelligence.
The ongoing U.S.-Iran war has concretized fears over an emergent alliance between China, Russia, and Iran. Chinese satellites have reportedly helped map U.S. basing infrastructure in the Persian Gulf ahead of deadly missile and drone strikes, while the integration of the Russian and Iranian defense industrial bases , previously done to the sole benefit of Moscow, is now aiding Tehran’s efforts to replenish its munitions stockpiles. This cooperation is in many ways opportunistic rather than strategic. Nevertheless, it suggests that rumors of the demise of the so-called “axis of authoritarians”—following the failure of Moscow and Beijing to react to the removal of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro—were exaggerated. It also underscores how unforeseen cooperation between like-minded geopolitical rivals poses a serious risk to U.S. national security.
While these threats appear most acutely within the security domain, this is hardly the only area where China and Russia have sought to strengthen collaboration. In the trade and economic space, efforts by the two countries to control critical supply chains, apply pressure to U.S. allies, and coordinate sanctions evasion for themselves as well as their fellow autocratic hangers-on, all represent important considerations the United States must account for in conceptualizing any emergent China-Russia “no-limits” partnership. For this reason, CSIS conducted a series of TTXs in 2025 and 2026 to better understand various facets of the China-Russia partnership and how coordination across a range of sectors, including economic, may or may not prejudice U.S. interests in the region. Findings from the previous two TTXs suggest that the strength of this cooperation varies significantly depending on the sector. In the economic and trade space, there may be potential for cooperation in some industries, but China and Russia could find themselves at odds in others.
The economic dimension certainly contains the most widespread array of interests for the two powers. It is also where China far outpaces Russia in terms of both the breadth and depth of engagement. For most countries in the region, China is the number one or number two trade partner, as well as one of the largest sources of development finance and foreign direct investment. As a result, China exerts a powerful gravitational pull through its economic presence in the region. Russia, for its part, has carved out a niche in the fuel and fertilizer markets and in some cases has been able to effectively leverage its lighter trade footprint for political advantage. Ecuador, for instance, appeared on the verge of supplying legacy Russian and Soviet weapons to Ukraine (via the United States), when Russian sanctions and enhanced phytosanitary checks on the country’s banana industry forced President Daniel Noboa to walk back the plan. The incident underscored the role of media and information influence when paired with economic pressure, as both RT and Sputnik raced to amplify statements by the Russian foreign ministry that providing arms to Ukraine, however indirectly, would make Ecuador and its people belligerents in the ongoing war. It also serves as a troubling portent of the kinds of influence China could wield should it pursue coercive economic measures against the region.
Furthermore, both China and Russia have pursued convergent investment projects targeting Bolivia’s critical minerals sector. Former Bolivian President Luis Arce signed agreements with Chinese battery maker CATL and Russia’s Uranium One Group to develop the country’s sizeable lithium reserves in conjunction with Bolivia’s state-owned mining company. However, this proposed project drew protests and civil society opposition. Meanwhile, the election of Rodrigo Paz Pereira in 2025 has brought about a reorientation toward the United States with respect to Bolivia’s international cooperation priorities.
Another area ripe for China-Russia cooperation in LAC concerns sanctions evasion. A combination of Russian maintenance and Chinese demand for energy was essential to keeping the Maduro regime afloat in Venezuela following U.S. sectoral sanctions against the oil industry. As Maduro sought to hang on to power following a brazen election theft , the importance of China and Russia as economic lifelines grew, though in the aftermath of Operation Absolute Resolve, Chinese and Russian economic influence seems to have dissipated significantly in Venezuela. However diminished, Chinese and Russian influence in Venezuela has not disappeared entirely, and both countries can play spoiler roles as Caracas looks to renegotiate its massive external public debt. Elsewhere in the Western Hemisphere, the authoritarian Ortega-Murillo regime in Nicaragua continues to strengthen its partnerships with China and Russia, including granting Chinese mining companies control over vast swathes of its territory.
As Maduro sought to hang on to power following a brazen election theft, the importance of China and Russia as economic lifelines grew, though in the aftermath of Operation Absolute Resolve, Chinese and Russian economic influence seems to have dissipated significantly in Venezuela.
Beijing and Moscow have also championed de-dollarization as a means of reducing their exposure to U.S. sanctions architecture. China, in particular, has provided billions of dollars in currency swap lines to Argentina and is pushing for more of its trade with LAC to be denominated in yuan. Not only have China and Russia provided an economic lifeline to authoritarian allies in the Americas, but both have benefited from relatively unfettered trade with LAC countries as the United States and Europe raise new trade barriers. In the wake of U.S. and European sanctions on Russian oil and gas, the Kremlin stepped up its exports of diesel to countries including Brazil, which is now the largest importer in the world and has consistently opposed all sanctions regimes not explicitly authorized by the UN Security Council. Latin America’s natural resource wealth is also increasingly important to sustain Russia’s war economy—and potentially, a future wartime China.
